children.title: Graphical Localizations
children.top_down_role: Local graph restrictions and localized branches of set-valued mappings.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{gph}F_{U,V}=\operatorname{gph}F\cap(U\times V)\).

notation.meaning: graphical localization of F to U and V

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Neighborhood restriction of a set-valued mapping around a reference graph point.

source_refs.locator: 4.1.2 Neighborhood Characterizations of Metric Regularity and Lipschitzian Behavior p. 382
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(V\) of \(\bar y\), the graphical localization of \(F\) is the mapping \(F_{U,V}:U\rightrightarrows V\) defined by \[F_{U,V}(x):=F(x)\cap V\quad(x\in U).\] Equivalently, its graph is \[\operatorname{gph}F_{U,V}=\operatorname{gph}F\cap(U\times V).\] Thus only graph points whose coordinates lie in the prescribed neighborhoods are retained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A graphical localization restricts a set-valued mapping’s graph to chosen neighborhoods of a reference graph point.
knowledge_statements.title: Graphical Localizations

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1.2 Neighborhood Characterizations of Metric Regularity and Lipschitzian Behavior p. 382
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nested neighborhood restrictions around a fixed graph point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(U'\subset U\) and \(V'\subset V\) are neighborhoods of \(\bar x\) and \(\bar y\), respectively, then \[(F_{U,V})_{U',V'}=F_{U',V'},\qquad \operatorname{gph}F_{U',V'}=\operatorname{gph}F_{U,V}\cap(U'\times V').\] Hence any two graphical localizations at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) agree after restriction to the intersections of their neighborhoods.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeated graphical localization is restriction to the smaller product neighborhood, so localizations at one graph point represent the same mapping germ.
assumptions_latex: \(U'\subset U\) and \(V'\subset V\) are neighborhoods of the reference coordinates.
knowledge_statements.title: Nested Localization and Mapping Germ

children.title: Inverse-Mapping Localizations
children.top_down_role: Local inverse images and inverse branches used to express mapping stability.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((F_{U,V})^{-1}(y)=F^{-1}(y)\cap U\) for every \(y\in V\).

notation.meaning: graphical localization of F to U and V

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inverse representation of a graphical localization near \((\bar x,\bar y)\).

source_refs.locator: 4.1.2 Neighborhood Characterizations of Metric Regularity and Lipschitzian Behavior p. 382
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\) and \(V\) be neighborhoods of \(\bar x\) and \(\bar y\), respectively, and let \(F_{U,V}(x)=F(x)\cap V\) for \(x\in U\). The inverse localization is represented by \[(F_{U,V})^{-1}(y)=\{x\in U:y\in F(x)\}=F^{-1}(y)\cap U\quad(y\in V).\] Its graph is the coordinate reversal of the localized graph: \[\operatorname{gph}(F_{U,V})^{-1}=\{(y,x):(x,y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\cap(U\times V)\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inverting a graphical localization restricts each inverse image to the chosen neighborhood of the reference input.
knowledge_statements.title: Inverse-Mapping Localizations

knowledge_statements.title: Implicit-System Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-valued generalized equation used to encode parameter-dependent solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The parameterized implicit system associated with \(G\) is \[0\in G(p,x).\] Its solution mapping \(S:P\rightrightarrows X\) is defined by \[S(p):=\{x\in X:0\in G(p,x)\}.\] Consequently, the feasible parameter-state pairs admit the graph representation \[\operatorname{gph}S=\{(p,x)\in P\times X:(p,x,0)\in\operatorname{gph}G\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An implicit generalized equation induces a solution mapping whose graph consists exactly of parameter-state pairs with zero residual.

notation.meaning: solution mapping induced by the implicit system

children.title: Parameterized Solution Mappings
children.top_down_role: Solution-set mappings induced by varying parameters in localized systems.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S(p)=G_p^{-1}(0)\) for every \(p\in P\).

notation.meaning: partial mapping obtained by fixing p

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Solution multifunction obtained by fixing the parameter in an implicit system.

source_refs.locator: 4.1.2 Neighborhood Characterizations of Metric Regularity and Lipschitzian Behavior p. 382
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each parameter \(p\in P\), define the partial mapping \(G_p:X\rightrightarrows Y\) by \(G_p(x):=G(p,x)\). The parameterized solution mapping of the generalized equation \(0\in G(p,x)\) is \[S:P\rightrightarrows X,\qquad S(p):=\{x\in X:0\in G_p(x)\}=G_p^{-1}(0).\] At a reference solution \((\bar p,\bar x)\), one has \(\bar x\in S(\bar p)\) exactly when \(0\in G(\bar p,\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixing a parameter turns the implicit system into a set-valued mapping, and its zero inverse image is the parameter’s solution set.
knowledge_statements.title: Parameterized Solution Mappings

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1.2 Neighborhood Characterizations of Metric Regularity and Lipschitzian Behavior p. 382
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Parameter and State Fibers of the Solution Relation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fiber and projection identities for the zero relation of an implicit system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(S(p):=\{x:0\in G(p,x)\}\), the inverse fiber at \(x\) is \[S^{-1}(x)=\{p\in P:0\in G(p,x)\}.\] Consequently, \[\operatorname{dom}S=\{p\in P:\exists x\in X\text{ with }0\in G(p,x)\},\qquad \operatorname{rge}S=\{x\in X:\exists p\in P\text{ with }0\in G(p,x)\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixing the parameter gives a state-solution fiber, while fixing the state gives the parameters for which that state solves the system; domain and range are the corresponding projections.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S^{-1}(x)=\{p:0\in G(p,x)\},\quad\operatorname{dom}S=\operatorname{proj}_P\{(p,x):0\in G(p,x)\}.

notation.meaning: Parameters for which \(x\) is a solution

knowledge_statements.title: Parameter and State Fibers of the Solution Relation

children.title: Implicit-to-Solution Map Passage
children.top_down_role: The correspondence between localized implicit systems and their solution-mapping representations.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{gph}S=\Phi^{-1}(\operatorname{gph}G)\), where \(\Phi(p,x)=(p,x,0)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact graph passage from a generalized equation to its solution multifunction.

source_refs.locator: 4.1.2 Neighborhood Characterizations of Metric Regularity and Lipschitzian Behavior p. 382
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the zero-section embedding \(\Phi:P\times X\to P\times X\times Y\) by \(\Phi(p,x):=(p,x,0)\). Passage from the implicit system \(0\in G(p,x)\) to its solution mapping is the exact graph identity \[\operatorname{gph}S=\Phi^{-1}(\operatorname{gph}G)=\{(p,x):(p,x,0)\in\operatorname{gph}G\}.\] Hence any local property of solutions near \((\bar p,\bar x)\) concerns the intersection of \(\operatorname{gph}G\) with the zero section near \((\bar p,\bar x,0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The solution graph is the inverse image of the implicit mapping’s graph under the zero-section embedding.
knowledge_statements.title: Implicit-to-Solution Map Passage

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1.2 Neighborhood Characterizations of Metric Regularity and Lipschitzian Behavior p. 382
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closedness Transfer through the Zero Section
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-way transfer of graph closedness from an implicit residual to its solution map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Phi(p,x)=(p,x,0)\). Since \(\Phi\) is continuous and \(\operatorname{gph}S=\Phi^{-1}(\operatorname{gph}G)\), closedness of \(\operatorname{gph}G\) implies closedness of \(\operatorname{gph}S\). Locally, if \(\operatorname{gph}G\) is locally closed at \((\bar p,\bar x,0)\), then \(\operatorname{gph}S\) is locally closed at \((\bar p,\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The zero-section pullback transfers global or local graph closedness from the residual mapping to its solution mapping.
assumptions_latex: For the local conclusion, \(\operatorname{gph}G\) is locally closed at \((\bar p,\bar x,0)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{gph}G\text{ locally closed at }(\bar p,\bar x,0)\Longrightarrow\operatorname{gph}S\text{ locally closed at }(\bar p,\bar x).
knowledge_statements.title: Closedness Transfer through the Zero Section

children.title: Local Branch Representation
children.top_down_role: Single-valued or set-valued local branches selected from parameterized solution sets.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{gph}s=\operatorname{gph}S\cap(U\times V)\) for a single-valued local branch \(s:U\to V\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-valued graphical localization of a solution multifunction.

source_refs.locator: 4.1.2 Neighborhood Characterizations of Metric Regularity and Lipschitzian Behavior p. 382
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A local branch of \(S\) through \((\bar p,\bar x)\) is a single-valued mapping \(s:U\to V\), for neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar p\) and \(V\) of \(\bar x\), such that \(s(\bar p)=\bar x\) and \[S(p)\cap V=\{s(p)\}\quad(p\in U).\] Equivalently, \[\operatorname{gph}s=\operatorname{gph}S\cap(U\times V).\] Thus the localized solution multifunction has exactly one value at every parameter in \(U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local branch is a single-valued graphical localization of a solution mapping around a reference solution.
knowledge_statements.title: Local Branch Representation

children.title: Distance-to-Inverse Regularity
children.top_down_role: The residual and inverse-image distance viewpoint on metric regularity.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d(x,F^{-1}(y))\leq\kappa d(y,F(x))\) locally around \((\bar x,\bar y)\).

notation.meaning: distance from a point to a set, with distance to the empty set equal to infinity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard neighborhood definition of metric regularity via residual and inverse-image distances.

source_refs.locator: 1.2.3 Metric Regularity and Covering p. 56
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The mapping \(F\) is metrically regular around \((\bar x,\bar y)\) with constant \(\kappa\geq0\) if there exist neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(V\) of \(\bar y\) such that \[d(x,F^{-1}(y))\leq\kappa\,d(y,F(x))\quad\text{for all }(x,y)\in U\times V.\] Here \(d(z,\varnothing):=+\infty\). The least admissible constant is the exact regularity modulus \(\operatorname{reg}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Metric regularity bounds distance to an exact inverse image by a constant times the residual distance to the mapping value.
knowledge_statements.title: Distance-to-Inverse Regularity

children.title: Covering Behavior
children.top_down_role: Image-ball coverage properties used to express local surjectivity.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B_Y(y,cr)\subset F(B_X(x,r))\) in a localized regime.

notation.meaning: open ball of radius r in the indicated space

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local ball-covering predicate at graph points near the reference pair.

source_refs.locator: 1.2.3 Metric Regularity and Covering p. 56
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The mapping \(F\) has local covering behavior with rate \(c>0\) around \((\bar x,\bar y)\) if there are neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\), \(V\) of \(\bar y\), and \(\varepsilon>0\) such that, whenever \((x,y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\cap(U\times V)\) and \(0<r<\varepsilon\) with \(B_X(x,r)\subset U\), one has \[B_Y(y,cr)\cap V\subset F(B_X(x,r)).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nearby graph points cover output balls whose radius is a fixed positive multiple of the input-ball radius.
knowledge_statements.title: Covering Behavior

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2.3 Metric Regularity and Covering p. 56

children.title: Linear Openness
children.top_down_role: Open behavior measured through a linear relation between source and image neighborhoods.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B_Y(y,cr)\cap V\subset F(B_X(x,r))\) locally for some \(c>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear openness around a graph point, uniform over nearby graph points.

source_refs.locator: 1.2.3 Metric Regularity and Covering p. 56
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The mapping \(F\) is open at a linear rate around \((\bar x,\bar y)\) if there exist \(c>0\), neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(V\) of \(\bar y\), and \(\varepsilon>0\) such that \[B_Y(y,cr)\cap V\subset F(B_X(x,r))\] for every \((x,y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\cap(U\times V)\) and every \(r\in(0,\varepsilon)\) satisfying \(B_X(x,r)\subset U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linear openness means that nearby input balls map onto localized output balls with proportionally scaled radii.
knowledge_statements.title: Linear Openness

children.title: Covering–Openness Correspondence
children.top_down_role: The quantitative passage between covering descriptions and linear openness descriptions.

knowledge_statements.title: Covering–Openness Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard local equivalence for a set-valued mapping with locally closed graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The following are equivalent around \((\bar x,\bar y)\): \(F\) is metrically regular with some constant \(\kappa>0\), and \(F\) is open at a linear rate with some \(c>0\). Quantitatively, every valid regularity constant \(\kappa\) yields every covering rate \(c<1/\kappa\), and every valid covering rate \(c\) yields every regularity constant \(\kappa>1/c\). Consequently, \[\operatorname{sur}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)=\frac{1}{\operatorname{reg}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)},\] with the standard conventions for \(0\) and \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Metric regularity and linear openness are equivalent local properties, and their exact constants are reciprocal.
assumptions_latex: \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\), \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\), and \(\operatorname{gph}F\) is locally closed near \((\bar x,\bar y)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{sur}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)=1/\operatorname{reg}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)\).

children.title: Localized Covering Regimes
children.top_down_role: Pointwise and neighborhood settings in which covering behavior is imposed.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The covering inclusion is required only on a prescribed local graph restriction and within prescribed neighborhoods.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covering property formulated for a fixed graphical localization.

source_refs.locator: 4.1.2 Neighborhood Characterizations of Metric Regularity and Lipschitzian Behavior p. 382
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(V\) of \(\bar y\), and let \(F_{U,V}(x)=F(x)\cap V\) for \(x\in U\). A localized covering regime with rate \(c>0\) holds if some \(\varepsilon>0\) satisfies \[B_Y(y,cr)\cap V\subset F_{U,V}(B_X(x,r)\cap U)\] whenever \((x,y)\in\operatorname{gph}F_{U,V}\) and \(0<r<\varepsilon\). The neighborhoods and radius threshold are part of the regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A localized covering regime imposes the ball-covering inclusion only on a fixed graph restriction and for sufficiently small radii.
knowledge_statements.title: Localized Covering Regimes

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1.2 Neighborhood Characterizations of Metric Regularity and Lipschitzian Behavior p. 382
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covering imposed only at the reference graph point rather than uniformly at nearby graph points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The mapping \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) covers at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) with rate \(c>0\) if some \(\varepsilon>0\) satisfies \[B_Y(\bar y,cr)\subset F(B_X(\bar x,r))\qquad(0<r<\varepsilon).\] The centers remain fixed at \((\bar x,\bar y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pointwise covering requires proportional ball coverage only at the reference graph point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B_Y(\bar y,cr)\subset F(B_X(\bar x,r))\) for all sufficiently small \(r>0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Pointwise Linear Covering Regime

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pointwise Covering Need Not Be Neighborhood-Uniform
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict boundary between fixed-reference coverage and uniform coverage around a graph point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \[f(0)=0,\qquad f(x)=x+x^3\sin(1/x^2)\quad(x\ne0),\] the mapping \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) has a positive pointwise linear covering rate at \((0,0)\), but no positive rate works uniformly at all graph points near \((0,0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pointwise linear covering can hold at the reference point while every neighborhood-uniform covering rate fails.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) covers linearly at \((0,0)\) pointwise but is not open at any positive linear rate around \((0,0)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Pointwise Covering Need Not Be Neighborhood-Uniform

children.title: Aubin Property of the Inverse
children.top_down_role: The inverse-map Lipschitzian counterpart of metric regularity.

knowledge_statements.title: Aubin Property of the Inverse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inverse-map equivalence using the localized Aubin distance inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The inverse \(F^{-1}:Y\rightrightarrows X\) has the Aubin property around \((\bar y,\bar x)\) with constant \(\kappa\geq0\) if neighborhoods \(V\) of \(\bar y\) and \(U\) of \(\bar x\) satisfy \[d\bigl(x,F^{-1}(y_2)\bigr)\leq\kappa d(y_1,y_2)\quad\text{for all }y_1,y_2\in V\text{ and }x\in F^{-1}(y_1)\cap U.\] This property is equivalent to metric regularity of \(F\) around \((\bar x,\bar y)\), and the exact moduli satisfy \[\operatorname{lip}F^{-1}(\bar y\mid\bar x)=\operatorname{reg}F(\bar x\mid\bar y).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Metric regularity of a mapping is exactly the localized Lipschitz-like, or Aubin, property of its inverse, with the same modulus.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is metrically regular around \((\bar x,\bar y)\) exactly when \(F^{-1}\) has the Aubin property around \((\bar y,\bar x)\), and \(\operatorname{lip}F^{-1}(\bar y\mid\bar x)=\operatorname{reg}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)\).

notation.meaning: distance from a point to a set, with distance to the empty set equal to infinity
exact Aubin modulus of the inverse mapping

children.title: Exact Regularity Modulus
children.top_down_role: Sharp conditioning values attached to distance-to-inverse regularity.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{reg}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)\) is the infimum of the admissible regularity constants.

notation.meaning: distance from a point to a set, with distance to the empty set equal to positive infinity
inverse image of a point under the set-valued mapping

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local exact modulus for metric regularity at a graph point.

source_refs.locator: 1.2.3 Metric Regularity and Covering p. 56
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The exact regularity modulus of \(F\) at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) is
\[
\operatorname{reg}F(\bar x\mid\bar y):=\inf\bigl\{\kappa\geq0:\ \exists\text{ neighborhoods }U\text{ of }\bar x,
V\text{ of }\bar y\text{ such that }d(x,F^{-1}(y))\leq\kappa d(y,F(x))
\text{ for all }(x,y)\in U\times V\bigr\}.
\]
The infimum of the empty set is understood as \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exact regularity modulus is the infimum of all constants in the local residual-to-solution distance estimate.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Regularity Modulus

source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

children.title: Exact Openness Modulus
children.top_down_role: Sharp rates attached to linear openness or covering behavior.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{lop}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)\) is the supremum of the admissible linear covering rates.

notation.meaning: open ball of radius r centered at z

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact linear-openness modulus, using uniform covering near the graph point.

source_refs.locator: 1.2.3 Metric Regularity and Covering p. 56
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The exact openness modulus of \(F\) at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) is
\[
\operatorname{lop}F(\bar x\mid\bar y):=\sup\bigl\{c\geq0:\ \exists\text{ neighborhoods }U\text{ of }\bar x,
V\text{ of }\bar y,\ \exists\varepsilon>0,
\ B(y,ct)\subset F(B(x,t))
\text{ whenever }(x,y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\cap(U\times V),\ 0<t<\varepsilon\bigr\}.
\]
The supremum of the empty set is \(0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exact openness modulus is the supremum of local rates at which images of balls cover corresponding balls.

children.top_down_role: Sharp inverse-mapping Lipschitz rates associated with the Aubin property.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The exact Lipschitz modulus of the inverse at \((\bar y,\bar x)\) is
\[
\operatorname{lip}F^{-1}(\bar y\mid\bar x):=\inf\bigl\{\kappa\geq0:\ \exists\text{ neighborhoods }V\text{ of }\bar y,
U\text{ of }\bar x\text{ such that }
e(F^{-1}(y_1)\cap U,F^{-1}(y_2))\leq\kappa d(y_1,y_2)
\text{ for all }y_1,y_2\in V\bigr\}.
\]
An empty admissible set gives value \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This modulus is the infimum of constants governing the local Lipschitz-like variation of the inverse map.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Lipschitz Modulus

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Metric regularity of \(F\) at \((\bar x,\bar y)\), linear openness of \(F\) there, and the Aubin property of \(F^{-1}\) at \((\bar y,\bar x)\) are equivalent. Their exact moduli satisfy
\[
\operatorname{reg}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)
=\operatorname{lip}F^{-1}(\bar y\mid\bar x)
=\frac{1}{\operatorname{lop}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)}.
\]
The identity is interpreted in the extended nonnegative reals with \(1/0=+\infty\) and \(1/(+\infty)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exact regularity modulus equals the inverse map’s exact Lipschitz modulus and is the reciprocal of the exact openness rate.
knowledge_statements.title: Reciprocal Modulus Correspondence

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the exact-modulus correspondence, failure of every finite metric-regularity estimate is equivalent to zero exact openness and an infinite inverse Lipschitz modulus:
\[
\operatorname{reg}F=+\infty\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\operatorname{lop}F=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\operatorname{lip}F^{-1}=+\infty.
\]
At the opposite boundary,
\[
\operatorname{reg}F=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\operatorname{lop}F=+\infty\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\operatorname{lip}F^{-1}=0.
\]
All moduli are evaluated at the corresponding graph points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zero and infinite exact moduli occur in reciprocal triples, covering complete failure and the opposite zero-constant boundary regime.
knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Modulus Regimes

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(\mathbb R\), the full-valued mapping \(F(x)=\mathbb R\) has exact triple \[(\operatorname{reg}F,\operatorname{lop}F,\operatorname{lip}F^{-1})=(0,+\infty,0)\] at every graph point. For the constant singleton mapping \(G(x)=\{0\}\), the exact triple at every \((\bar x,0)\) is \[(\operatorname{reg}G,\operatorname{lop}G,\operatorname{lip}G^{-1})=(+\infty,0,+\infty).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Full-valued and constant-singleton real multifunctions realize the two reciprocal zero-infinity regimes.
assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb R\rightrightarrows\mathbb R\) is defined by \(F(x)=\mathbb R\).

children.top_down_role: Fixed-target mapping regularity underlying local error bounds.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The infimum of the admissible constants \(\kappa\) is the exact subregularity modulus \(\operatorname{subreg}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The mapping \(F\) is metrically subregular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) if there exist a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and a constant \(\kappa\geq0\) such that
\[
d(x,F^{-1}(\bar y))\leq\kappa d(\bar y,F(x))
\qquad\text{for every }x\in U.
\]
Unlike metric regularity, the target is fixed at \(\bar y\). The exact subregularity modulus is the infimum of all admissible constants \(\kappa\), with value \(+\infty\) if none exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Metric subregularity bounds local distance to the fixed-target solution set by the residual at that same target.
knowledge_statements.title: Metric Subregularity

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1.2 Neighborhood Characterizations of Metric Regularity and Lipschitzian Behavior p. 382
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact scalar growth-rate representation of fixed-target metric subregularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S:=F^{-1}(\bar y)\) and define
\[
\operatorname{Er}F(\bar x\mid\bar y):=\liminf_{\substack{x\to\bar x\\x\notin S}}\frac{\operatorname{dist}(\bar y,F(x))}{d_X(x,S)}.
\]
Then \(F\) is metrically subregular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) if and only if \(\operatorname{Er}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)>0\), and
\[
\operatorname{subreg}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)=\frac{1}{\operatorname{Er}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)},
\]
where \(1/(+\infty)=0\) and \(1/0=+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Metric subregularity is equivalent to positive lower growth of the fixed-target residual relative to solution-set distance, with reciprocal exact modulus.
assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are metric spaces, \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\), and \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is metrically subregular at }(\bar x,\bar y)\iff \operatorname{Er}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)>0.

notation.meaning: Lower residual-growth rate relative to solution-set distance.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Residual-Growth Characterization

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The inverse \(S=F^{-1}\) is calm at \((\bar y,\bar x)\) if there exist neighborhoods \(V\) of \(\bar y\) and \(U\) of \(\bar x\), and \(\kappa\geq0\), such that
\[
e(S(y)\cap U,S(\bar y))\leq\kappa d(y,\bar y)
\qquad\text{for every }y\in V.
\]
This property is equivalent to metric subregularity of \(F\) at \((\bar x,\bar y)\), and the infima of their admissible constants coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Metric subregularity of a mapping is equivalent, with the same exact constant, to calmness of its inverse.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniform Fixed-Target Subregularity of Parameter Slices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Common-neighborhood, common-modulus fixed-target error bound for nearby parameter slices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S(p):=\{x:\bar y\in F(p,x)\}\). The slices \(F_p(x):=F(p,x)\) are uniformly metrically subregular near \((\bar p,\bar x,\bar y)\) if there exist neighborhoods \(W\) of \(\bar p\) and \(U\) of \(\bar x\), and \(\kappa<\infty\), such that \(S(p)\ne\varnothing\) and
\[d(x,S(p))\le\kappa d(\bar y,F(p,x))\qquad\text{for all }(p,x)\in W\times U.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One state neighborhood and one residual-bound constant work for every nearby fixed-parameter slice.
assumptions_latex: \(P,X,Y\) are metric spaces and \(\bar y\in F(\bar p,\bar x)\).
Nearby fixed-target solution sets are nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The slice family has common local subregularity data over the parameter neighborhood.

notation.meaning: fixed-target solution set of the p-slice

knowledge_statements.title: Uniform Fixed-Target Subregularity of Parameter Slices

assumptions_latex: \(P,X,Y\) are metric spaces and \(F:P\times X\rightrightarrows Y\).
\(\bar y\in F(\bar p,\bar x)\), and \(S(p):=\{x:\bar y\in F(p,x)\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: One constant and fixed neighborhoods control the subregularity estimates for all nearby parameters.

notation.meaning: fixed-target solution set for parameter p

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform fixed-target subregularity of parameterized slices near a reference parameter and point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The family \(F_p\) is uniformly metrically subregular near \((\bar p,\bar x,\bar y)\) if there exist neighborhoods \(W\) of \(\bar p\) and \(U\) of \(\bar x\), and a constant \(\kappa\geq0\), such that
\[
d(x,S(p))\leq\kappa d(\bar y,F(p,x))
\qquad\text{for every }(p,x)\in W\times U.
\]
The same \(W\), \(U\), and \(\kappa\) must work simultaneously for all parameters \(p\in W\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform subregularity uses one residual-bound constant and common neighborhoods for every nearby parameter slice.
knowledge_statements.title: Uniform Subregularity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formula is a coherent uniform fixed-target error-bound condition, but no source is supplied to establish that this exact quantifier pattern and terminology are the intended notion of uniform subregularity in the immutable container.

children.title: Parametric Subregularity
children.top_down_role: Subregularity behavior for mappings whose systems vary with an external parameter.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Slice Moduli Need Not Be Uniform
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between selection-relative parametric subregularity and uniform subregularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(p,x)=\{px\}\) on \(\mathbb R^2\), fix \(\bar y=0\), and choose \(x_p=0\). Every slice is metrically subregular at \((0,0)\): for \(p\ne0\) its exact modulus is \(1/|p|\), while for \(p=0\) its solution set is all of \(\mathbb R\) and its exact modulus is \(0\). Hence the family is selection-relative parametrically subregular, but no finite modulus works uniformly for all \(p\) near \(0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every slice can be subregular even though its exact moduli diverge near the reference parameter.
assumptions_latex: All spaces are \(\mathbb R\) with the usual metric.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Slice-wise parametric subregularity does not imply uniform subregularity.
knowledge_statements.title: Slice Moduli Need Not Be Uniform

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Slice-wise subregularity along a designated local solution selection, without uniform constants or neighborhoods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S(p):=\{x:\bar y\in F(p,x)\}\). The family is parametrically metrically subregular along a designated local selection \(p\mapsto x_p\) if there are neighborhoods \(W\) of \(\bar p\) and \(U\) of \(\bar x\) such that \(x_{\bar p}=\bar x\), \(x_p\in S(p)\cap U\), and, for every \(p\in W\), there exist a neighborhood \(U_p\) of \(x_p\) and \(\kappa_p<\infty\) satisfying
\[d(x,S(p))\le\kappa_p d(\bar y,F(p,x))\qquad(x\in U_p).\]
No common \(U_p\) or \(\kappa_p\) is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each nearby parameter slice is subregular at a designated nearby solution, but its localization and modulus may depend on the parameter.
assumptions_latex: \(P,X,Y\) are metric spaces and \(\bar y\in F(\bar p,\bar x)\).
A designated solution selection remains in a fixed neighborhood of \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every selected nearby slice graph point has an ordinary fixed-target metric-subregularity estimate.

notation.meaning: designated nearby solution of the p-slice

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inverse-map representation along the same designated solution selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every fixed \(p\), metric subregularity of \(F_p\) at \((x_p,\bar y)\) is equivalent to calmness of \(F_p^{-1}\) at \((\bar y,x_p)\), with the same exact modulus. Consequently, selection-relative parametric subregularity is equivalently a parameter-indexed family of calm inverse slices, without a uniform calmness modulus requirement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parametric slice-wise subregularity is the same as calmness of each inverse slice along the selected solutions.
assumptions_latex: The ordinary metric-subregularity/calmness equivalence is applied separately to each parameter slice.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{subreg}F_p(x_p\mid\bar y)=\operatorname{clm}F_p^{-1}(\bar y\mid x_p)\) for each nearby p.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parameterwise subregularity without a uniform modulus requirement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The family is parametrically metrically subregular near \(\bar p\) at the fixed target \(\bar y\) if, for every parameter \(p\) in some neighborhood \(W\) of \(\bar p\), there exist a neighborhood \(U_p\) of a designated point \(x_p\in S(p)\) and a constant \(\kappa_p\geq0\) satisfying
\[
d(x,S(p))\leq\kappa_p d(\bar y,F(p,x))
\qquad\text{for every }x\in U_p.
\]
Neither \(U_p\) nor \(\kappa_p\) is required to be independent of \(p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parametric subregularity requires subregularity of nearby parameter slices but permits slice-dependent constants and neighborhoods.
knowledge_statements.title: Parametric Subregularity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports this terminology or quantifier structure. In addition, the designated points \(x_p\) are not constrained to remain near \(\bar x\), so the stated property does not yet give a reliable local parametric notion at the reference pair.

children.title: Base-Point Uniformity
children.top_down_role: Uniform control as reference points vary within a designated set.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-target error bound uniform over nearby parameters and nearby solution base points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S(p):=\{x:\bar y\in F(p,x)\}\). Base-point uniformity at \((\bar p,\bar x,\bar y)\) means that there exist neighborhoods \(W\) of \(\bar p\) and \(U\) of \(\bar x\), numbers \(r>0\) and \(\kappa\ge0\), such that \(S(p)\cap U\ne\varnothing\) for every \(p\in W\) and
\[d(x,S(p))\le\kappa d(\bar y,F(p,x))\]
for every \(p\in W\), \(\hat x\in S(p)\cap U\), and \(x\in B_X(\hat x,r)\cap U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One radius and one error-bound constant work around every nearby solution base point, with nearby solutions required to persist.
assumptions_latex: \(P,X,Y\) are metric spaces and \(F:P\times X\rightrightarrows Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The fixed-target slice error bound has common localization data as both the parameter and solution base point vary.

notation.meaning: fixed-target solution set for parameter p
radius-r ball about the selected solution base point

knowledge_statements.title: Base-Point-Uniform Slice Error Bound

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantifier boundary for moving-base formulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If the condition is quantified only over \(\hat x\in S(p)\cap U\) without requiring \(S(p)\cap U\ne\varnothing\), then it is vacuous for parameters whose nearby slice has no solution and therefore does not provide a uniform feasibility error bound for those parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A moving-base estimate says nothing for an empty nearby solution slice unless solution persistence is imposed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Nonemptiness of nearby localized solution sets is essential to a nonvacuous base-point-uniform regime.
knowledge_statements.title: Vacuity Without Solution Persistence

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relation to a common-neighborhood uniform slice estimate when solutions persist uniformly near the reference point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A common-neighborhood estimate
\[d(x,S(p))\le\kappa d(\bar y,F(p,x))\qquad(p,x)\in W\times U\]
implies base-point uniformity. Conversely, if the base-point-uniform estimate holds and, after shrinking to neighborhoods \(W'\subset W\) and \(U'\subset U\), every \(S(p)\) meets \(U'\) and \(\operatorname{diam}U'<r\), then the common-neighborhood estimate holds on \(W'\times U'\) with the same \(\kappa\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With uniform local solution persistence, moving-base and common-neighborhood formulations agree after shrinking the state neighborhood.
assumptions_latex: The base-point-uniform estimate has radius \(r\) and modulus \(\kappa\).
Every nearby slice has a solution in the shrunken state neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The two local formulations have the same admissible modulus after neighborhood shrinking.
knowledge_statements.title: Local Equivalence After Neighborhood Shrinking

assumptions_latex: \(P,X,Y\) are metric spaces, \(F:P\times X\rightrightarrows Y\), and \(S(p):=\{x:\bar y\in F(p,x)\}\).
\((\bar p,\bar x)\) is a reference solution pair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The same local error-bound data apply around every nearby solution base point.

notation.meaning: fixed-target solution set at parameter p
ball in X centered at x with radius r

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniformity with respect to both parameters and nearby solution base points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Base-point uniformity holds if there exist neighborhoods \(W\) of \(\bar p\) and \(U\) of \(\bar x\), constants \(r>0\) and \(\kappa\geq0\), such that for every \(p\in W\), every \(\hat x\in S(p)\cap U\), and every \(x\in B_X(\hat x,r)\cap U\),
\[
d(x,S(p))\leq\kappa d(\bar y,F(p,x)).
\]
Thus the radius and modulus do not change when the base solution \(\hat x\) varies locally.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Base-point uniformity requires one radius and error-bound constant around every nearby parameterized solution.
knowledge_statements.title: Base-Point Uniformity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition is internally defined, but no evidence establishes it as the intended base-point-uniform variant. Its relation to the preceding uniform estimate is also source-sensitive because the distance remains to the full set \(S(p)\), independently of the selected base point.

children.title: Parameterwise Versus Joint Control
children.top_down_role: The distinction between separate parameterwise estimates and estimates uniform across parameter families.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Joint Control Does Not Imply Slice Control
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure caused by loss of feasibility in fixed-parameter slices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P=X=Y=\mathbb R\), \(F(p,x)=\{p\}\), and \(\bar y=0\). For the joint mapping \(H(p,x)=F(p,x)\),
\[H^{-1}(0)=\{0\}\times\mathbb R,\qquad d((p,x),H^{-1}(0))=|p|=d(0,H(p,x)),\]
so joint metric subregularity holds with exact modulus \(1\). In contrast, \(S(p)=\varnothing\) for every \(p\ne0\), so no neighborhood of \(0\) supports a nonvacuous parameter-uniform slice error bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Joint subregularity can hold by moving the parameter even though nearby fixed-parameter slices have no solutions.
assumptions_latex: The product carries the maximum metric.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Joint metric subregularity does not imply parameterwise or uniform fixed-slice subregularity.

notation.meaning: fixed-target solution set of the p-slice

knowledge_statements.title: Joint Control Does Not Imply Slice Control

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniform Slice Control Implies Joint Subregularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-way comparison under a product metric and fixed target.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H(p,x):=F(p,x)\), \(S(p):=\{x:\bar y\in F(p,x)\}\), and \(Z:=H^{-1}(\bar y)\). If, locally,
\[d_X(x,S(p))\le\kappa d_Y(\bar y,F(p,x))\]
for all nearby \((p,x)\), then under the maximum product metric
\[d_{P\times X}((p,x),Z)\le\kappa d_Y(\bar y,H(p,x)).\]
Thus uniform fixed-parameter slice control implies metric subregularity of the joint mapping at the reference point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A uniform slice error bound implies joint product-space subregularity because a solution can be sought while holding the parameter fixed.
assumptions_latex: Nearby slice solution sets are nonempty.
\(P\times X\) carries the maximum product metric.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H\) is metrically subregular at \(((\bar p,\bar x),\bar y)\) with an admissible modulus \(\kappa\).

notation.meaning: mapping with parameter and state treated as one joint variable

knowledge_statements.title: Uniform Slice Control Implies Joint Subregularity

assumptions_latex: For comparison, joint subregularity treats \((p,x)\) as one variable, while slice-uniform subregularity keeps \(p\) fixed in the solution distance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Joint subregularity does not imply parameter-uniform subregularity of the slices.

notation.meaning: parameterized set-valued mapping in the counterexample

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp distinction between moving in product space and controlling each fixed parameter slice.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F(p,x)=\{p\}\) and fix \(\bar y=0\). As a mapping of the joint variable \((p,x)\), its zero set is \(F^{-1}(0)=\{0\}\times\mathbb R\), and
\[
d((p,x),F^{-1}(0))=|p|=d(0,F(p,x)),
\]
so joint metric subregularity holds with constant \(1\). However, the slice solution set is \(S(p)=\mathbb R\) when \(p=0\) and \(S(p)=\varnothing\) when \(p\neq0\). Hence no neighborhood of \(0\) admits a uniform slice estimate \(d(x,S(p))\leq\kappa d(0,F(p,x))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Joint product-space subregularity can hold although nearby fixed-parameter slices lack solutions and therefore admit no uniform slice estimate.
knowledge_statements.title: Parameterwise Versus Joint Control

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed example is mathematically coherent and does separate joint product-space subregularity from uniform slice control, but the record supplies neither a source nor an explicit standard-field rationale. The evidence contract therefore prevents candidate-review acceptance.

children.top_down_role: Non-Lipschitz residual and inverse-stability regimes.

children.title: Hölder Subregularity
children.top_down_role: Fixed-target residual control governed by a Hölder growth scale.

assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are metric spaces, \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\), and \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The residual raised to \(q\) locally bounds distance to the fixed-target solution set.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-target Hölder subregularity with exponent \(q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The mapping \(F\) is Hölder metrically subregular of order \(q\) at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) if there exist a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and a constant \(\kappa\geq0\) such that
\[
d(x,F^{-1}(\bar y))\leq\kappa\bigl[d(\bar y,F(x))\bigr]^q
\qquad\text{for every }x\in U.
\]
The exact Hölder subregularity modulus of order \(q\) is the infimum of the admissible constants \(\kappa\). For \(q=1\), this reduces to ordinary metric subregularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hölder subregularity bounds solution-set distance by a fixed power of the residual; exponent one recovers metric subregularity.
knowledge_statements.title: Hölder Subregularity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formula is a standard-looking fixed-target Hölder error bound and correctly reduces to metric subregularity at \(q=1\), but no source is supplied. Hölder order conventions vary between residual powers and inverse exponents, so direct evidence is needed before accepting this exact version.

children.title: Hölder Calmness
children.top_down_role: Inverse solution-map stability governed by a Hölder growth scale.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are metric spaces, \(S:Y\rightrightarrows X\), and \((\bar y,\bar x)\in\operatorname{gph}S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\) is Hölder calm of order \(q\) at \((\bar y,\bar x)\).

notation.meaning: Distance from a point to a set, with distance to the empty set equal to positive infinity.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the standard local graph-point definition for a set-valued solution mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The mapping \(S\) is Hölder calm of order \(q\) at \((\bar y,\bar x)\) if there exist neighborhoods \(V\) of \(\bar y\) and \(U\) of \(\bar x\), and a constant \(\kappa\geq 0\), such that
\[
\operatorname{dist}(x,S(\bar y))\leq \kappa d_Y(y,\bar y)^q
\]
for every \(y\in V\) and every \(x\in S(y)\cap U\). The infimum of all admissible constants \(\kappa\) is the Hölder calmness modulus of order \(q\) at \((\bar y,\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nearby solution values cannot depart from the reference solution set faster than a constant times the parameter displacement raised to the Hölder exponent.
knowledge_statements.title: Hölder Calmness

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically precise and fits the leaf, but no source with a specific Hölder-calmness locator is supplied.

children.title: Hölder Exponent Regimes
children.top_down_role: Qualitative regimes distinguished by the exponent used in nonlinear residual control.

assumptions_latex: \(S:Y\rightrightarrows X\) is Hölder calm of order \(q\in(0,1]\) at \((\bar y,\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\) is locally Hölder calm of order \(r\) at \((\bar y,\bar x)\).

notation.meaning: Radius of the localized parameter neighborhood.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies exponents on the usual range \((0,1]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose the calmness inequality of order \(q\) holds with constant \(\kappa\) whenever \(d_Y(y,\bar y)\leq\delta\), where \(0<\delta<\infty\). For every \(r\in(0,q)\),
\[
d_Y(y,\bar y)^q\leq \delta^{q-r}d_Y(y,\bar y)^r.
\]
Consequently, the same localization is Hölder calm of order \(r\) with constant \(\kappa\delta^{q-r}\). Thus larger exponents express stronger local stability; \(q=1\) is the Lipschitz endpoint, while \(0<q<1\) is the proper Hölder regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Hölder estimate with exponent q implies every weaker estimate with a smaller positive exponent; exponent one is precisely the Lipschitz endpoint.
knowledge_statements.title: Hölder Exponent Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exponent-monotonicity statement is correct and the property kind fits, but the record supplies no inspectable source locator.

children.title: Residual–Inverse Hölder Correspondence
children.top_down_role: The relationship between Hölder subregularity and inverse Hölder calmness.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are metric spaces, \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\), and \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Hölder metric subregularity of \(F\) is equivalent to Hölder calmness of \(F^{-1}\), with the same order and modulus.

notation.meaning: Distance residual at the reference output.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the fixed-output form of Hölder metric subregularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The mapping \(F\) is Hölder metrically subregular of order \(q\) at \((\bar x,\bar y)\), meaning that for some neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(\kappa\geq0\),
\[
\operatorname{dist}(x,F^{-1}(\bar y))\leq\kappa\operatorname{dist}(\bar y,F(x))^q\quad(x\in U),
\]
if and only if \(S=F^{-1}\) is Hölder calm of order \(q\) at \((\bar y,\bar x)\). Under corresponding localizations, the admissible constants are identical; hence the exact Hölder subregularity modulus of \(F\) equals the exact Hölder calmness modulus of \(F^{-1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The residual error bound for a mapping is exactly the Hölder calmness estimate for its inverse solution map, with unchanged exponent and modulus.
knowledge_statements.title: Residual–Inverse Hölder Correspondence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The residual–inverse equivalence and equality of exact moduli require an authoritative Hölder-specific source; none is cited.

children.title: Lipschitz Transition Boundary
children.top_down_role: The interface between genuinely Hölder behavior and the Lipschitz-scale regime.

knowledge_statements.title: Lipschitz Transition Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies exponent one as the sharp transition to Lipschitz calmness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(q=1\), Hölder calmness is exactly Lipschitz calmness. For every \(q\in(0,1)\), Lipschitz calmness locally implies Hölder calmness of order \(q\), but the converse fails. In particular, the singleton-valued mapping \(S_q:\mathbb R\rightrightarrows\mathbb R\) defined by \(S_q(y)=\{|y|^q\}\) is Hölder calm of order \(q\) at \((0,0)\) with exact modulus \(1\), but it is not Lipschitz calm there.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exponent one is the Lipschitz boundary: every Lipschitz estimate gives lower-order Hölder estimates, while the mapping taking y to the singleton containing |y|^q shows that a proper Hölder estimate need not be Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_q\) is Hölder calm of order \(q\) at \((0,0)\) but is not Lipschitz calm there.

children.title: Single-Valued Inverse Localizations
children.top_down_role: Local inverse branches associated with strong metric regularity.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are metric spaces, \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\), and \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A localized inverse of \(F\) is single-valued and Lipschitz near \(\bar y\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local inverse-branch representation of strong metric regularity.

source_refs.locator: 4.1.2 Neighborhood Characterizations of Metric Regularity and Lipschitzian Behavior p. 382
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The mapping \(F\) is strongly metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) precisely when there exist neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(V\) of \(\bar y\), together with a single-valued Lipschitz mapping \(s:V\to U\), such that \(s(\bar y)=\bar x\) and
\[
F^{-1}(y)\cap U=\{s(y)\}\quad(y\in V).
\]
Thus the localized inverse mapping \(y\mapsto F^{-1}(y)\cap U\) is represented by one Lipschitz branch. Its least local Lipschitz constant is the modulus associated with this strong metric regularity localization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong metric regularity means that the inverse has exactly one nearby solution for each nearby output, and this solution varies Lipschitz continuously.
knowledge_statements.title: Single-Valued Inverse Localizations

children.title: Strong Implicit-Mapping Regime
children.top_down_role: Locally unique implicit solution branches generated by strong metric regularity.

knowledge_statements.title: Strong Implicit-Mapping Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Right-hand-side parameterization of the strong implicit-mapping principle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\), \(Y\), and \(P\) be metric spaces. Suppose \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) has a Lipschitz inverse localization \(s:V\to U\) at \((\bar x,\bar y)\), and let \(h:P\to Y\) be Lipschitz near \(\bar p\), with \(h(\bar p)=\bar y\). After shrinking a neighborhood \(W\) of \(\bar p\) so that \(h(W)\subset V\), the inclusion \(h(p)\in F(x)\) has exactly one solution \(x\in U\), namely \(x(p)=s(h(p))\), for every \(p\in W\). If \(s\) and \(h|_W\) have Lipschitz constants \(L_s\) and \(L_h\), respectively, then \[d_X(x(p_1),x(p_2))\leq L_sL_h d_P(p_1,p_2)\] for all \(p_1,p_2\in W\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Composing a strongly regular inverse branch with a locally Lipschitz right-hand side produces the unique local solution branch, whose Lipschitz constant is at most the product of the two component constants.
assumptions_latex: \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) has a Lipschitz inverse localization \(s:V\to U\) at \((\bar x,\bar y)\).
\(h:P\to Y\) is Lipschitz near \(\bar p\), with \(h(\bar p)=\bar y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The nearby inclusion \(h(p)\in F(x)\) has the unique local solution branch \(x(p)=s(h(p))\), which is Lipschitz.

notation.meaning: Lipschitz inverse localization of the strongly regular mapping.

children.title: Strong Metric Subregularity
children.top_down_role: Subregularity coupled with isolated reference solutions.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are metric spaces, \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\), and \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is strongly metrically subregular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\).

notation.meaning: Residual distance from the reference output to the image set.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the isolated-solution error-bound definition.

source_refs.locator: 4.2.2 Pointbased Characterizations of Covering and Metric Regularity p. 394
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The mapping \(F\) is strongly metrically subregular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) if there exist a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and a constant \(\kappa\geq0\) such that
\[
d_X(x,\bar x)\leq\kappa\operatorname{dist}(\bar y,F(x))\quad(x\in U).
\]
The convention is \(\operatorname{dist}(\bar y,\varnothing)=+\infty\). This inequality forces \(F^{-1}(\bar y)\cap U=\{\bar x\}\), so the reference point is an isolated local solution. The infimum of all admissible constants is the strong metric subregularity modulus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong metric subregularity is a residual error bound measured from one isolated reference solution rather than from the entire solution set.
knowledge_statements.title: Strong Metric Subregularity

source_witnesses.locator: 4.2.2 Pointbased Characterizations of Covering and Metric Regularity p. 394
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent formulation of the strong fixed-target regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S:=F^{-1}(\bar y)\). Then \(F\) is strongly metrically subregular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) if and only if \(F\) is metrically subregular there and \(\bar x\) is isolated in \(S\). Under these conditions, sufficiently near \(\bar x\), \(d_X(x,S)=d_X(x,\bar x)\), and the exact metric-subregularity and strong metric-subregularity moduli coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong metric subregularity is metric subregularity together with local isolation of the reference solution.
assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are metric spaces, \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\), and \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is strongly metrically subregular at }(\bar x,\bar y)\iff F\text{ is metrically subregular there and }\bar x\text{ is isolated in }F^{-1}(\bar y).
knowledge_statements.title: Subregularity Plus Solution Isolation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact scalar growth-rate representation of strong metric subregularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[
|F|^{\downarrow}(\bar x\mid\bar y):=\liminf_{\substack{x\to\bar x\\x\ne\bar x}}\frac{\operatorname{dist}(\bar y,F(x))}{d_X(x,\bar x)}.
\]
Then \(F\) is strongly metrically subregular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) if and only if \(|F|^{\downarrow}(\bar x\mid\bar y)>0\), and
\[
\operatorname{subreg}_{\mathrm{s}}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)=\frac{1}{|F|^{\downarrow}(\bar x\mid\bar y)},
\]
with \(1/(+\infty)=0\) and \(1/0=+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong metric subregularity is equivalent to positive residual growth away from the reference point, with reciprocal exact modulus.
assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are metric spaces, \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\), and \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is strongly metrically subregular at }(\bar x,\bar y)\iff |F|^{\downarrow}(\bar x\mid\bar y)>0.
knowledge_statements.title: Steepest Displacement-Rate Characterization

children.title: Isolated Calmness
children.top_down_role: The inverse solution-map counterpart of strong metric subregularity.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\) is isolated calm at \((\bar y,\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inverse-map counterpart of strong metric subregularity.

source_refs.locator: 4.1.2 Neighborhood Characterizations of Metric Regularity and Lipschitzian Behavior p. 382

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The mapping \(S\) is isolated calm at \((\bar y,\bar x)\) if there exist neighborhoods \(V\) of \(\bar y\) and \(U\) of \(\bar x\), and a constant \(\kappa\geq0\), such that
\[
S(y)\cap U\subseteq\{x\in X:d_X(x,\bar x)\leq\kappa d_Y(y,\bar y)\}
\]
for every \(y\in V\), and \(S(\bar y)\cap U=\{\bar x\}\). Equivalently, for \(S=F^{-1}\), isolated calmness at \((\bar y,\bar x)\) is strong metric subregularity of \(F\) at \((\bar x,\bar y)\), with equal exact moduli.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An isolated calm solution map has one reference solution locally, and every nearby local solution remains within a Lipschitz cone around it.
knowledge_statements.title: Isolated Calmness

children.top_down_role: Regularity centered at an individual graph point.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are metric spaces, \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\), and \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is metrically regular at the graph point \((\bar x,\bar y)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The mapping \(F\) is pointwise metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) if there exist neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(V\) of \(\bar y\), and a constant \(\kappa\geq0\), such that
\[
\operatorname{dist}(x,F^{-1}(y))\leq\kappa\operatorname{dist}(y,F(x))
\]
for every \((x,y)\in U\times V\). The property is centered at the single graph point \((\bar x,\bar y)\); its exact pointwise modulus is the infimum of the constants obtainable after arbitrary shrinking of \(U\) and \(V\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pointwise regularity is the standard metric-regularity inequality localized around one specified point of the mapping's graph.

children.title: Neighborhood Regularity
children.top_down_role: Regularity maintained throughout a local graph neighborhood.

knowledge_statements.title: Neighborhood Regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A common modulus is required across nearby graph points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be metric spaces. The mapping \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) has neighborhood metric regularity around \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\) if there exist an open product neighborhood \(O\subseteq X\times Y\) of \((\bar x,\bar y)\) and a constant \(\kappa\geq0\) such that, for every \((x_0,y_0)\in\operatorname{gph}F\cap O\), the mapping \(F\) is metrically regular at \((x_0,y_0)\) with an admissible modulus no greater than \(\kappa\). The point-dependent localization neighborhoods may be chosen inside \(O\), while \(\kappa\) is common to all nearby graph points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Neighborhood regularity requires metric regularity at every nearby graph point with one common bound, although the individual localization neighborhoods may vary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is uniformly metrically regular throughout a neighborhood of \((\bar x,\bar y)\) in its graph.

notation.meaning: Open product neighborhood in the product metric topology.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalence of Pointwise and Neighborhood Regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence under the immutable seed's convention allowing point-dependent localization neighborhoods while requiring one common modulus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\operatorname{nreg}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)\) denote the infimum of common bounds admissible in the neighborhood-regularity definition. Under that definition, \[F\text{ is neighborhood metrically regular around }(\bar x,\bar y)\iff F\text{ is metrically regular at }(\bar x,\bar y),\] and \[\operatorname{nreg}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)=\operatorname{reg}F(\bar x\mid\bar y).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the supplied neighborhood convention, neighborhood and ordinary pointwise metric regularity are equivalent and have the same exact modulus.
assumptions_latex: Neighborhood regularity is interpreted exactly as in the immutable seed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{nreg}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)=\operatorname{reg}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)\), with simultaneous finiteness.

children.title: Nonlocal Regularity Scale Family
children.top_down_role: Regularity over nonlocal sets, bounded regions, or parameter families.

children.title: Semilocal Regularity
children.top_down_role: Regularity over an extended neighborhood or bounded region anchored at a reference configuration.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is semilocally metrically regular on \(A\) around \(\bar y\).

notation.meaning: Prescribed input region on which the estimate is uniform.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the uniform-on-input-region, local-in-output convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Relative to a prescribed set \(A\subseteq X\), the mapping \(F\) is semilocally metrically regular on \(A\) around \(\bar y\) if there exist a neighborhood \(V\) of \(\bar y\) and a constant \(\kappa\geq0\) such that
\[
\operatorname{dist}(x,F^{-1}(y))\leq\kappa\operatorname{dist}(y,F(x))
\]
for every \(x\in A\) and every \(y\in V\). Thus localization is retained in the output variable, whereas the estimate is uniform over the entire designated input region. Taking \(A\) to be a neighborhood recovers a local form; taking \(A=X\) gives a one-sided nonlocal form.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Semilocal regularity keeps the output near a reference value while requiring one metric-regularity estimate uniformly over a prescribed input region.
knowledge_statements.title: Semilocal Regularity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated convention is coherent, but “semilocal metric regularity” is not sufficiently standardized to accept this exact quantifier pattern without an authoritative locator.

children.title: Global Regularity
children.top_down_role: Regularity imposed throughout the full domain under consideration.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are metric spaces and \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is globally metrically regular with modulus at most \(\kappa\).

notation.meaning: Residual distance from the output to the image.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the all-input, all-output metric-regularity inequality.

source_refs.locator: 1.2.3 Metric Regularity and Covering p. 56
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The mapping \(F\) is globally metrically regular if there exists a finite constant \(\kappa\geq0\) such that
\[
\operatorname{dist}(x,F^{-1}(y))\leq\kappa\operatorname{dist}(y,F(x))
\]
for every \(x\in X\) and every \(y\in Y\), using the convention that distance to the empty set is \(+\infty\). No localization neighborhoods are imposed. The least admissible \(\kappa\) is the global metric-regularity modulus. This global property implies every pointwise, neighborhood, and semilocal restriction obtained by limiting the quantified input and output sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Global metric regularity requires one residual-to-solution-distance bound for every input and output, without localization.
knowledge_statements.title: Global Regularity

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2.3 Metric Regularity and Covering p. 56
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonempty-graph consequence of the all-output quantifier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\operatorname{gph}F\neq\varnothing\) and \(F\) is globally metrically regular with a finite modulus, then \(F^{-1}(y)\neq\varnothing\) for every \(y\in Y\); equivalently, \(F(X)=Y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty globally metrically regular multifunction must be surjective.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is globally metrically regular with finite modulus.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F(X)=Y.
knowledge_statements.title: Global Regularity Forces Surjectivity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent inverse formulation for a multifunction with nonempty graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) have nonempty graph. Then \(F\) is globally metrically regular with constant \(\kappa\) if and only if
\[
e(F^{-1}(y_1),F^{-1}(y_2))\leq \kappa d_Y(y_1,y_2)\qquad(y_1,y_2\in Y),
\]
where \(e(A,B):=\sup_{a\in A}\operatorname{dist}(a,B)\). Consequently, the exact global regularity modulus is the least global one-sided-excess Lipschitz constant of \(F^{-1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Global metric regularity is equivalent to the inverse multifunction being globally Lipschitz in one-sided excess, with the same exact constant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{reg}_{\mathrm{glob}}F=\inf\{\kappa:e(F^{-1}(y_1),F^{-1}(y_2))\leq\kappa d_Y(y_1,y_2)\ \forall y_1,y_2\in Y\}\).

notation.meaning: One-sided excess of A over B.

knowledge_statements.title: Global Inverse-Excess Characterization

children.top_down_role: Regularity estimates controlled uniformly over a family of points, sets, or parameters.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{reg}_{A,B}F\leq\kappa\).

notation.meaning: Distance from a point to a set, with distance to the empty set equal to infinity.
Inverse image of a point under the multifunction.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The mapping \(F\) is uniformly metrically regular on \(A\times B\) with modulus \(\kappa\geq0\) if
\[
d(x,F^{-1}(y))\leq \kappa d(y,F(x))
\]
for every \(x\in A\) and \(y\in B\). The least admissible \(\kappa\), with value \(+\infty\) when none exists, is the uniform regularity modulus \(\operatorname{reg}_{A,B}F\). Unlike pointwise regularity, the same constant and the same prescribed sets serve all reference graph points in \(A\times B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform regularity requires one error-bound constant to work for every tested pair in fixed domain and range sets.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Monotonicity under Restriction of Test Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order property of the prescribed-set uniform modulus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(A'\subseteq A\subseteq X\), \(B'\subseteq B\subseteq Y\), and \(\operatorname{gph}F\cap(A'\times B')\neq\varnothing\), then
\[
\operatorname{reg}_{A',B'}F\leq \operatorname{reg}_{A,B}F.
\]
Thus every uniform regularity estimate on \(A\times B\) remains valid, with the same constant, after either test set is restricted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restricting the tested input or output set cannot increase the uniform regularity modulus.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{reg}_{A',B'}F\leq \operatorname{reg}_{A,B}F\).
knowledge_statements.title: Monotonicity under Restriction of Test Sets

children.title: Scale-Transition Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Conditions governing passage between semilocal, global, and uniform regimes.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is locally metrically regular at every graph point but has no finite uniform regularity modulus on \((0,\infty)^2\).

notation.meaning: Exact local metric-regularity modulus of a single-valued map.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between pointwise local and uniform nonlocal regularity.

source_refs.locator: 4.1.2 Neighborhood Characterizations of Metric Regularity and Lipschitzian Behavior p. 382
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(x>0\), the inverse function theorem gives local metric regularity of \(f\) at \((x,x^2)\), with exact local modulus
\[
\operatorname{reg}f(x\mid x^2)=\frac{1}{2x}.
\]
Consequently these local moduli are unbounded as \(x\downarrow0\). Hence pointwise local regularity at every graph point does not imply uniform regularity on the whole domain and range: no finite \(\kappa\) satisfies \(d(x,f^{-1}(y))\leq\kappa |y-f(x)|\) for all \(x,y>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The squaring map is regular around every positive point, but its local moduli diverge near zero, preventing a uniform global constant.
knowledge_statements.title: Scale-Transition Boundaries

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive implications among global, prescribed-set uniform, and pointwise regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\), global metric regularity with constant \(\kappa\) is exactly uniform metric regularity on \(X\times Y\) with that constant. More generally, uniform metric regularity on \(A\times B\) with constant \(\kappa\) implies pointwise metric regularity with modulus at most \(\kappa\) at every \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\cap(\operatorname{int}A\times\operatorname{int}B)\). The converse passage from pointwise estimates requires a common bound on common neighborhoods and fails in general.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Global regularity is full-set uniform regularity, and prescribed-set uniform regularity yields pointwise regularity at interior graph points; pointwise estimates need not globalize.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{reg}_{X,Y}F=\operatorname{reg}_{\mathrm{glob}}F\), and \(\operatorname{reg}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)\leq\operatorname{reg}_{A,B}F\) at interior graph points.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal tangent-surjectivity criterion avoiding Asplund dual calculus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A Banach-space primal regularity condition is the existence of neighborhoods \(U,V\) and \(\kappa>0\) such that, for every \((x,y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\cap(U\times V)\) and every \(v\in Y\), there exists \(u\in X\) satisfying
\[
v\in DF(x,y)(u),\qquad \|u\|\leq\kappa\|v\|.
\]
Uniform contingent solvability of all range directions yields local linear openness of \(F\), hence metric regularity around \((\bar x,\bar y)\) with modulus no larger than \(\kappa\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniformly solving every infinitesimal range direction through the graphical derivative gives a primal Banach-space regularity certificate.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The mapping \(F\) is metrically regular around \((\bar x,\bar y)\) with modulus at most \(\kappa\) if there are neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(V\) of \(\bar y\) such that
\[
d_X\bigl(x,F^{-1}(y)\bigr)\leq\kappa d_Y\bigl(y,F(x)\bigr)
\]
for every \((x,y)\in U\times V\), where distance to the empty set is \(+\infty\). The least admissible constant is \(\operatorname{reg}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)\). This definition uses only distances and inverse images, so it remains meaningful in general metric spaces without linear or dual structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In arbitrary metric spaces, metric regularity is a local distance-to-solution error bound with one constant valid on a product of neighborhoods.

\]

children.title: Nonlinear Metric Alternatives
children.top_down_role: Slope, covering, or variational routes used when linear dual tools are unavailable.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hölder Regularity Without Linear Metric Regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separating example showing that Hölder metric regularity is strictly broader than linear metric regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an odd integer \(m\geq3\), let \(F:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be \(F(x)=x^m\). Around \((0,0)\), its inverse satisfies a Hölder estimate
\[
|x-F^{-1}(y)|\leq C_m|x^m-y|^{1/m}
\]
for a constant \(C_m>0\), so \(F\) is Hölder metrically regular of order \(1/m\). It is not linearly metrically regular at \((0,0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An odd power map has Hölder inverse regularity at zero but no finite linear metric-regularity modulus there.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is Hölder metrically regular of order }1/m\text{ at }(0,0)\text{ but is not metrically regular there}.

notation.meaning: A positive constant depending only on the odd exponent.

knowledge_statements.title: Hölder Regularity Without Linear Metric Regularity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonlinear residual-to-solution estimate replacing the linear metric-regularity modulus by a gauge.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\omega:[0,+\infty]\to[0,+\infty]\) be nondecreasing, satisfy \(\omega(0)=0\), and be continuous at \(0\). The mapping \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) is \(\omega\)-metrically regular around \((\bar x,\bar y)\) if neighborhoods \(U,V\) exist such that
\[
d_X(x,F^{-1}(y))\leq \omega\!\left(d_Y(y,F(x))\right)
\]
for every \((x,y)\in U\times V\). The choice \(\omega(t)=\kappa t\) gives ordinary metric regularity; \(\omega(t)=\kappa t^q\), \(0<q\leq1\), gives the standard Hölder form of order \(q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gauge metric regularity bounds solution distance by a nonlinear function of the residual, with linear and Hölder bounds as special cases.
assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are metric spaces, \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\), and \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\).
\(\omega\) is nondecreasing, \(\omega(0)=0\), and continuous at zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d_X(x,F^{-1}(y))\leq\omega(d_Y(y,F(x)))\quad\text{locally}.

notation.meaning: Distances in the domain and range metric spaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Gauge Metric Regularity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local covering form equivalent to gauge metric regularity for a locally invertible gauge.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\omega:[0,\varepsilon)\to[0,\omega(\varepsilon))\) be continuous and strictly increasing with \(\omega(0)=0\), and put \(\phi=\omega^{-1}\). After localizing to sufficiently small neighborhoods and radii, \(\omega\)-metric regularity is equivalent to the graph-centered covering property \[B_Y(y,\phi(t))\cap V\subset F(B_X(x,t))\] for every nearby \((x,y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\) and every sufficiently small \(t>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a continuous strictly increasing gauge, gauge metric regularity is equivalent to local openness with output radius given by the inverse gauge.
assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are metric spaces and \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\).
\(\omega\) is continuous and strictly increasing near zero, with \(\omega(0)=0\).
The regularity estimate and covering inclusion are localized to suitably shrunk neighborhoods and sufficiently small radii.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\omega\text{-metric regularity}\Longleftrightarrow B_Y(y,\omega^{-1}(t))\cap V\subset F(B_X(x,t))\) locally.

notation.meaning: Local inverse of the nonlinear regularity gauge.
Open metric balls in the domain and range.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong-Slope Certificate for Gauge Error Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal complete-metric-space certificate for a locally uniform gauge residual bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each nearby \(y\), define \(g_y(x):=\omega(d_Y(y,F(x)))\) on a complete closed localization \(C\). Assume \(g_y\) is lower semicontinuous, \(\omega(t)>0\) for \(t>0\), and there is \(\delta>0\) such that \[|\nabla g_y|(x)\ge 1\] whenever \(x\in C\), \(0<g_y(x)<\delta\), and \(y\) is sufficiently near \(\bar y\). For points in a smaller localization whose relevant Ekeland comparison balls remain in \(C\), \[d_X(x,F^{-1}(y))\le g_y(x)=\omega(d_Y(y,F(x))).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A uniform unit lower bound on the strong slope of the gauge-composed residual certifies the corresponding nonlinear metric-regularity estimate on an interior localization.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a complete closed localization containing \(\bar x\).
For each nearby \(y\), \(g_y(x)=\omega(d_Y(y,F(x)))\) is lower semicontinuous on \(C\).
There is \(\delta>0\) such that \(|\nabla g_y|(x)\ge1\) at every relevant point with \(0<g_y(x)<\delta\).
The conclusion is restricted to a smaller localization whose comparison balls remain in \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d_X(x,F^{-1}(y))\le\omega(d_Y(y,F(x)))\quad\text{locally around }(\bar x,\bar y).

notation.meaning: strong slope of the residual function at x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gauge-based nonlinear replacement for linear metric regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The mapping \(F\) is \(\omega\)-metrically regular around \((\bar x,\bar y)\) if there exist neighborhoods \(U\) and \(V\) such that
\[
d_X(x,F^{-1}(y))\leq\omega\!\left(d_Y(y,F(x))\right)
\]
for every \((x,y)\in U\times V\). Linear metric regularity is recovered with \(\omega(t)=\kappa t\); choosing \(\omega(t)=\kappa t^q\) gives Hölder metric regularity of order \(q>0\). The formulation is entirely metric and therefore avoids coderivative calculus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonlinear metric regularity replaces the linear residual bound by an increasing gauge, including Hölder error bounds as a special case.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonlinear Metric Alternatives

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The gauge-based definition is plausible and fits the leaf, but no source is supplied for the exact gauge assumptions or for treating every q>0 as the stated Holder regularity convention. assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are arbitrary Banach spaces and \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) has locally closed graph at \((\bar x,\bar y)\).
