notation.meaning: Sequential limiting coderivative based on limiting graph normals.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of limiting-coderivative criteria outside Asplund spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In a general non-Asplund Banach space, local closedness of \(\operatorname{gph}F\) does not by itself supply the fuzzy normal-cone sum rules and sequential approximation properties used by the standard limiting-coderivative criterion. Therefore the finite-dimensional equivalence
\[
F\text{ metrically regular around }(\bar x,\bar y)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(0)=\{0\}
\]
may not be invoked without additional compactness, convexity, smooth-renorming, or calculus assumptions. Primal metric or slope criteria remain meaningful without those dual hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Outside Asplund spaces, the usual limiting-coderivative equivalence requires extra assumptions; local closedness alone does not justify transferring it.
knowledge_statements.title: Asplund-Free Validity Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The warning is directionally plausible, but no boundary theorem or counterexample is cited. Because the validity of limiting-normal and coderivative criteria outside Asplund spaces depends on the precise normal construction and auxiliary compactness or calculus assumptions, the asserted failure boundary requires a source.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a closed convex graph, the limiting and convex normal cones coincide. Consequently
\[
D^*F(x,y)(y^*)=
\left\{x^*:\langle x^*,u-x\rangle-\langle y^*,v-y\rangle\leq0
\text{ for all }(u,v)\in\operatorname{gph}F\right\}.
\]
Thus coderivative membership is determined by one global supporting inequality rather than by sequential nonconvex limiting constructions. This representation permits convex separation and open-mapping arguments in regularity certification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a closed convex graph, coderivative membership is exactly a global supporting inequality over the graph.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a convex graph, regularity criteria may be expressed with convex normals, and for a polyhedral graph the relevant normal structure is determined by finitely many faces. For a nonconvex graph, the corresponding criterion must use an appropriate nonconvex normal or coderivative and its required qualification hypotheses. In particular, replacing \(N_{\operatorname{gph}F}(x,y)\) by \(N_{\operatorname{gph}F}^{\mathrm{conv}}(x,y)\), or retaining a finite-face test after polyhedrality is lost, need not preserve either necessity or sufficiency for metric regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Regularity tests transfer between graph regimes only after replacing geometry-specific normals and qualifications; convex or finite-face tests cannot generally be reused unchanged for nonconvex graphs.
knowledge_statements.title: Geometry-Dependent Criterion Transfer

children.title: Polyhedral-to-Nonconvex Boundary
children.top_down_role: Loss of finite combinatorial structure and its consequences for regularity analysis.

assumptions_latex: The multifunction is considered at a graph point where local linear openness is being tested.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Loss of polyhedral geometry removes finite-face error-bound guarantees; a nonpolyhedral mapping can fail every positive linear covering estimate.

notation.meaning: closed unit ball in the scalar space

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete failure of a positive linear covering rate after leaving the polyhedral graph regime.

source_refs.locator: 4.2.2 Pointbased Characterizations of Covering and Metric Regularity p. 394
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb R\rightrightarrows\mathbb R\) be given by \(F(x)=\{x^2\}\). Its graph is smooth but nonpolyhedral near \((0,0)\). For every \(c>0\) and every sufficiently small \(t>0\), the inclusion \[0+c t\mathbb B\subset F(0+t\mathbb B)\] fails, because \(F([-t,t])=[0,t^2]\) contains no neighborhood of \(0\). Hence \(F\) is not open at a linear rate and is not metrically regular at \((0,0)\), illustrating that polyhedral finite-face error-bound conclusions do not survive arbitrary nonpolyhedral deformation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The nonpolyhedral map x↦x² covers only [0,t²] from a radius-t neighborhood, so it has no positive linear openness rate at zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral-to-Nonconvex Boundary

source_witnesses.locator: 4.2.2 Pointbased Characterizations of Covering and Metric Regularity p. 394

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonpolyhedrality Alone Does Not Destroy Regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Converse boundary showing that loss of finite polyhedral structure removes a guarantee but is not itself an obstruction to metric regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be defined by \(F(x)=x+x^2\). Its graph is nonpolyhedral in every neighborhood of \((0,0)\), while \(F'(0)=1\). Hence \(F\) is strongly metrically regular around \((0,0)\), and its exact metric-regularity modulus is \(\operatorname{reg}F(0\mid 0)=1\). Thus leaving the polyhedral regime does not by itself imply failure of metric regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The nonpolyhedral map x↦x+x² is strongly metrically regular at zero, so nonpolyhedrality alone does not cause regularity failure.
assumptions_latex: Regularity is considered at \((\bar x,\bar y)=(0,0)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is strongly metrically regular around \((0,0)\) and \(\operatorname{reg}F(0\mid0)=1\), despite its locally nonpolyhedral graph.

notation.meaning: Exact metric-regularity modulus at the reference graph point.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonpolyhedrality Alone Does Not Destroy Regularity

children.title: Linear Surjectivity
children.top_down_role: Surjectivity properties of bounded linear operators underlying regularity results.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Linear surjectivity is the condition \(A(X)=Y\).

notation.meaning: range of the linear operator A

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Banach-space surjectivity condition underlying linear openness and metric regularity.

source_refs.locator: 1.2.3 Metric Regularity and Covering p. 56

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The bounded linear operator \(A:X\to Y\) is surjective precisely when \[A(X)=Y,\] equivalently, when for every \(y\in Y\) there exists \(x\in X\) satisfying \(Ax=y\). In the metric-regularity setting, this is the qualitative condition that permits a positive linear covering modulus and a finite inverse-distance bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded linear operator is surjective when every target vector has at least one preimage.
knowledge_statements.title: Linear Surjectivity

children.title: Linear Open-Mapping Principle
children.top_down_role: Open behavior of surjective linear operators as a precursor to nonlinear covering results.

assumptions_latex: \(A:X\to Y\) is bounded, linear, and surjective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists \(c>0\) such that \(c\mathbb B_Y\subset A(\mathbb B_X)\).

notation.meaning: closed unit ball of a normed space Z

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative Banach open-mapping theorem for a surjective bounded linear operator.

source_refs.locator: 1.2.3 Metric Regularity and Covering p. 56
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exists a constant \(c>0\) such that \[c\mathbb B_Y\subset A(\mathbb B_X).\] By linearity and translation, for every \(x\in X\) and every \(t>0\), \[Ax+c t\mathbb B_Y\subset A(x+t\mathbb B_X).\] Thus a bounded surjective linear operator maps every open subset of \(X\) to an open subset of \(Y\) and is open at a uniform linear rate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every bounded surjective linear operator between Banach spaces maps balls onto sets containing proportionally sized balls.
knowledge_statements.title: Linear Open-Mapping Principle

children.title: Surjectivity–Openness Correspondence
children.top_down_role: The passage from algebraic range coverage to quantitative open behavior.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Surjectivity, positive linear openness, and metric regularity are equivalent for \(A\).

notation.meaning: closed unit ball of a normed space Z
inverse image of y under A

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global equivalence for bounded linear operators between Banach spaces.

source_refs.locator: 1.2.3 Metric Regularity and Covering p. 56
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The following are equivalent: \(A(X)=Y\); there exists \(c>0\) with \(c\mathbb B_Y\subset A(\mathbb B_X)\); and there exists \(\kappa<\infty\) such that \[\operatorname{dist}(x,A^{-1}(y))\leq \kappa\lVert Ax-y\rVert\qquad(x\in X,\ y\in Y).\] When the covering inclusion holds with \(c\), the distance estimate holds with \(\kappa=1/c\), up to passage to nonattained exact moduli. Conversely, any finite metric-regularity bound implies linear openness and therefore surjectivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a bounded linear operator, surjectivity, openness at a positive linear rate, and a global inverse-distance error bound are equivalent.
knowledge_statements.title: Surjectivity–Openness Correspondence

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2.3 Metric Regularity and Covering p. 56

children.title: Linear Conditioning Constants
children.top_down_role: Quantitative measures controlling openness and inverse stability for linear operators.

assumptions_latex: \(A:X\to Y\) is bounded, linear, and surjective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The exact regularity modulus is the reciprocal of the surjection modulus, which equals the adjoint lower bound.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact primal and dual conditioning constants for a surjective bounded linear operator.

source_refs.locator: 4.2.2 Pointbased Characterizations of Covering and Metric Regularity p. 394
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[\operatorname{sur}A:=\sup\{c\geq0:c\mathbb B_Y\subset A(\mathbb B_X)\}.\] Then \[\operatorname{sur}A=\inf_{\lVert y^*\rVert=1}\lVert A^*y^*\rVert>0,\qquad \operatorname{reg}A=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sur}A}.\] Here \(\operatorname{reg}A\) is the infimum of all \(\kappa\) for which \(\operatorname{dist}(x,A^{-1}(y))\leq\kappa\lVert Ax-y\rVert\) holds globally. Thus the primal covering radius, the adjoint bounded-below constant, and the inverse-distance conditioning constant encode the same linear conditioning.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A surjective operator’s covering modulus equals its adjoint’s minimum gain, and its exact metric-regularity modulus is the reciprocal.
knowledge_statements.title: Linear Conditioning Constants

source_witnesses.locator: 4.2.2 Pointbased Characterizations of Covering and Metric Regularity p. 394
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quotient-operator representation of the exact linear conditioning constants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\widetilde A:X/\ker A\to Y\) be defined by \(\widetilde A[x]=Ax\). Then \(\widetilde A\) is a bounded linear isomorphism and
\[
\operatorname{reg}A=\|\widetilde A^{-1}\|=\sup_{\|y\|\leq1}\inf_{Ax=y}\|x\|,
\qquad
\operatorname{sur}A=\|\widetilde A^{-1}\|^{-1}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After factoring out the kernel, a surjective operator is an isomorphism whose inverse norm is the exact regularity modulus.
assumptions_latex: \(A:X\to Y\) is bounded, linear, and surjective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{reg}A=\|\widetilde A^{-1}\|\) and \(\operatorname{sur}A=1/\|\widetilde A^{-1}\|\).

notation.meaning: operator induced by A on the quotient by its kernel
coset of x in the quotient space

knowledge_statements.title: Quotient-Space Condition Number

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Euclidean formula for the linear conditioning constants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a full-row-rank matrix \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\),
\[
\operatorname{sur}A=\sigma_{\min}(A)=\sqrt{\lambda_{\min}(AA^{\mathsf T})},
\qquad
\operatorname{reg}A=\|A^\dagger\|_2=\frac1{\sigma_{\min}(A)}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a full-row-rank Euclidean matrix, the covering modulus is its smallest singular value and the regularity modulus is the norm of its Moore–Penrose inverse.
assumptions_latex: The domain and range have Euclidean norms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{sur}A=\sigma_{\min}(A)\) and \(\operatorname{reg}A=\|A^\dagger\|_2=1/\sigma_{\min}(A)\).

notation.meaning: smallest singular value of the full-row-rank matrix

knowledge_statements.title: Euclidean Singular-Value Specialization

children.title: Nonsurjective Failure Regime
children.top_down_role: Regularity limitations caused by deficient operator range.

assumptions_latex: \(A:X\to Y\) is bounded and linear but not surjective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The operator has zero linear covering modulus and no finite metric-regularity modulus.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of linear openness and metric regularity when surjectivity is absent.

source_refs.locator: 1.2.3 Metric Regularity and Covering p. 56
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(c>0\), the inclusion \[c\mathbb B_Y\subset A(\mathbb B_X)\] fails; otherwise scaling would give \(A(X)=Y\). Consequently, \(A\) is not open at any positive linear rate. It also admits no finite constant \(\kappa\) satisfying \(\operatorname{dist}(x,A^{-1}(y))\leq\kappa\lVert Ax-y\rVert\) for all nearby graph data, since such metric regularity would imply local linear openness and hence, by linearity, surjectivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonsurjective bounded linear operator contains no target ball in its image and therefore cannot be linearly open or metrically regular.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonsurjective Failure Regime

children.title: Smooth Surjective-Derivative Regime
children.top_down_role: Differentiable mappings organized by derivative surjectivity.

assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to Y\) is continuously Fréchet differentiable near \(\bar x\).
The derivative \(Df(\bar x):X\to Y\) is surjective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The mapping \(f\) is locally open at a linear rate and metrically regular near \((\bar x,f(\bar x))\).

notation.meaning: Fréchet derivative of f at x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth Banach-space Lyusternik–Graves theorem at a surjective derivative.

source_refs.locator: 4.2.3 Metric Regularity under Perturbations p. 399
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(c\) satisfying \(0<c<\operatorname{sur}Df(\bar x)\), there are neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(V\) of \(f(\bar x)\) such that, whenever \(x\in U\) and \(t>0\) is sufficiently small, \[f(x)+ct\mathbb B_Y\subset f(x+t\mathbb B_X).\] Equivalently, after possibly shrinking \(U\) and \(V\), \[\operatorname{dist}(x,f^{-1}(y))\leq c^{-1}\lVert f(x)-y\rVert\qquad(x\in U,\ y\in V).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuously differentiable map whose derivative is surjective at a point is locally linearly open and metrically regular there.
knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Surjective-Derivative Regime

source_witnesses.locator: 4.2.3 Metric Regularity under Perturbations p. 399
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact-modulus refinement of the smooth Lyusternik–Graves theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At \((\bar x,f(\bar x))\),
\[
\operatorname{sur}(f;\bar x\mid f(\bar x))=\operatorname{sur}Df(\bar x),
\qquad
\operatorname{reg}(f;\bar x\mid f(\bar x))=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sur}Df(\bar x)}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a continuously differentiable map with surjective derivative, the exact local covering rate equals the derivative's surjection modulus and the exact regularity modulus is its reciprocal.
assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to Y\) is continuously Fréchet differentiable near \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The exact local covering and regularity moduli of \(f\) coincide with those determined by \(Df(\bar x)\).

notation.meaning: exact local linear-covering modulus of f

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Smooth Regularity Modulus

children.title: Strict-Differentiability Perturbation Regime
children.top_down_role: Perturbation extensions based on strict first-order approximation.

assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to Y\) is strictly Fréchet differentiable at \(\bar x\) with derivative \(A\).
The bounded linear operator \(A:X\to Y\) is surjective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The strict first-order perturbation preserves every local covering rate below \(\operatorname{sur}A\).

notation.meaning: strict derivative of f at the reference point

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lyusternik–Graves perturbation theorem under strict differentiability rather than continuous differentiability.

source_refs.locator: 4.2.3 Metric Regularity under Perturbations p. 399
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Strict differentiability means \[\lim_{x,x'\to\bar x,\ x\ne x'}\frac{\lVert f(x)-f(x')-A(x-x')\rVert}{\lVert x-x'\rVert}=0.\] For every \(c\) with \(0<c<\operatorname{sur}A\), there exists a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) such that, for \(x\in U\) and all sufficiently small \(t>0\), \[f(x)+ct\mathbb B_Y\subset f(x+t\mathbb B_X).\] Hence \(f\) is metrically regular at \((\bar x,f(\bar x))\) with modulus at most \(1/c\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strictly differentiable map with surjective strict derivative retains every covering rate below the derivative’s surjection modulus.
knowledge_statements.title: Strict-Differentiability Perturbation Regime

source_witnesses.locator: 4.2.3 Metric Regularity under Perturbations p. 399
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact-modulus form of the strictly differentiable Lyusternik–Graves regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Writing \(\bar y=f(\bar x)\),
\[
\operatorname{sur}(f;\bar x\mid\bar y)=\operatorname{sur}A,
\qquad
\operatorname{reg}(f;\bar x\mid\bar y)=\frac1{\operatorname{sur}A}.
\]
Every positive covering rate below \(\operatorname{sur}A\) is locally admissible; the endpoint rate need not be attained on a fixed neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strictly differentiable mapping and its surjective strict derivative have the same exact covering modulus and reciprocal exact regularity modulus, although the endpoint covering rate need not be attained.
assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to Y\) is strictly Fréchet differentiable at \(\bar x\) with derivative \(A\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The exact local moduli of \(f\) equal those determined by \(A\).
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Strict-Derivative Moduli

children.title: Set-Valued Extensions
children.top_down_role: Covering principles for mappings whose values are sets.

assumptions_latex: \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) is metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) with modulus \(\kappa\).
\(g:X\to Y\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\) with constant \(\ell\) and \(\kappa\ell<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The perturbed multifunction \(F+g\) remains metrically regular, with modulus at most \(\kappa/(1-\kappa\ell)\).

notation.meaning: pointwise sum of F and g

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-valued Lyusternik–Graves stability under a small single-valued Lipschitz perturbation.

source_refs.locator: 4.2.3 Metric Regularity under Perturbations p. 399
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\bar z=\bar y+g(\bar x)\). Then \(F+g\) is metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar z)\). More precisely, after restricting to suitable neighborhoods, \[\operatorname{dist}\bigl(x,(F+g)^{-1}(z)\bigr)\leq \frac{\kappa}{1-\kappa\ell}\operatorname{dist}\bigl(z,F(x)+g(x)\bigr).\] Thus the set-valued inverse-distance estimate survives a Lipschitz perturbation whenever the perturbation slope is strictly smaller than the reciprocal regularity margin.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A metrically regular multifunction remains regular after a Lipschitz perturbation whose slope is smaller than its inverse regularity margin.
knowledge_statements.title: Set-Valued Extensions

knowledge_statements.title: Metric-Space Extensions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Purely metric equivalence between local covering and inverse-distance regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The local estimate \[d\bigl(x,F^{-1}(y)\bigr)\leq\kappa d\bigl(y,F(x)\bigr)\] for \(x\) near \(\bar x\) and \(y\) near \(\bar y\) is equivalent to local linear openness: for every \(c<1/\kappa\), after shrinking neighborhoods, \[B_Y(y,ct)\subset F\bigl(B_X(x,t)\bigr)\] whenever \((x,y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\) is nearby and \(t>0\) is sufficiently small. Consequently, the exact regularity modulus is the reciprocal of the exact covering modulus, with the convention \(1/0=+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For multifunctions between metric spaces, local inverse-distance regularity and local linear covering are equivalent, with reciprocal exact moduli.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Metric regularity with constant \(\kappa\) is equivalent to linear openness with any reciprocal rate below \(1/\kappa\).

notation.meaning: closed metric ball of radius t centered at x
distance from a point to a set

The supremum of admissible \(c\) is the local covering modulus.

children.title: Metric Completeness Regimes
children.top_down_role: Ambient completeness conditions supporting metric-space covering principles.

knowledge_statements.title: Metric Completeness Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Completeness assumptions used by differentiability-free iterative covering arguments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,d_X)\) and \((Y,d_Y)\) be metric spaces, let \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\), and let \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\). For \(r,s>0\), set \(G_{r,s}:=\operatorname{gph}F\cap(\overline B_X(\bar x,r)\times\overline B_Y(\bar y,s))\). A local iterative covering argument has the required completeness regime whenever its iterates remain in \(G_{r,s}\) and \(G_{r,s}\) is complete under a product metric. In particular, this holds if \(X\) and \(Y\) are complete and \(G_{r,s}\) is closed in \(X\times Y\). Thus completeness of the ambient spaces may be replaced by completeness of the localized graph region containing the iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A differentiability-free covering iteration only needs its localized graph region to be complete. Completeness of both ambient spaces together with closedness of that region is a standard sufficient condition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Completeness is required only for the localized graph region containing the iteration.

notation.meaning: Closed ball of radius r about x in X
Set-valued mapping from X to subsets of Y

children.title: Differentiability-Free Boundary

knowledge_statements.title: Differentiability-Free Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp strict-rate boundary in a differentiability-free covering perturbation theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be Banach spaces. Suppose \(f:X\to Y\) is linearly open around \((\bar x,f(\bar x))\) with an admissible rate \(c>0\), and \(g:X\to Y\) is Lipschitz near \(\bar x\) with modulus \(\ell<c\). Then \(f+g\) is linearly open around \((\bar x,f(\bar x)+g(\bar x))\) at every rate \(c'\) satisfying \(0<c'<c-\ell\). The strict inequality cannot generally be replaced by \(\ell\le c\): for \(X=Y=\mathbb R\), \(f(x)=x\), \(g(x)=-x\), and \(\bar x=0\), one has \(c=\ell=1\), while \(f+g\equiv0\) is not linearly open.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Lipschitz perturbation preserves linear openness when its modulus is strictly smaller than the original covering rate. At equality, complete cancellation can destroy openness.
assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to Y\) is linearly open around \((\bar x,f(\bar x))\) with rate \(c>0\).
\(g:X\to Y\) is Lipschitz near \(\bar x\) with modulus \(\ell<c\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The perturbed mapping is linearly open at every rate \(c'\) with \(0<c'<c-\ell\), whereas equality \(\ell=c\) need not preserve openness.

notation.meaning: Admissible linear-openness rate of the unperturbed mapping
Local Lipschitz modulus of the perturbation
Guaranteed linear-openness rate of the perturbed mapping

knowledge_statements.title: Graphical Regularity Criteria
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph-local error-bound formulation of metric regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) be a mapping between metric spaces and let \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\). The mapping \(F\) is metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) if there exist neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(V\) of \(\bar y\), and a constant \(\kappa\ge0\), such that \[d_X(x,F^{-1}(y))\le \kappa d_Y(y,F(x))\] for every \((x,y)\in U\times V\), with distance to the empty set defined as \(+\infty\). The infimum of all such locally admissible constants is the exact modulus \(\operatorname{reg}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Metric regularity is the local error bound controlling distance to an inverse image by the residual distance to the mapping value; the least local bound is its exact modulus.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed local error bound characterizes metric regularity at \((\bar x,\bar y)\).

notation.meaning: Distance from a point to a set, with distance to the empty set equal to positive infinity

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A mapping \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) satisfies the graphical openness criterion at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) with rate \(c>0\) if there are neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(V\) of \(\bar y\), and \(\varepsilon>0\), such that
\[
B_Y(y,ct)\subset F(B_X(x,t))
\]
whenever \((x,y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\cap(U\times V)\) and \(0<t<\varepsilon\) with the balls confined to the chosen localization. The supremum of all admissible rates, over shrinking neighborhoods, is the exact linear-openness bound \(\operatorname{lop}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linear openness means that images of every sufficiently small ball around a nearby graph point cover a proportionally sized ball in the range.
knowledge_statements.title: Graphical Openness Criteria

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose there are neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(V\) of \(\bar y\), and \(\kappa>0\), such that for every \((x,y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\cap(U\times V)\) and every \(v\in Y\), one can find \(u\in X\) satisfying
\[
v\in DF(x\mid y)(u),\qquad \|u\|\le\kappa\|v\|.
\]
Under the local closedness and completeness hypotheses supporting the tangent iteration, this uniform tangent surjectivity implies that \(F\) is open at every rate \(c<1/\kappa\), and hence is metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) with \(\operatorname{reg}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)\le\kappa\).

children.title: Regularity–Openness Criterion Transfer
children.top_down_role: The correspondence between graphical tests expressed through regularity or openness.

knowledge_statements.title: Regularity–Openness Criterion Transfer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative correspondence between regularity error bounds and graph-centered covering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) be a mapping between metric spaces and let \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\). Metric regularity of \(F\) at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) is equivalent to linear openness of \(F\) around \((\bar x,\bar y)\). More quantitatively, every locally admissible covering rate \(c>0\) yields a metric-regularity bound \(1/c\), and every locally admissible metric-regularity bound \(\kappa>0\) yields, after shrinking the neighborhoods if necessary, every covering rate \(c\) satisfying \(0<c<1/\kappa\). Consequently, \[\operatorname{reg}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)=\frac{1}{\operatorname{lop}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)},\] with the extended-real conventions \(1/0=+\infty\) and \(1/(+\infty)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Metric regularity and graph-centered linear openness are equivalent. Their locally admissible constants transfer reciprocally, and their exact moduli are reciprocals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Metric regularity and linear openness are equivalent, with \(\operatorname{reg}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)=1/\operatorname{lop}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)\).

children.title: Levy–Rockafellar Criterion for Strong Subregularity
children.top_down_role: The graphical-derivative criterion for isolated solution behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Levy–Rockafellar Criterion for Strong Subregularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Levy–Rockafellar graphical-derivative criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be finite-dimensional normed spaces, and let \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) have locally closed graph at \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\). Then \(F\) is strongly metrically subregular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\), meaning that there exist \(\kappa\ge0\) and a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) such that \[\|x-\bar x\|\le\kappa d(\bar y,F(x))\qquad\text{for every }x\in U,\] if and only if \[DF(\bar x\mid\bar y)^{-1}(0)=\{0\}.\] Equivalently, the tangent cone to \(\operatorname{gph}F\) at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) contains no nonzero horizontal direction \((u,0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite-dimensional mapping with locally closed graph, strong metric subregularity is equivalent to the absence of nonzero horizontal tangent directions at the reference graph point.
assumptions_latex: \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) has locally closed graph at \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strong metric subregularity is equivalent to \(DF(\bar x\mid\bar y)^{-1}(0)=\{0\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Assume that
\[
\frac{f(\bar x+t u')-f(\bar x)}{t}\to df(\bar x)(u)
\]
whenever \(t\downarrow0\) and \(u'\to u\). Then \(f\) is strongly metrically subregular at \((\bar x,f(\bar x))\) if and only if there exists \(\alpha>0\) such that
\[
\|df(\bar x)(u)\|\ge\alpha\|u\|\qquad(u\in X).
\]
Equivalently, \(df(\bar x)^{-1}(0)=\{0\}\). Under the displayed lower bound, every \(\kappa>1/\alpha\) is locally admissible in \(\|x-\bar x\|\le\kappa\|f(x)-f(\bar x)\|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite-dimensional semidifferentiable map, strong subregularity is equivalent to the semiderivative being uniformly bounded away from zero on unit directions.
knowledge_statements.title: Semiderivative Criteria

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:X\to Y\) be Hadamard semidifferentiable at \(\bar x\), where \(X,Y\) are finite-dimensional normed spaces, and let \(\bar y=f(\bar x)\). Set \[\alpha:=\inf_{\|u\|=1}\|df(\bar x)(u)\|.\] Then \[\operatorname{subreg}_{s}f(\bar x\mid\bar y)=\alpha^{-1},\] with \(1/0=+\infty\). Thus strong metric subregularity holds exactly when \(\alpha>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exact strong-subregularity modulus is the reciprocal of the least semiderivative norm over unit directions.
assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to Y\) is Hadamard semidifferentiable at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{subreg}_{s}f(\bar x\mid f(\bar x))=(\inf_{\|u\|=1}\|df(\bar x)(u)\|)^{-1}\).

assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are normed spaces and \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\).
The strict graphical derivative is defined through tangents generated uniformly by pairs of graph points converging to \((\bar x,\bar y)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A uniform bounded right-inverse condition for the strict graphical derivative is the strict primal criterion for metric regularity.

notation.meaning: Strict graphical derivative of F at the reference graph point

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict graphical-derivative right-inverse criterion; exact variant requires source confirmation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The strict graphical-derivative criterion with bound \(\kappa>0\) is
\[
\forall v\in Y\quad\exists u\in X:\qquad v\in D_{*}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)(u),\qquad \|u\|\le\kappa\|v\|.
\]
Here strictness requires the underlying difference quotients to remain valid uniformly as both base graph points approach \((\bar x,\bar y)\), rather than only along arcs based at that point. Under the appropriate local closedness and compactness hypotheses, this bounded right-inverse condition yields linear openness at every rate below \(1/\kappa\), hence metric regularity. The precise converse and the choice among strict contingent derivative variants depend on the adopted definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict graphical criteria require uniformly solvable range directions while nearby graph base points move; this stronger control supports metric regularity rather than only isolated behavior.
knowledge_statements.title: Strict Graphical-Derivative Criteria

assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to Y\) maps normed spaces and \(\bar x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Hadamard semidifferentiability is point-based, whereas strict differentiability is uniform over pairs of nearby base points.

source_refs.locator: 3.2.4 Graphical Regularity of Lipschitzian Mappings p. 327

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The point-based Hadamard regime requires, for every \(u\in X\),
\[
\frac{f(\bar x+t u')-f(\bar x)}{t}\to df(\bar x)(u)
\quad\text{whenever }t\downarrow0,\ u'\to u.
\]
The strict first-order regime requires a bounded linear operator \(A:X\to Y\) such that
\[
\frac{\|f(x)-f(x')-A(x-x')\|}{\|x-x'\|}\to0
\]
as distinct \(x,x'\to\bar x\). Strict differentiability implies Hadamard semidifferentiability with \(df(\bar x)(u)=Au\), but the converse generally fails because the first limit keeps one base point fixed while the second moves both base points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Semidifferentiability approximates directions from one fixed point; strict differentiability controls differences uniformly between every pair of nearby points.
knowledge_statements.title: Directional Approximation Regimes

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Structure of a Lipschitz Hadamard Semiderivative
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic homogeneity and continuity of the point-based directional model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(u,v\in X\) and \(\lambda\geq0\),
\[
df(\bar x)(\lambda u)=\lambda df(\bar x)(u),
\qquad
\|df(\bar x)(u)-df(\bar x)(v)\|\leq L\|u-v\|.
\]
Thus the semiderivative is continuous and positively homogeneous, but it need not be linear.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Hadamard semiderivative of a locally Lipschitz map is positively homogeneous and Lipschitz continuous, although it may be nonlinear.
assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to Y\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\) with constant \(L\).
\(f\) is Hadamard semidifferentiable at \(\bar x\) in every direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(df(\bar x)\) is positively homogeneous and \(L\)-Lipschitz on \(X\).

notation.meaning: Hadamard semiderivative at the fixed base point

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Absolute value separates semiderivative subregularity from strict regularity criteria.

source_refs.locator: 3.2.4 Graphical Regularity of Lipschitzian Mappings p. 327

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f(x)=|x|\), the Hadamard semiderivative at zero is
\[
df(0)(u)=|u|,
\]
so \(|df(0)(u)|=|u|\) and \(f\) is strongly metrically subregular at \((0,0)\). However, \(f\) is not strictly differentiable at zero: difference quotients from the positive and negative sides would require incompatible linear derivatives. Moreover, \(f\) is not metrically regular at \((0,0)\), since \(f^{-1}(y)=\varnothing\) for every \(y<0\). Thus a nondegenerate point-based semiderivative can certify isolated solution behavior without supplying the moving-base uniformity needed for full regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Absolute value has a nondegenerate semiderivative and is strongly subregular at zero, yet it is neither strictly differentiable nor metrically regular there.
knowledge_statements.title: Strictness Gap

children.title: Finite-Dimensional Mordukhovich Criterion
children.top_down_role: The exact limiting-coderivative criterion in finite dimensions.

assumptions_latex: \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) has locally closed graph at \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Metric regularity is equivalent to \(\ker D^{*}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact finite-dimensional limiting-coderivative criterion for metric regularity.

source_refs.locator: 4.2.2 Pointbased Characterizations of Covering and Metric Regularity p. 394
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the limiting coderivative by
\[
D^{*}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)(y^{*})=\{x^{*}\mid(x^{*},-y^{*})\in N_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)\}.
\]
Then \(F\) is metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) if and only if
\[
\ker D^{*}F(\bar x\mid\bar y):=\{y^{*}\mid0\in D^{*}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)(y^{*})\}=\{0\}.
\]
Equivalently, no nonzero range covector \(y^{*}\) produces the zero domain covector through the limiting normal cone to the graph. This equivalence uses finite dimensionality; infinite-dimensional versions require additional geometric hypotheses or modified coderivatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions, metric regularity holds exactly when the limiting coderivative has no nonzero range covector mapped to the zero domain covector.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Dimensional Mordukhovich Criterion

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each \(y^*\in Y^*\), the normal limiting coderivative of \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) is
\[
D_N^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*):=\{x^*\in X^*:(x^*,-y^*)\in N_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)\}.
\]
Here \(N_{\operatorname{gph}F}\) is the limiting normal cone obtained from weak-star limits of nearby Fréchet normals in the dual product space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The normal coderivative consists of dual pairs whose signed product belongs to the limiting normal cone of the graph.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The inclusion
\[
D_M^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(0)\subset D_N^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(0)

gives the implication
\[
D_N^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(0)=\{0\}\ \Longrightarrow\ D_M^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(0)=\{0\}.
\]
Thus a normal-coderivative zero-kernel test is formally stronger. Equivalence follows whenever the two coderivatives agree at \(0\); without such an agreement condition, the reverse implication is not justified by inclusion alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A trivial normal-coderivative kernel is stronger than a trivial mixed-coderivative kernel; equivalence needs an additional coincidence condition.
knowledge_statements.title: Criterion Sharpness Comparison

children.title: Coderivative Equivalence Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Settings where the alternative dual constructions cease to yield interchangeable criteria.

assumptions_latex: The relevant nearby Fréchet-normal sequences are bounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Equivalence holds when weak-star convergence of output covectors can be upgraded to norm convergence; otherwise only inclusion is assured.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topological boundary separating equality from strict inclusion.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Equality \(D_M^*F(\bar x,\bar y)=D_N^*F(\bar x,\bar y)\) is ensured when every bounded output-dual sequence used in the normal construction has a norm-convergent subsequence with the same limit, as in finite-dimensional \(Y\). The equivalence mechanism fails in infinite-dimensional duals admitting bounded sequences \(y_k^*\overset{w^*}{\longrightarrow}y^*\) with no norm-convergent subsequence. Such sequences may enter \(D_N^*F\) but are excluded from the defining limits of \(D_M^*F\), so only \(D_M^*F\subset D_N^*F\) remains automatic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Normal and mixed coderivatives coincide under output-dual norm compactness; weak-star-only convergence is the mechanism permitting strict inclusion.

assumptions_latex: \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) has locally closed graph near \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{reg}F(\bar x,\bar y)=1/c\), using \(1/0=+\infty\) and \(1/(+\infty)=0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[
c:=\lim_{\delta\downarrow0}\inf\{\|x^*\|:(x,y)\in\operatorname{gph}F,\ \|x-\bar x\|<\delta,\ \|y-\bar y\|<\delta,\ y^*\in Y^*,\ \|y^*\|=1,\ x^*\in\widehat D^*F(x,y)(y^*)\}.
\]
With the convention \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\), the exact metric-regularity modulus satisfies
\[
\operatorname{reg}F(\bar x,\bar y)=c^{-1},
\]
where \(1/0=+\infty\) and \(1/(+\infty)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exact regularity modulus is the reciprocal of the limiting lower norm of nearby normalized Fréchet coderivatives.

children.title: Strong-Slope Criteria
children.top_down_role: Local primal slope tests for regularity and residual bounds.

assumptions_latex: \((X,d_X)\) is a complete metric space, \((Y,d_Y)\) is a metric space, and \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\).
\((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\), and for every nearby \(y\), the residual \(\varphi_y(x):=\operatorname{dist}(y,F(x))\) is lower semicontinuous on the relevant neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A uniform lower bound on \(|\nabla\varphi_y|\) yields metric regularity with modulus at most \(1/\tau\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform local residual-slope sufficient criterion.

source_refs.locator: 4.1.2 Neighborhood Characterizations of Metric Regularity and Lipschitzian Behavior p. 382
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(y\in Y\), define \(\varphi_y:X\to[0,+\infty]\) by \(\varphi_y(x):=\operatorname{dist}(y,F(x))\). Assume that some \(\tau>0\) satisfies
\[
|\nabla\varphi_y|(x):=\limsup_{u\to x,\,u\ne x}\frac{[\varphi_y(x)-\varphi_y(u)]_+}{d_X(x,u)}\ge\tau
\]
for all nearby \((x,y)\) for which \(0<\varphi_y(x)\) is sufficiently small. Then, after shrinking the neighborhoods,
\[
\operatorname{dist}(x,F^{-1}(y))\le\tau^{-1}\operatorname{dist}(y,F(x)).
\]
Consequently, \(F\) is metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) with modulus at most \(\tau^{-1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A uniform positive strong slope of the residual implies a local error bound and hence metric regularity.
knowledge_statements.title: Strong-Slope Criteria

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1.2 Neighborhood Characterizations of Metric Regularity and Lipschitzian Behavior p. 382
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong-Slope Separation Is Not Necessary for an Error Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary showing that the uniform strong-slope condition is sufficient but not generally necessary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(f:\mathbb R\to[0,+\infty)\) by \(f(0)=0\) and
\[
f(x)=|x|\bigl(2+\sin(1/|x|)\bigr)\quad(x\ne0).
\]
Then \(f^{-1}(0)=\{0\}\) and
\[
|x|\leq f(x)
\]
for every \(x\). Nevertheless, there are differentiability points \(x_n\to0\), \(x_n\ne0\), at which \(f'(x_n)=0\), and hence \(|\nabla f|(x_n)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An oscillatory continuous residual has a global error bound although its strong slope vanishes at infeasible points approaching the zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{dist}(x,f^{-1}(0))\leq f(x)\text{ globally, while }\inf_{0<|x|<\delta}|\nabla f|(x)=0\text{ for every }\delta>0.
knowledge_statements.title: Strong-Slope Separation Is Not Necessary for an Error Bound

children.title: Nonlocal-Slope Criteria
children.top_down_role: Slope criteria adapted to semilocal and global estimates.

assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to[0,+\infty]\) is lower semicontinuous and its zero set \(S:=\{u\in X:f(u)=0\}\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(|\nabla f|^{\diamond}(x)\ge\tau\) for every \(x\in X\setminus S\) with \(f(x)<+\infty\), then \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le f(x)/\tau\) for every \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global nonlocal-slope error-bound criterion underlying semilocal regularity estimates.

source_refs.locator: 4.1 Neighborhood Criteria and Exact Bounds p. 378
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(x\in X\) with \(f(x)<+\infty\), define
\[
|\nabla f|^{\diamond}(x):=\sup_{u\in X,\,u\ne x}\frac{[f(x)-f(u)]_+}{d(x,u)}.
\]
If a constant \(\tau>0\) satisfies \(|\nabla f|^{\diamond}(x)\ge\tau\) for every \(x\in X\setminus S\) with \(f(x)<+\infty\), then
\[
\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le\frac{f(x)}{\tau}
\]
for every \(x\in X\), with the inequality interpreted in the extended-real sense when \(f(x)=+\infty\). Applied uniformly to residual functions \(f=\varphi_y\), this yields the corresponding semilocal regularity estimates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A global positive nonlocal-slope bound gives an error bound; uniform application to residual functions yields semilocal regularity estimates.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonlocal-Slope Criteria

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1 Neighborhood Criteria and Exact Bounds p. 378
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise comparison between global and local descent measures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\),
\[
|\nabla f|(x)\leq |\nabla f|^{\diamond}(x).
\]
The inequality can be strict.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The nonlocal slope is at least the strong slope and may be strictly larger.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |\nabla f|(x)\leq|\nabla f|^{\diamond}(x).
knowledge_statements.title: Nonlocal Slope Dominates Strong Slope

children.title: Subdifferential Slope Criteria
children.top_down_role: Dualized slope tests for Banach and Asplund settings.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correct inequality direction and boundary of direct pointwise dualization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is finite at \(x\), then
\[
|\nabla f|(x)\leq\operatorname{dist}\bigl(0,\widehat\partial f(x)\bigr),
\]
with \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\varnothing)=+\infty\). Consequently, a pointwise positive lower bound on Fréchet-subgradient norms does not, through this inequality alone, imply a positive strong-slope bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fréchet-subgradient distance bounds the strong slope from above, so pointwise subgradient separation alone cannot be transferred to the primal slope theorem by reversing this inequality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |\nabla f|(x)\leq\operatorname{dist}(0,\widehat\partial f(x)).
knowledge_statements.title: Pointwise Strong-Slope and Fréchet-Subgradient Relation

assumptions_latex: Each nearby residual \(\varphi_y(x):=\operatorname{dist}(y,F(x))\) is lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A uniform positive lower bound on Fréchet subgradient norms implies the corresponding strong-slope regularity estimate.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual sufficient condition obtained from Fréchet subgradient norms.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A subdifferential slope condition with constant \(\tau>0\) is
\[
\inf\{\|x^*\|:x^*\in\widehat\partial\varphi_y(x)\}\ge\tau
\]
for every nearby \((x,y)\) satisfying \(0<\varphi_y(x)\) sufficiently small, with \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\). Since
\[
|\nabla\varphi_y|(x)\ge\operatorname{dist}(0,\widehat\partial\varphi_y(x)),
\]
this condition implies the strong-slope bound and therefore the associated local error bound and metric-regularity estimate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniformly positive Fréchet-subgradient norms imply the strong-slope condition and its metric-regularity estimate.
knowledge_statements.title: Subdifferential Slope Criteria

children.title: Ekeland Variational Route
children.top_down_role: Variational-principle derivations of regularity and error-bound criteria.

assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and bounded below.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Ekeland's principle converts failure of an error bound into a nearby point with slope below the proposed bound.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ekeland-based contradiction route from slope bounds to error bounds.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.1 Ekeland Variational Principle p. 204
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(f(x_0)\le\inf f+\varepsilon\) and \(\lambda>0\), then there exists \(x_\varepsilon\) with \(d(x_\varepsilon,x_0)\le\lambda\), \(f(x_\varepsilon)\le f(x_0)\), and
\[
f(x_\varepsilon)<f(x)+\frac{\varepsilon}{\lambda}d(x,x_\varepsilon)
\]
for every \(x\ne x_\varepsilon\). Hence \(|\nabla f|(x_\varepsilon)\le\varepsilon/\lambda\). Applied to a residual function, a hypothesized failure of its error bound produces a point contradicting any uniform slope lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ekeland's principle turns a failed residual error bound into a nearby point of small slope, enabling regularity proofs by contradiction.
knowledge_statements.title: Ekeland Variational Route

children.title: Sum Mappings
children.top_down_role: Transfer of regularity properties under additive mapping constructions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact additive rule for a constant single-valued summand.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) be metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\), where \(Y\) is a normed space, and let \(c\in Y\). For \((F+c)(x):=F(x)+c\),
\[\operatorname{reg}(F+c)(\bar x\mid\bar y+c)=\operatorname{reg}F(\bar x\mid\bar y).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding a constant translates the graph and preserves the exact metric-regularity modulus.
assumptions_latex: \(Y\) is a normed space and \(c\in Y\).
\(F\) is metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F+c\) is metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y+c)\) with the same exact modulus.

notation.meaning: constant translate of the values of F

knowledge_statements.title: Translation Invariance of Metric Regularity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient Banach-space formulation of the Lyusternik–Graves perturbation principle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X,Y\) be Banach spaces, let \(\operatorname{gph}F\) be locally closed near \((\bar x,\bar y)\), and suppose \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) has a local metric-regularity estimate with constant \(\kappa\). If \(g:X\to Y\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\) with constant \(L\) and \(\kappa L<1\), then \(F+g\) is metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y+g(\bar x))\), with
\[\operatorname{reg}(F+g)(\bar x\mid\bar y+g(\bar x))\le\frac{\kappa}{1-\kappa L}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sufficiently small Lipschitz perturbation preserves metric regularity, with an explicit degraded modulus.
assumptions_latex: \(\operatorname{gph}F\) is locally closed near the reference graph point.
\(F\) admits regularity constant \(\kappa\), \(g\) admits local Lipschitz constant \(L\), and \(\kappa L<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F+g\) is metrically regular with modulus at most \(\kappa/(1-\kappa L)\).

notation.meaning: local Lipschitz constant of the perturbation

knowledge_statements.title: Small-Lipschitz Additive Perturbation Theorem

assumptions_latex: \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) is metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) with modulus \(\kappa\).
\(g:X\to Y\) is Lipschitz near \(\bar x\) with constant \(L\), and \(\kappa L<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F+g\) is metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y+g(\bar x))\) with modulus at most \(\kappa/(1-\kappa L)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lipschitz perturbation rule for a regular set-valued mapping.

source_refs.locator: 1.2.3 Metric Regularity and Covering p. 56

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \((F+g)(x):=\{y+g(x):y\in F(x)\}\). If \(F\) is metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) with modulus bounded by \(\kappa\), while \(g\) is locally Lipschitz at \(\bar x\) with constant \(L\) satisfying \(\kappa L<1\), then \(F+g\) is metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y+g(\bar x))\). Its regularity modulus admits the estimate
\[
\operatorname{reg}(F+g)(\bar x,\bar y+g(\bar x))\le\frac{\kappa}{1-\kappa L}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding a Lipschitz perturbation preserves metric regularity when its Lipschitz constant is smaller than the reciprocal regularity modulus.
knowledge_statements.title: Sum Mappings

children.title: Product Mappings
children.top_down_role: Transfer of regularity properties under Cartesian or componentwise product constructions.

assumptions_latex: \(F_i:X_i\rightrightarrows Y_i\) has locally closed graph near \((\bar x_i,\bar y_i)\), for \(i=1,2\).\)
The product spaces carry maximum metrics.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{reg}(F_1\times F_2)((\bar x_1,\bar x_2)\mid(\bar y_1,\bar y_2))=\max_{i=1,2}\operatorname{reg}F_i(\bar x_i\mid\bar y_i).\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independent Cartesian products under maximum product metrics.

source_refs.locator: 4.1.2 Neighborhood Characterizations of Metric Regularity and Lipschitzian Behavior p. 382
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \((F_1\times F_2)(x_1,x_2):=F_1(x_1)\times F_2(x_2)\). Then \(F_1\times F_2\) is metrically regular at \(((\bar x_1,\bar x_2),(\bar y_1,\bar y_2))\) if and only if each \(F_i\) is metrically regular at \((\bar x_i,\bar y_i)\). With maximum product metrics, the exact modulus satisfies \[\operatorname{reg}(F_1\times F_2)((\bar x_1,\bar x_2)\mid(\bar y_1,\bar y_2))=\max_{i=1,2}\operatorname{reg}F_i(\bar x_i\mid\bar y_i).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An independent product mapping is metrically regular exactly when every component is; under maximum metrics its exact modulus is the largest component modulus.
knowledge_statements.title: Product Mappings

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1.2 Neighborhood Characterizations of Metric Regularity and Lipschitzian Behavior p. 382

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite independent products under maximum product metrics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(i=1,\ldots,m\), let \(F_i:X_i\rightrightarrows Y_i\) be metrically subregular at \((\bar x_i,\bar y_i)\). Under maximum product metrics, \(F=\prod_iF_i\) is metrically subregular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) if and only if every \(F_i\) is, and
\[\operatorname{subreg}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)=\max_i\operatorname{subreg}F_i(\bar x_i\mid\bar y_i).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite independent products preserve metric subregularity, with exact maximum modulus under maximum metrics.
assumptions_latex: The product is finite and independent: \(F(x_1,\ldots,x_m)=\prod_iF_i(x_i)\).
The domain and codomain products use maximum metrics.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{subreg}(\prod_iF_i)=\max_i\operatorname{subreg}F_i\) at the product reference point.
knowledge_statements.title: Subregularity of Independent Products

assumptions_latex: \(F,G:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^q\) have locally closed graphs near \((\bar x,\bar y_F)\) and \((\bar x,\bar y_G)\), respectively.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[D^*F(\bar x\mid\bar y_F)(0)\cap\bigl[-D^*G(\bar x\mid\bar y_G)(0)\bigr]=\{0\}.\]

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the fixed decomposition \(\bar y=\bar y_F+\bar y_G\), the basic finite-dimensional abnormal-multiplier qualification is \[D^*F(\bar x\mid\bar y_F)(0)\cap\bigl[-D^*G(\bar x\mid\bar y_G)(0)\bigr]=\{0\}.\] A coderivative sum rule additionally requires the applicable hypotheses controlling nearby decompositions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compactness qualification retaining locally relevant decompositions in limiting coderivative sum calculus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(S(x,y):=\{(u,v)\in F(x)\times G(x):u+v=y\}\). The decomposition mapping is inner semicompact at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) relative to \(\operatorname{gph}(F+G)\) if every sequence \((x_k,y_k)\to(\bar x,\bar y)\), with \(y_k\in F(x_k)+G(x_k)\), admits decompositions \((u_k,v_k)\in S(x_k,y_k)\) having a subsequence converging to an element of \(S(\bar x,\bar y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nearby convergent sum-graph sequence must admit decompositions with a subsequence converging to a reference decomposition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\) retains a convergent subsequence of decompositions along every sequence in \(\operatorname{gph}(F+G)\) approaching \((\bar x,\bar y)\).

notation.meaning: mapping of additive decompositions of y at x

knowledge_statements.title: Inner-Semicompact Decomposition Qualification

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Automatic Qualification for a Lipschitz Summand
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Automatic no-abnormal-cancellation and decomposition-compactness regime for a single-valued Lipschitz perturbation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(g:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^q\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\), then \(D^*g(\bar x)(0)=\{0\}\). Hence \[D^*F(\bar x\mid\bar y_F)(0)\cap[-D^*g(\bar x)(0)]=\{0\}.\] Moreover, each \(y\in(F+g)(x)\) has the unique decomposition \((y-g(x),g(x))\), and continuity of \(g\) makes the decomposition mapping inner semicompact locally.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A locally Lipschitz single-valued summand makes the abnormal-multiplier test automatic, and its unique continuous decomposition supplies the required compactness.
assumptions_latex: \(g:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^q\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D^*F(\bar x\mid\bar y_F)(0)\cap[-D^*g(\bar x)(0)]=\{0\}\), and the additive decomposition mapping is locally inner semicompact.
knowledge_statements.title: Automatic Qualification for a Lipschitz Summand

children.title: Componentwise Product Control
children.top_down_role: Relationships between component regularity and regularity of the product mapping.

assumptions_latex: For \(i=1,\ldots,m\), \(X_i\) and \(Y_i\) are metric spaces and \(F_i:X_i\rightrightarrows Y_i\) satisfies a metric-regularity estimate near \((\bar x_i,\bar y_i)\) with constant \(\kappa_i>0\).
The finite product spaces \(X:=\prod_{i=1}^mX_i\) and \(Y:=\prod_{i=1}^mY_i\) carry their maximum product metrics.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[d_X\bigl(x,F^{-1}(y)\bigr)\le \left(\max_{1\le i\le m}\kappa_i\right)d_Y\bigl(y,F(x)\bigr)\] for all \((x,y)\) sufficiently near \((\bar x,\bar y)\).

notation.meaning: distances induced by the maximum product metrics

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative local componentwise control for finite independent products.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:=\prod_{i=1}^mF_i\), \(\bar x:=(\bar x_i)_{i=1}^m\), and \(\bar y:=(\bar y_i)_{i=1}^m\). For all \((x,y)\) sufficiently near \((\bar x,\bar y)\), \[d_X\bigl(x,F^{-1}(y)\bigr)\le \left(\max_{1\le i\le m}\kappa_i\right)d_Y\bigl(y,F(x)\bigr).\] Thus the maximum component constant is an admissible local regularity constant for the product mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite independent product with maximum metrics, the largest component regularity constant is an admissible local regularity constant for the product.
knowledge_statements.title: Componentwise Product Control

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite Product Control for Matching Ell-p Metrics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Admissible componentwise regularity bound for finite independent products with matching product metrics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(1\le p<\infty\), let \(F_i:X_i\rightrightarrows Y_i\) be metrically regular near \((\bar x_i,\bar y_i)\) with constants \(\kappa_i\), and equip \(X=\prod_{i=1}^mX_i\) and \(Y=\prod_{i=1}^mY_i\) with the corresponding \(\ell^p\) product metrics. For \(F=\prod_{i=1}^mF_i\),
\[d_X(x,F^{-1}(y))\le\bigl(\max_i\kappa_i\bigr)d_Y(y,F(x))\]
locally at \((\bar x,\bar y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With matching finite ell-p product metrics, the largest component regularity constant controls the independent product.
assumptions_latex: Each component estimate holds on a neighborhood of its reference graph point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max_i\kappa_i\) is an admissible local regularity constant for \(\prod_iF_i\).
knowledge_statements.title: Finite Product Control for Matching Ell-p Metrics

children.title: Coupling Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Loss of regularity caused by incompatible summands or interacting product components.

assumptions_latex: The domain is \(\mathbb R\), each component codomain is \(\mathbb R\), and the joint codomain is \(\mathbb R^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[F_1\text{ and }F_2\text{ are metrically regular at }(0,0),\quad F\text{ is not metrically regular at }(0,(0,0)).\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counterexample showing that shared-variable coupling can destroy joint metric regularity.

source_refs.locator: 1.2.3 Metric Regularity and Covering p. 56
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F_1(x):=x\), \(F_2(x):=x\), and \(F(x):=(F_1(x),F_2(x))=(x,x)\). Each \(F_i\) is metrically regular at \((0,0)\) with exact modulus \(1\), whereas \(F\) is not metrically regular at \((0,(0,0))\). Its range is the diagonal \(\{(t,t):t\in\mathbb R\}\subset\mathbb R^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The two identity components are metrically regular, but their shared-variable diagonal mapping is not metrically regular as a map into the plane.
knowledge_statements.title: Coupling Failure Boundaries

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cancellation Can Destroy Regularity of a Sum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp additive-coupling boundary for individually regular scalar summands.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(F_1(x)=x\) and \(F_2(x)=-x\) on \(\mathbb R\). Each \(F_i\) is metrically regular at \((0,0)\) with exact modulus \(1\), but
\[(F_1+F_2)(x)=0\]
is not metrically regular at \((0,0)\), since \((F_1+F_2)^{-1}(y)=\varnothing\) for every \(y\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two individually regular summands can cancel, producing a constant mapping that is not metrically regular.
assumptions_latex: The domain and codomain are \(\mathbb R\) with the usual metric.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Metric regularity of both summands does not imply metric regularity of their pointwise sum.

children.title: Composition Calculus
children.top_down_role: Regularity transfer through chained single-valued or set-valued mappings.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) and \(g:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^p\) are continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\) and \(f(\bar x)\), respectively.
\(Df(\bar x):\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) and \(Dg(f(\bar x)):\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^p\) are surjective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g\circ f\) is metrically regular at \((\bar x,g(f(\bar x)))\).

notation.meaning: Fréchet derivative of the inner map
Fréchet derivative of the outer map

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient smooth finite-dimensional composition rule based on surjectivity of both component derivatives.

source_refs.locator: 4.2.2 Pointbased Characterizations of Covering and Metric Regularity p. 394

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h:=g\circ f\). If \(Df(\bar x)\) and \(Dg(f(\bar x))\) are surjective, then \(h\) is metrically regular at \((\bar x,h(\bar x))\). Equivalently, \(h^{-1}\) has the Aubin property at \((h(\bar x),\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A composition of continuously differentiable finite-dimensional maps is metrically regular when both component derivatives at the reference points are surjective.
knowledge_statements.title: Composition Calculus

source_witnesses.locator: 4.2.2 Pointbased Characterizations of Covering and Metric Regularity p. 394
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of the componentwise sufficient condition in the smooth composition rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^2\) and \(g:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R\) be \(f(x)=(x,0)\) and \(g(u,v)=u\). Then \(Df(0):\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^2\) is not surjective, while \((g\circ f)(x)=x\) and \(D(g\circ f)(0)=1\). Thus \(g\circ f\) is metrically regular although the inner component derivative is not surjective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An embedding followed by its matching projection composes to the identity, so regularity of the composition does not require every component derivative to be surjective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g\circ f=\operatorname{id}_{\mathbb R}\) is metrically regular, but \(Df(0)\) is not surjective.
knowledge_statements.title: Component Surjectivity Is Not Necessary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient first-order criterion for metric regularity of a smooth finite-dimensional composition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h:=g\circ f\), where \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) and \(g:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^p\) are continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\) and \(f(\bar x)\). Then \(h\) is metrically regular at \((\bar x,h(\bar x))\) if and only if \[Dh(\bar x)=Dg(f(\bar x))Df(\bar x):\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^p\] is surjective. Equivalently, \[\ker\bigl(Dh(\bar x)^*\bigr)=\{0\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth finite-dimensional composition is metrically regular exactly when its product derivative is surjective, equivalently when the adjoint product has trivial kernel.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) and \(g:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^p\) are continuously differentiable near the reference points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g\circ f\) is metrically regular at \((\bar x,g(f(\bar x)))\) if and only if \(Dg(f(\bar x))Df(\bar x)\) is surjective.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Smooth Composition Criterion

children.title: Inverse-Image Calculus
children.top_down_role: Regularity transfer to constraint preimages under a mapping.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are metric spaces, \(f:X\to Y\) is continuous at \(\bar x\), and \(\bar y:=f(\bar x)\).
There are neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(V\) of \(\bar y\) such that \(d_X(x,f^{-1}(y))\le\kappa d_Y(y,f(x))\) for every \((x,y)\in U\times V\).
\(S\subset Y\) is closed near \(\bar y\) and \(\bar y\in S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[d_X\bigl(x,f^{-1}(S)\bigr)\le\kappa d_Y\bigl(f(x),S\bigr)\] for every \(x\) in a sufficiently small neighborhood of \(\bar x\).

notation.meaning: inverse image of the target set
distances in the domain and codomain
distance from a point to a set in the indicated metric

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the stated local metric-regularity estimate and continuity of \(f\) at \(\bar x\), there is a neighborhood \(U'\) of \(\bar x\) such that \[d_X\bigl(x,f^{-1}(S)\bigr)\le\kappa d_Y\bigl(f(x),S\bigr)\qquad\text{for every }x\in U'.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local metric-regularity estimate for a continuous mapping yields a local error bound for the inverse image of a closed target set containing the reference value.

\(G:\mathbb R^m\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^p\) has locally closed graph near \((f(\bar x),\bar z)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[D^*G(f(\bar x)\mid\bar z)(0)\cap\ker Df(\bar x)^*=\{0\}.\]

adjoint derivative of the inner mapping

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The finite-dimensional composition qualification at \((\bar x,\bar z)\) is \[D^*G(f(\bar x)\mid\bar z)(0)\cap\ker Df(\bar x)^*=\{0\}.\] Under this condition, the limiting-coderivative chain-rule inclusion is \[D^*(G\circ f)(\bar x\mid\bar z)(z^*)\subset Df(\bar x)^*D^*G(f(\bar x)\mid\bar z)(z^*)\qquad\text{for every }z^*\in\mathbb R^p.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions, the composition qualification excludes every nonzero zero-direction outer coderivative multiplier annihilated by the adjoint derivative, and it yields the limiting-coderivative chain-rule inclusion.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\).\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{f^{-1}(C)}(\bar x)\subset Df(\bar x)^*N_C(f(\bar x)).\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limiting-normal geometry of a smooth constraint preimage.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M:=f^{-1}(C)\). Under the stated normal qualification, every limiting normal to the preimage admits an outer-normal multiplier representation: \[N_M(\bar x)\subset Df(\bar x)^*N_C(f(\bar x)).\] Thus, for each \(x^*\in N_M(\bar x)\), there exists \(y^*\in N_C(f(\bar x))\) such that \(x^*=Df(\bar x)^*y^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the normal qualification, every limiting normal to a smooth preimage is the adjoint derivative applied to a normal of the target set.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tangent Cone to a Smooth Preimage under an Error Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Contingent-tangent geometry of a smooth finite-dimensional constraint preimage under a local constraint error bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M:=f^{-1}(C)\), where \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\in M\) and \(C\subset\mathbb R^m\) is closed near \(f(\bar x)\). If \[d(x,M)\leq\kappa d(f(x),C)\] locally at \(\bar x\), then \[T_M(\bar x)=\{u\in\mathbb R^n:Df(\bar x)u\in T_C(f(\bar x))\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under a local constraint error bound, the contingent tangent cone to a smooth preimage is exactly the derivative preimage of the target tangent cone.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\).
\(C\subset\mathbb R^m\) is closed near \(f(\bar x)\), and \(\bar x\in f^{-1}(C)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[T_{f^{-1}(C)}(\bar x)=\{u:Df(\bar x)u\in T_C(f(\bar x))\}.\]

notation.meaning: contingent tangent cone to C at y

knowledge_statements.title: Tangent Cone to a Smooth Preimage under an Error Bound

children.title: Chain-Rule Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Configurations where intermediate mapping behavior obstructs regularity transfer.

notation.meaning: derivative of the inner mapping at zero

source_refs.locator: 3.3 SNC Calculus for Sets and Mappings p. 341

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x):=x^2\), \(C:=\{0\}\), and \(\bar x:=0\), \[f^{-1}(C)=\{0\},\qquad N_{f^{-1}(C)}(0)=\mathbb R,\qquad Df(0)^*N_C(0)=\{0\}.\] Consequently, \[N_{f^{-1}(C)}(0)\not\subset Df(0)^*N_C(0),\] and the qualification \(N_C(0)\cap\ker Df(0)^*=\{0\}\) fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the squared mapping and the zero target, the preimage normal cone is the whole line while the adjoint-derivative image of the target normal cone is zero, so the normal-chain inclusion fails.
knowledge_statements.title: Chain-Rule Failure Boundaries

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3 SNC Calculus for Sets and Mappings p. 341

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Qualification Failure Need Not Force Chain-Rule Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary showing that the normal qualification is sufficient for the general rule but not necessary for every individual preimage.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be the constant map \(f(x)=0\), let \(C=\{0\}\), and take \(\bar x=0\). Then \(f^{-1}(C)=\mathbb R\), so \[N_{f^{-1}(C)}(0)=\{0\}=Df(0)^*N_C(0).\] Nevertheless, \(N_C(0)=\mathbb R\) and \(\ker Df(0)^*=\mathbb R\), hence \[N_C(0)\cap\ker Df(0)^*=\mathbb R\ne\{0\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a constant map into a singleton target, the qualification fails maximally although the preimage normal formula still holds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The qualification fails, but \(N_{f^{-1}(C)}(0)=Df(0)^*N_C(0)=\{0\}\).

children.title: Intersection Regularity
children.top_down_role: Regularity properties of families of sets near a common point.

assumptions_latex: \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\) are closed subsets of a normed space \(X\).\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d(x,\bigcap_i(C_i-z_i))\le\kappa\max_i d(x,C_i-z_i)\) locally and uniformly for small \(z_i\).\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform local regularity under independent translations of sets.

source_refs.locator: 5.4.1 Linear Subextremality of Set Systems p. 110
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The collection \(\{C_1,\ldots,C_m\}\) is locally intersection regular at \(\bar x\) if there exist \(\kappa>0\) and neighborhoods of \(\bar x\) and the zero translation such that, for every nearby \(x\) and all sufficiently small \(z_i\), \[d\left(x,\bigcap_{i=1}^m(C_i-z_i)\right)\le\kappa\max_{1\le i\le m}d(x,C_i-z_i),\] whenever the translated intersection is locally nonempty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Intersection regularity is a uniform local error bound that remains valid under sufficiently small independent translations of all sets.
knowledge_statements.title: Intersection Regularity

source_witnesses.locator: 5.4.1 Linear Subextremality of Set Systems p. 110
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed definition is a uniform translated error-bound property, but the cited locator concerns linear subextremality and does not clearly establish that this is the intended local meaning of “Intersection Regularity.” The clause “whenever the translated intersection is locally nonempty” is also not formally localized. A source specifically defining the translated intersection property is required before choosing the mathematical version.

children.title: Transversality
children.top_down_role: Geometric compatibility of sets or mappings supporting stable intersections.

assumptions_latex: \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\subset\mathbb R^n\) are closed near \(\bar x\in\bigcap_i C_i\).\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v_i\in N_{C_i}(\bar x),\ \sum_i v_i=0\Longrightarrow v_1=\cdots=v_m=0.\)

notation.meaning: limiting normal cone to the ith set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional normal-cone transversality for a set system.

source_refs.locator: 5.3.3 Extremal Principle for Set-Valued Mappings p. 83
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The sets are transversal at \(\bar x\) in the limiting-normal sense if \[v_i\in N_{C_i}(\bar x)\ \text{for all }i,\qquad \sum_{i=1}^m v_i=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad v_1=\cdots=v_m=0.\] Equivalently, the individual limiting normal cones admit no nontrivial balanced collection of normals at the common point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Transversality excludes any nonzero collection of limiting normals to the sets that balances to zero at their common point.
knowledge_statements.title: Transversality

source_witnesses.locator: 5.3.3 Extremal Principle for Set-Valued Mappings p. 83
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional quantitative form of normal-cone transversality for a finite set system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For closed sets \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\subset\mathbb R^n\) and \(\bar x\in\bigcap_iC_i\), the limiting-normal transversality condition is equivalent to the existence of \(\alpha>0\) such that \[\left\|\sum_{i=1}^m v_i\right\|\geq\alpha\sum_{i=1}^m\|v_i\|\qquad\text{for all }v_i\in N_{C_i}(\bar x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions, absence of a nontrivial balanced collection of normals is equivalent to a positive uniform separation between the norm of their sum and the sum of their norms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Transversality holds if and only if there is \(\alpha>0\) such that \(\|\sum_i v_i\|\geq\alpha\sum_i\|v_i\|\) for every \(v_i\in N_{C_i}(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Quantitative Normal Separation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent tangent-space formulation for two embedded smooth manifolds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M_1,M_2\subset\mathbb R^n\) be embedded \(C^1\) submanifolds and \(\bar x\in M_1\cap M_2\). Then \[N_{M_1}(\bar x)\cap[-N_{M_2}(\bar x)]=\{0\}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad T_{M_1}(\bar x)+T_{M_2}(\bar x)=\mathbb R^n.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For two smooth manifolds, normal transversality is equivalent to their tangent spaces spanning the ambient space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[N_{M_1}(\bar x)\cap[-N_{M_2}(\bar x)]=\{0\}\iff T_{M_1}(\bar x)+T_{M_2}(\bar x)=\mathbb R^n.\]

notation.meaning: tangent space to M at x
normal space to M at x
