children.title: Linear Regularity
children.top_down_role: Distance control for feasibility systems formed from multiple sets.

assumptions_latex: \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\) are closed subsets of a normed space \(X\).\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d(x,C)\le\kappa\max_i d(x,C_i)\) for all nearby \(x\).\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local unperturbed error bound for finite set systems.

source_refs.locator: 5.4.1 Linear Subextremality of Set Systems p. 110
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The collection \(\{C_1,\ldots,C_m\}\) is locally linearly regular at \(\bar x\) if there exist \(\kappa>0\) and a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) such that \[d\left(x,\bigcap_{i=1}^m C_i\right)\le\kappa\max_{1\le i\le m}d(x,C_i)\qquad\text{for every }x\in U.\] The least admissible \(\kappa\) is the local linear-regularity modulus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set system is locally linearly regular when distance to its intersection is bounded linearly by the largest individual feasibility residual.
knowledge_statements.title: Linear Regularity

source_witnesses.locator: 5.4.1 Linear Subextremality of Set Systems p. 110
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical product-multifunction representation of the local feasibility error bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\) be closed subsets of a normed space \(X\), let \(\bar x\in C:=\bigcap_iC_i\), and equip \(X^m\) with the maximum product norm. Define \[\Phi(x):=(C_1-x)\times\cdots\times(C_m-x).\] Then \(\Phi^{-1}(0)=C\) and \(d(0,\Phi(x))=\max_i d(x,C_i)\). Consequently, the family is locally linearly regular at \(\bar x\) with constant \(\kappa\) if and only if \(\Phi\) is metrically subregular at \((\bar x,0)\) with the same constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite set family is locally linearly regular exactly when its canonical product residual multifunction is metrically subregular, with the same modulus.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[d(x,\bigcap_iC_i)\leq\kappa\max_i d(x,C_i)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad d(x,\Phi^{-1}(0))\leq\kappa d(0,\Phi(x))\] locally at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.title: Linear Regularity as Metric Subregularity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Relative-Interior Criterion for Convex Linear Regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex sufficient condition for bounded and hence local linear regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\subset\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty closed convex sets. If \[\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{ri}C_i\neq\varnothing,\] then for every bounded set \(B\subset\mathbb R^n\) there exists \(\kappa_B>0\) such that \[d\left(x,\bigcap_{i=1}^mC_i\right)\leq\kappa_B\max_i d(x,C_i)\qquad(x\in B).\] In particular, the family is locally linearly regular at every point of its intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closed convex sets with a common relative-interior point are linearly regular on every bounded region and hence locally linearly regular at each feasible point.
assumptions_latex: \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\subset\mathbb R^n\) are nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every bounded \(B\subset\mathbb R^n\), there is \(\kappa_B>0\) such that \(d(x,\bigcap_iC_i)\leq\kappa_B\max_i d(x,C_i)\) for all \(x\in B\).

notation.meaning: relative interior of a convex set

knowledge_statements.title: Relative-Interior Criterion for Convex Linear Regularity

assumptions_latex: \(A,B\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) are closed and \(\bar x\in A\cap B\).
\(N_A(\bar x)\cap[-N_B(\bar x)]=\{0\}\), where \(N\) is the limiting normal cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exist \(\kappa,\delta>0\) such that \(d(x,A\cap B)\leq\kappa\max\{d(x,A),d(x,B)\}\) for every \(x\in B_\delta(\bar x)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A,B\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be closed and let \(\bar x\in A\cap B\). If the limiting-normal transversality condition \[N_A(\bar x)\cap[-N_B(\bar x)]=\{0\}\] holds, then the pair \(\{A,B\}\) is locally linearly regular at \(\bar x\): there exist \(\kappa>0\) and \(\delta>0\) such that \[d(x,A\cap B)\leq\kappa\max\{d(x,A),d(x,B)\}\qquad\text{for all }x\in B_\delta(\bar x).\] Equivalently, the feasibility residual formed from the two individual distances supplies a local error bound for the intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For two closed Euclidean sets, exclusion of opposing nonzero normals at their common point yields a local linear error bound for their intersection.

If \[v_i\in N_{C_i}(\bar x),\qquad\sum_{i=1}^m v_i=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad v_1=\cdots=v_m=0,\] then there exist \(\kappa,\delta>0\) such that \[d(x,C)\leq\kappa\max_{1\leq i\leq m}d(x,C_i)\qquad(x\in B_\delta(\bar x)).\]

children.title: Tangential Intersection Failure
children.top_down_role: Loss of stable intersection behavior when component geometries align degenerately.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Higher-Order Tangential Contact Destroys Linear Regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A family of tangent curve-axis intersections whose individual residual vanishes superlinearly.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any \(p>1\), let \[A:=\{(s,0):s\in\mathbb R\},\qquad B_p:=\{(s,|s|^p):s\in\mathbb R\}.\] Then \(A\cap B_p=\{(0,0)\}\), and both sets have the horizontal tangent line at the origin. For \(x_t:=(t,0)\in A\), \[d(x_t,A\cap B_p)=|t|,\qquad d(x_t,A)=0,\qquad d(x_t,B_p)\leq |t|^p.\] Hence \[\frac{d(x_t,A\cap B_p)}{\max\{d(x_t,A),d(x_t,B_p)\}}\geq |t|^{1-p}\longrightarrow+\infty,\] so no local linear-regularity estimate holds. Moreover, \(N_A(0,0)=N_{B_p}(0,0)=\{0\}\times\mathbb R\), so the pair admits nonzero opposing normals and fails transversality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An axis and any graph with contact order greater than one have a superlinear individual residual but only linear distance to their singleton intersection; they also possess opposing normals.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is the horizontal axis and \(B_p\) is the graph of \(|s|^p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No \(\kappa,\delta>0\) satisfy \(d(x,A\cap B_p)\leq\kappa\max\{d(x,A),d(x,B_p)\}\) for every \(x\in B_\delta(0)\), and \(N_A(0)\cap[-N_{B_p}(0)]\neq\{0\}\).

notation.meaning: graph of the function s mapped to |s|^p

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No \(\kappa,\delta>0\) satisfy \(d(x,A\cap B)\leq\kappa\max\{d(x,A),d(x,B)\}\) throughout \(B_\delta(\bar x)\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A parabola tangent to its axis gives a concrete failure of linear intersection regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In \(\mathbb{R}^2\), set \(A=\{(s,0):s\in\mathbb{R}\}\), \(B=\{(s,s^2):s\in\mathbb{R}\}\), and \(\bar x=(0,0)\). Then \(A\cap B=\{\bar x\}\), while the two sets have the same tangent line at \(\bar x\). For \(x_t=(t,0)\in A\), one has \(d(x_t,A\cap B)=|t|\) and \(d(x_t,B)\leq t^2\). Consequently, \[\frac{d(x_t,A\cap B)}{\max\{d(x_t,A),d(x_t,B)\}}\geq\frac{1}{|t|}\longrightarrow+\infty.\] Hence no local linear intersection error bound holds at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The x-axis and a tangent parabola meet only at the origin, but their individual distance residual is quadratic while distance to the intersection is linear.
knowledge_statements.title: Tangential Intersection Failure

children.title: Sequential Normal Compactness
children.top_down_role: Normal-cone compactness behavior used in infinite-dimensional regularity analysis.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Banach space, \(\Omega\subset X\) is locally closed at \(\bar x\in\Omega\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(x_k\in\Omega\), \(x_k\to\bar x\), \(\varepsilon_k\downarrow0\), and \(x_k^*\in\widehat N_{\varepsilon_k}(x_k;\Omega)\), weak-star convergence \(x_k^*\xrightarrow{w^*}0\) implies \(\|x_k^*\|\to0\).

notation.meaning: Fréchet epsilon-normal cone to the set
weak-star convergence in the dual space

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical set-level sequential normal compactness formulated using nearby Fréchet epsilon-normals.

source_refs.locator: 1.1.4 Sequential Normal Compactness of Sets p. 27
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a Banach space and let \(\Omega\subset X\) be locally closed at \(\bar x\in\Omega\). The set \(\Omega\) is sequentially normally compact at \(\bar x\) if every sequence \((x_k,x_k^*,\varepsilon_k)\) satisfying \(x_k\in\Omega\), \(x_k\to\bar x\), \(\varepsilon_k\downarrow0\), \(x_k^*\in\widehat N_{\varepsilon_k}(x_k;\Omega)\), and \(x_k^*\xrightarrow{w^*}0\) also satisfies \(\|x_k^*\|\to0\). It is sequentially normally compact around \(\bar x\) when this property holds at every point of \(\Omega\) in some neighborhood of \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set is sequentially normally compact when nearby approximate Fréchet normals that converge weak-star to zero must also converge to zero in norm.
knowledge_statements.title: Sequential Normal Compactness

source_witnesses.locator: 1.1.4 Sequential Normal Compactness of Sets p. 27
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional regime in which sequential normal compactness is automatic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(X\) is finite-dimensional, then every set \(\Omega\subset X\) is sequentially normally compact at each \(\bar x\in\Omega\) where the SNC definition is considered. Indeed, weak-star convergence and norm convergence coincide in the finite-dimensional dual, so \(x_k^*\xrightarrow{w^*}0\) implies \(\|x_k^*\|\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: SNC is automatic in finite dimensions because weak-star and norm convergence coincide in the dual space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Omega\) is sequentially normally compact at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.title: Automatic SNC in Finite Dimensions

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is Asplund, \(A,B\subset X\) are locally closed near \(\bar x\in A\cap B\).
At least one of \(A\) and \(B\) is sequentially normally compact at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The qualification is \(N_A(\bar x)\cap[-N_B(\bar x)]=\{0\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be an Asplund space and let \(A,B\subset X\) be locally closed around \(\bar x\in A\cap B\). The basic intersection-calculus qualification at \(\bar x\) is \[N_A(\bar x)\cap[-N_B(\bar x)]=\{0\}.\] Equivalently, whenever \(a^*\in N_A(\bar x)\), \(b^*\in N_B(\bar x)\), and \(a^*+b^*=0\), one must have \(a^*=b^*=0\). Together with sequential normal compactness of at least one participating set, this condition rules out nonzero cancelling limiting normals and supports the limiting-normal intersection calculus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The intersection qualification excludes nonzero limiting normals to the two sets that cancel each other; one set also supplies sequential normal compactness.
knowledge_statements.title: Calculus Qualifications

knowledge_statements.scope_note: No-cancellation qualification for intersections of finitely many sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For locally closed sets \(A_1,\ldots,A_m\subset X\) containing \(\bar x\), the finite-family normal qualification is \[x_i^*\in N_{A_i}(\bar x)\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\quad \sum_{i=1}^m x_i^*=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x_1^*=\cdots=x_m^*=0.\] For \(m=2\), this is equivalent to \(N_{A_1}(\bar x)\cap[-N_{A_2}(\bar x)]=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite intersection is qualified when no nontrivial tuple of limiting normals sums to zero; its binary form is the seed condition.
assumptions_latex: \(A_1,\ldots,A_m\subset X\) are locally closed near \(\bar x\in\bigcap_iA_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_i x_i^*=0\) with \(x_i^*\in N_{A_i}(\bar x)\) implies \(x_i^*=0\) for every \(i\).

notation.meaning: limiting normal cone to the ith set

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Family Normal Qualification

children.title: Compactness-Supported Calculus
children.top_down_role: The role of sequential normal compactness in validating calculus transfers.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is Asplund and \(A,B\subset X\) are locally closed near \(\bar x\in A\cap B\).
One set is sequentially normally compact at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{A\cap B}(\bar x)\subset N_A(\bar x)+N_B(\bar x)\), and \(A\cap B\) is sequentially normally compact at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asplund-space intersection calculus supported by sequential normal compactness.

source_refs.locator: 3.3.1 Sequential Normal Compactness of Set Intersections and Inverse Images p. 341
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be Asplund, and let \(A,B\subset X\) be locally closed around \(\bar x\in A\cap B\). Suppose that one of the sets is sequentially normally compact at \(\bar x\) and that \[N_A(\bar x)\cap[-N_B(\bar x)]=\{0\}.\] Then every limiting normal to the intersection admits the calculus estimate \[N_{A\cap B}(\bar x)\subset N_A(\bar x)+N_B(\bar x).\] Under these hypotheses the intersection \(A\cap B\) is also sequentially normally compact at \(\bar x\), so the compactness property required by subsequent limiting-normal calculus is retained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sequential normal compactness plus the no-cancellation qualification yields the limiting-normal intersection rule and transfers compactness to the intersection.
knowledge_statements.title: Compactness-Supported Calculus

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3.1 Sequential Normal Compactness of Set Intersections and Inverse Images p. 341
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-family extension of compactness-supported limiting-normal intersection calculus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A_1,\ldots,A_m\subset X\) be locally closed near \(\bar x\in\bigcap_iA_i\). Suppose all but at most one of the sets are sequentially normally compact at \(\bar x\), and \[x_i^*\in N_{A_i}(\bar x),\quad \sum_{i=1}^m x_i^*=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x_1^*=\cdots=x_m^*=0.\] Then \[N_{\cap_{i=1}^mA_i}(\bar x)\subset\sum_{i=1}^mN_{A_i}(\bar x),\] and \(\bigcap_{i=1}^mA_i\) is sequentially normally compact at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite intersection, SNC of all but at most one set plus no cancellation yields the limiting-normal inclusion and transfers SNC to the intersection.
assumptions_latex: All but at most one \(A_i\) are SNC at \(\bar x\).
The finite-family normal qualification holds at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\cap_iA_i}(\bar x)\subset\sum_iN_{A_i}(\bar x)\), and \(\cap_iA_i\) is SNC at \(\bar x\).

notation.meaning: Minkowski sum of the limiting normal cones

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Intersection SNC Calculus

assumptions_latex: \(A,B\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) are closed near \(\bar x\in A\cap B\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exist \(\delta,c>0\) such that \(\|a^*+b^*\|\geq c\) for all nearby unit normals \(a^*\) and \(b^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional compactness turns pointwise normal qualification into a uniform nearby angle bound.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A,B\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be closed near \(\bar x\in A\cap B\), and suppose \(N_A(\bar x)\cap[-N_B(\bar x)]=\{0\}\). Then there exist \(\delta>0\) and \(c>0\) such that, whenever \(a\in A\cap B_\delta(\bar x)\), \(b\in B\cap B_\delta(\bar x)\), \(a^*\in N_A(a)\), \(b^*\in N_B(b)\), and \(\|a^*\|+\|b^*\|=1\), one has \[\|a^*+b^*\|\geq c.\] Thus the no-cancellation qualification persists quantitatively for nearby normal pairs in the finite-dimensional regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions, exclusion of cancelling normals at the reference point yields a uniform positive separation for normalized nearby normal pairs.
knowledge_statements.title: Qualification Stability Regimes

children.top_down_role: Failure of calculus caused by uncontrolled limiting normal sequences.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Banach space and \(\Omega\subset X\) is locally closed at \(\bar x\in\Omega\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Sequential normal compactness fails exactly when weak-star-null nearby Fréchet epsilon-normal sequences have norms bounded away from zero.

notation.meaning: Fréchet epsilon-normal cone to the set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential characterization of the escape mechanism that is the exact negation of canonical sequential normal compactness.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a Banach space and let \(\Omega\subset X\) be locally closed at \(\bar x\in\Omega\). Sequential normal compactness fails at \(\bar x\) if and only if there exist sequences \(x_k\in\Omega\), \(x_k\to\bar x\), \(\varepsilon_k\downarrow0\), and \(x_k^*\in\widehat N_{\varepsilon_k}(x_k;\Omega)\) such that \[x_k^*\xrightarrow{w^*}0\qquad\text{and}\qquad\inf_k\|x_k^*\|>0.\] After passing to a subsequence and rescaling the normals, the witnesses may equivalently be chosen with \(\|x_k^*\|=1\), with correspondingly rescaled tolerances still converging to zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sequential normal compactness fails precisely when nonvanishing nearby approximate Fréchet normals become invisible in the weak-star topology; normalized witnesses can be used after rescaling their tolerances.
knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Sequence Escape

children.title: Pointwise Error Bounds
children.top_down_role: Residual estimates centered at an individual reference solution.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exist \(\kappa,\delta>0\) such that \(d(x,S)\leq\kappa r(x)\) whenever \(d(x,\bar x)<\delta\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear residual error bound centered at one prescribed solution.

source_refs.locator: 4.2.2 Pointbased Characterizations of Covering and Metric Regularity p. 394
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space, let \(r:X\to[0,+\infty]\) be a residual, and set \(S=\{x\in X:r(x)=0\}\). For \(\bar x\in S\), a pointwise error bound holds at \(\bar x\) if there exist \(\kappa>0\) and \(\delta>0\) such that \[d(x,S)\leq\kappa r(x)\qquad\text{whenever }d(x,\bar x)<\delta.\] The least admissible asymptotic modulus is \[\operatorname{eb}(r;\bar x)=\limsup_{\substack{x\to\bar x\\x\notin S}}\frac{d(x,S)}{r(x)},\] with the quotient interpreted only where \(r(x)>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pointwise error bound controls distance to the residual zero set for all points sufficiently near one fixed solution.
knowledge_statements.title: Pointwise Error Bounds

source_witnesses.locator: 4.2.2 Pointbased Characterizations of Covering and Metric Regularity p. 394
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent pointwise characterization using residual growth away from the solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[\gamma(r;\bar x):=\liminf_{\substack{x\to\bar x\\x\notin S}}\frac{r(x)}{d(x,S)}.\] Then \[\operatorname{eb}(r;\bar x)=\frac{1}{\gamma(r;\bar x)},\] with \(1/0:=+\infty\) and \(1/(+\infty):=0\). Consequently, a pointwise error bound holds at \(\bar x\) exactly when \(\gamma(r;\bar x)>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pointwise error bound is equivalent to positive asymptotic residual growth per unit distance from the solution set.
assumptions_latex: Ratios are taken only for \(x\notin S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{eb}(r;\bar x)=1/\gamma(r;\bar x)\), so finiteness is equivalent to \(\gamma(r;\bar x)>0\).

notation.meaning: Pointwise residual-growth rate relative to solution distance

knowledge_statements.title: Reciprocal Residual-Growth Characterization

children.title: Local Error Bounds
children.top_down_role: Residual estimates valid near a solution or solution set.

assumptions_latex: \(S_0\subset S\) is a specified solution subset.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: One pair \((\kappa,U)\) satisfies \(d(x,S)\leq\kappa r(x)\) for all \(x\in U\), where \(U\) is a neighborhood of \(S_0\).

notation.meaning: solution subset around which uniformity is required

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform linear error bound on a neighborhood of a prescribed solution subset.

source_refs.locator: 4.1.2 Neighborhood Characterizations of Metric Regularity and Lipschitzian Behavior p. 382
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space, let \(r:X\to[0,+\infty]\), and define \(S=\{x\in X:r(x)=0\}\). Given a nonempty subset \(S_0\subset S\), a local error bound holds around \(S_0\) if there exist a neighborhood \(U\) of \(S_0\) and a constant \(\kappa>0\) such that \[d(x,S)\leq\kappa r(x)\qquad\text{for every }x\in U.\] Unlike a pointwise bound, the same neighborhood and modulus must work uniformly around all reference solutions in \(S_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local error bound uses one residual modulus throughout a neighborhood of an entire prescribed set of solutions.
knowledge_statements.title: Local Error Bounds

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1.2 Neighborhood Characterizations of Metric Regularity and Lipschitzian Behavior p. 382

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Local Error-Bound Modulus Around a Solution Subset
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Best uniform linear error-bound constant obtainable on a neighborhood of the prescribed solution subset.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S=r^{-1}(0)\) and \(\varnothing\neq S_0\subset S\). Define
\[
\operatorname{eb}_{\mathrm{loc}}(r;S_0):=
\inf_{U\supset S_0}\ \sup_{\substack{x\in U\\ r(x)>0}}
\frac{d(x,S)}{r(x)},
\]
where the infimum ranges over neighborhoods \(U\) of \(S_0\), \(\sup\varnothing=0\), and the value is \(+\infty\) if every such ratio supremum is infinite. A local error bound around \(S_0\) holds if and only if \(\operatorname{eb}_{\mathrm{loc}}(r;S_0)<+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exact local modulus is the best worst-case distance-to-residual ratio obtainable on a neighborhood of the prescribed solution subset.
assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a metric space, \(r:X\to[0,+\infty]\), \(S=r^{-1}(0)\), and \(\varnothing\neq S_0\subset S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A local error bound around \(S_0\) exists if and only if \(\operatorname{eb}_{\mathrm{loc}}(r;S_0)<+\infty\).

notation.meaning: Exact uniform local error-bound modulus around the prescribed solution subset.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Local Error-Bound Modulus Around a Solution Subset

children.title: Level-Set Error Bounds
children.top_down_role: Residual estimates controlled uniformly over designated level or sublevel sets.

assumptions_latex: \(R\subset X\) is the region on which the estimate is required.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is \(\kappa_\alpha<+\infty\) such that \(d(x,S_\alpha)\leq\kappa_\alpha[f(x)-\alpha]_+\) for all \(x\in R\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regional linear error bound for a fixed sublevel set of an extended-real-valued function.

source_refs.locator: 4.1.2 Neighborhood Characterizations of Metric Regularity and Lipschitzian Behavior p. 382
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space, let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), fix \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\), and suppose \(S_\alpha=\{x\in X:f(x)\leq\alpha\}\neq\varnothing\). A level-set error bound holds on a region \(R\subset X\) if there exists \(\kappa_\alpha<+\infty\) such that \[d(x,S_\alpha)\leq\kappa_\alpha[f(x)-\alpha]_+\qquad\text{for all }x\in R.\] The modulus may depend on the selected level \(\alpha\) and on the prescribed region \(R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a fixed level, excess function value controls distance to the corresponding sublevel set throughout the prescribed region.
knowledge_statements.title: Level-Set Error Bounds

assumptions_latex: \(r:X\to[0,+\infty]\) has nonempty zero set \(S\) in a metric space \(X\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space, let \(r:X\to[0,+\infty]\), and suppose that \(S=\{x\in X:r(x)=0\}\neq\varnothing\). For a bounded set \(R\subset X\), a bounded-region error bound holds on \(R\) if there exists \(\kappa_R<+\infty\) such that \[d(x,S)\leq\kappa_R r(x)\qquad\text{for all }x\in R.\] The constant is uniform over \(R\) but may grow when \(R\) is replaced by a larger bounded region; no assertion is made about a single global modulus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On each selected bounded region, one finite constant controls distance to the solution set, although the constant may grow with the region.
knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Region Error Bounds

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space, let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), and let \(I\subset\mathbb{R}\) be a nonempty interval such that \(S_\alpha=\{x\in X:f(x)\leq\alpha\}\neq\varnothing\) for every \(\alpha\in I\). The level-set error bounds are uniform on \(R\subset X\) over \(I\) if there exists a single \(\kappa<+\infty\) satisfying \[d(x,S_\alpha)\leq\kappa[f(x)-\alpha]_+\qquad\text{for every }x\in R\text{ and }\alpha\in I.\] Thus neither the level nor the point may change the modulus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sublevel uniformity means one modulus controls distance to every sublevel set for all levels in the chosen interval and all points in the region.
knowledge_statements.title: Sublevel Uniformity

children.title: Region-Dependent Moduli
children.top_down_role: Conditioning values whose size depends on the selected level set or bounded region.

assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a metric space, \(S\subset X\) is nonempty and closed, and \(r:X\to[0,\infty)\) satisfies \(S=\{x:r(x)=0\}\).
\(\mathcal R\) is a family of nonempty subsets of \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For each \(R\in\mathcal R\), \(\kappa(R)\) is the infimum of all error-bound moduli valid throughout \(R\), and it may equal \(+\infty\).

notation.meaning: Distance from a point to the solution set
Exact error-bound modulus on a region

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact moduli are indexed by prescribed regions and may grow as regions expand.

source_refs.locator: 4.1 Neighborhood Criteria and Exact Bounds p. 378
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[
\kappa(R):=\inf\bigl\{\kappa\geq0: d(x,S)\leq\kappa r(x)\ \text{for every }x\in R\bigr\},
\]
with \(\inf\varnothing:=+\infty\). If \(R_1\subset R_2\), then \(\kappa(R_1)\leq\kappa(R_2)\). Thus an exhaustion \(R_1\subset R_2\subset\cdots\) can have finite regional moduli while \(\sup_n\kappa(R_n)=+\infty\), in which case those regional estimates furnish no uniform finite modulus on the union.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The regional modulus is the infimum of the constants controlling distance by the residual on that region. It is monotone under region enlargement, and finite moduli on every member of an exhaustion need not yield a uniform modulus on the union.
knowledge_statements.title: Region-Dependent Moduli

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1 Neighborhood Criteria and Exact Bounds p. 378
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Regional Modulus as a Supremum of Pointwise Ratios
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent quotient representation of the exact modulus on a prescribed region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every nonempty region \(R\subset X\), \[\kappa(R)=\sup_{\substack{x\in R\\x\notin S}}\frac{d(x,S)}{r(x)},\] with \(\sup\varnothing:=0\) and an unbounded supremum interpreted as \(+\infty\). Thus \(\kappa(R)<+\infty\) exactly when the distance-to-residual ratio is bounded on \(R\setminus S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exact regional modulus is the supremum of the distance-to-residual ratio over infeasible points in the region.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\kappa(R)=\sup_{x\in R\setminus S}d(x,S)/r(x)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Regional Modulus as a Supremum of Pointwise Ratios

children.title: Unbounded-Region Breakdown
children.top_down_role: Loss of uniform residual control as the region expands without boundedness.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every bounded interval admits an error bound, but no finite error-bound modulus works on all of \(\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A bounded residual cannot globally control an unbounded distance to the solution set.

source_refs.locator: 5.10 Residues and Error Bounds p. 475
source_refs.source_title: The Linear Complementarity Problem

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(R>0\) and every \(|x|\leq R\),
\[
d(x,S)=|x|=(1+|x|)r(x)\leq(1+R)r(x).
\]
Hence a finite error-bound modulus exists on each bounded interval. If a global constant \(\kappa<\infty\) existed, then \(|x|\leq\kappa |x|/(1+|x|)\) for every nonzero \(x\), implying \(1+|x|\leq\kappa\), which is impossible as \(|x|\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This residual controls distance on every bounded interval, but its saturation at infinity prevents any global linear error bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded-Region Breakdown

source_witnesses.locator: 5.10 Residues and Error Bounds p. 475
source_witnesses.source_title: The Linear Complementarity Problem

children.title: Global Error Bounds
children.top_down_role: Residual estimates uniform over the full domain or feasibility region.

assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a metric space, \(S\subset X\) is nonempty and closed, and \(r:X\to[0,\infty)\) has zero set \(S\).
\(D\subset X\) is the full domain or feasibility region under consideration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A global error bound holds exactly when one finite modulus controls \(d(x,S)\) by \(r(x)\) for every \(x\in D\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform linear residual estimate over the entire prescribed domain.

source_refs.locator: 4.1 Neighborhood Criteria and Exact Bounds p. 378
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The residual \(r\) admits a global error bound on \(D\) if there exists \(\kappa<\infty\) such that
\[
d(x,S)\leq\kappa r(x)\qquad\text{for every }x\in D.
\]
Its exact global modulus is
\[
\operatorname{eb}(r;D):=\inf\bigl\{\kappa\geq0:d(x,S)\leq\kappa r(x)\ \text{for every }x\in D\bigr\},
\]
where the value is \(+\infty\) if no such finite constant exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A global error bound uses one finite constant to control distance to the solution set throughout the entire designated domain.
knowledge_statements.title: Global Error Bounds

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1 Neighborhood Criteria and Exact Bounds p. 378
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Ratio Formula for the Exact Global Modulus
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent supremum representation of the exact global linear error-bound modulus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the notation of the accepted seed, define
\[
Q:=\sup\left\{\frac{d(x,S)}{r(x)}:x\in D,\ r(x)>0\right\},
\]
with \(\sup\varnothing=0\). Then
\[
\operatorname{eb}(r;D)=Q.
\]
Thus a finite global error bound exists exactly when the positive-residual distance ratios are uniformly bounded on \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exact global error-bound modulus is the worst distance-to-solution divided by positive residual over the designated domain.
assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a metric space, \(S=r^{-1}(0)\neq\varnothing\), and \(D\subset X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{eb}(r;D)=\sup_{x\in D,\ r(x)>0}d(x,S)/r(x)\).

notation.meaning: Worst positive-residual distance ratio on the designated domain.

knowledge_statements.title: Ratio Formula for the Exact Global Modulus

children.title: Nonlinear Growth Error-Bound Family
children.top_down_role: Residual estimates with nonlinear growth scales.

children.title: Hölder Error Bounds
children.top_down_role: Residual estimates governed by a power-type growth scale.

assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a metric space, \(S\subset X\) is nonempty and closed, and \(r:X\to[0,\infty]\) has zero set \(S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed inequality defines a Hölder error bound of order \(q\) on \(D\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Power-type nonlinear error bound; the case \(q=1\) is Lipschitz.

source_refs.locator: 4.1 Neighborhood Criteria and Exact Bounds p. 378
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A Hölder error bound of order \(q\) holds on \(D\) when
\[
d(x,S)\leq\kappa\,r(x)^q\qquad\text{for every }x\in D.
\]
For a local bound at \(\bar x\in S\), the same inequality is required only for \(x\in D\cap U\), where \(U\) is some neighborhood of \(\bar x\). The convention \(0^q=0\) makes the estimate consistent on \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Hölder error bound controls distance to the solution set by a positive power of the residual.
knowledge_statements.title: Hölder Error Bounds

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1 Neighborhood Criteria and Exact Bounds p. 378
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact asymptotic modulus for a fixed Hölder order at one solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\bar x\in S\) and \(q\in(0,1]\), define \[\operatorname{heb}_q(r;\bar x):=\limsup_{\substack{x\to\bar x\\x\notin S}}\frac{d(x,S)}{r(x)^q}.\] A pointwise Hölder error bound of order \(q\) holds at \(\bar x\) if and only if \(\operatorname{heb}_q(r;\bar x)<+\infty\); this value is the infimum of all locally admissible moduli.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exact pointwise Hölder modulus is the limsup of solution distance divided by the q-th power of the residual.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Finiteness of \(\operatorname{heb}_q(r;\bar x)\) is equivalent to a pointwise order-\(q\) Hölder error bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Pointwise Hölder Error-Bound Modulus

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordering of Hölder error-bound strengths on a residual-bounded region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(0<q_1<q_2\leq1\), \(0\leq r(x)\leq\delta\), and \(d(x,S)\leq\kappa r(x)^{q_2}\). Then \[d(x,S)\leq\kappa\delta^{q_2-q_1}r(x)^{q_1}.\] Hence an order-\(q_2\) bound implies every lower-order bound locally, while the converse need not hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a residual-bounded region, a higher Hölder order implies every lower order with an explicit modulus adjustment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The order-\(q_1\) bound holds with modulus \(\kappa\delta^{q_2-q_1}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Monotonicity of Local Hölder Orders

children.title: General Nonlinear Error Bounds
children.top_down_role: Residual estimates governed by non-power growth functions.

assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a metric space, \(S\subset X\) is nonempty and closed, and \(r:X\to[0,\infty]\) has zero set \(S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed estimate is a nonlinear error bound with growth function \(\varphi\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General residual-to-distance estimate encompassing linear and Hölder scales.

source_refs.locator: 4.1 Neighborhood Criteria and Exact Bounds p. 378
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A nonlinear error bound with growth function \(\varphi\) holds on \(D\) if
\[
d(x,S)\leq\varphi(r(x))\qquad\text{for every }x\in D.
\]
A scaled form permits \(d(x,S)\leq\kappa\varphi(r(x))\) with \(\kappa>0\). The linear choice \(\varphi(t)=t\) gives a Lipschitz error bound, while \(\varphi(t)=t^q\) with \(q\in(0,1)\) gives a Hölder error bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonlinear error bound controls solution distance through a nondecreasing growth function applied to the residual.
knowledge_statements.title: General Nonlinear Error Bounds

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1 Neighborhood Criteria and Exact Bounds p. 378
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A nonlinear error bound represented as a linear bound for a growth-transformed residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S=r^{-1}(0)\), and suppose \(\varphi:[0,+\infty]\to[0,+\infty]\) is nondecreasing, \(\varphi(0)=0\), and \(\varphi(t)>0\) for every \(t>0\). Define \(\widetilde r:=\varphi\circ r\). Then \(\widetilde r^{-1}(0)=S\), and for every \(D\subset X\) and \(\kappa>0\),
\[
d(x,S)\leq\kappa\varphi(r(x))\quad(x\in D)
\]
if and only if
\[
d(x,S)\leq\kappa\widetilde r(x)\quad(x\in D).
\]
Thus a nonlinear error bound is a linear error bound for the admissibly transformed residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-definite growth transformation converts a nonlinear error bound into an ordinary linear bound for a residual with the same zero set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d(x,S)\leq\kappa\varphi(r(x))\iff d(x,S)\leq\kappa\widetilde r(x)\) on \(D\), and \(\widetilde r^{-1}(0)=S\).

notation.meaning: Growth-transformed residual preserving the original zero set.

knowledge_statements.title: Transformed-Residual Representation

children.title: Growth-Function Regimes
children.top_down_role: Classes of nonlinear growth scales used to calibrate residual control.

assumptions_latex: \(\delta>0\), and \(\varphi:[0,\delta]\to[0,\infty)\) is nondecreasing with \(\varphi(0)=0\) and \(\varphi(t)>0\) for every \(t\in(0,\delta]\).
The estimate \(d(x,S)\leq\kappa\varphi(r(x))\) is considered only at points satisfying \(0\leq r(x)\leq\delta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The asymptotic ratio \(\varphi(t)/t\) classifies the growth function as below the linear scale, comparable with it, or above it near zero.

notation.meaning: Growth ratio relative to the linear scale

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classification is by comparison of the growth function with the linear scale near zero.

source_refs.locator: 4.1 Neighborhood Criteria and Exact Bounds p. 378
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(\rho(t):=\varphi(t)/t\) for \(t\in(0,\delta]\). The growth function is comparable with the linear scale near zero when
\[
0<\liminf_{t\downarrow0}\rho(t)\leq\limsup_{t\downarrow0}\rho(t)<\infty.
\]
It lies below the linear scale when \(\rho(t)\to0\), and above the linear scale when \(\rho(t)\to+\infty\). For \(\varphi(t)=t^q\), these regimes correspond respectively to \(q=1\), \(q>1\), and \(0<q<1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near zero, the ratio of a growth function to the identity determines whether it is comparable with, below, or above the linear scale.
knowledge_statements.title: Growth-Function Regimes

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1 Neighborhood Criteria and Exact Bounds p. 378
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of the three simple limiting regimes when the linear-scale ratio oscillates near zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\underline\rho:=\liminf_{t\downarrow0}\varphi(t)/t\) and \(\overline\rho:=\limsup_{t\downarrow0}\varphi(t)/t\). Two-sided comparability with the linear scale holds exactly when \(0<\underline\rho\leq\overline\rho<+\infty\). The limits \(\varphi(t)/t\to0\) and \(\varphi(t)/t\to+\infty\) are the pure below-linear and above-linear regimes. If neither limit holds and two-sided comparability fails, the scale is oscillatory or one-sided degenerate and cannot be assigned to one of those three pure regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The three simple ratio regimes do not cover scales whose ratio to the identity oscillates or degenerates only on subsequences.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pair \((\underline\rho,\overline\rho)\) identifies comparability and the residual mixed or oscillatory failure cases.

notation.meaning: Lower and upper asymptotic ratios of the growth scale to the identity

knowledge_statements.title: Nonexhaustive Limiting-Ratio Regimes

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local implication between nonlinear error bounds induced by asymptotically ordered growth scales.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(d(x,S)\leq\kappa\varphi(r(x))\) whenever \(r(x)\leq\delta\). If \(\varphi(t)\leq C\psi(t)\) on \([0,\delta]\), then \[d(x,S)\leq\kappa C\psi(r(x))\] on the same region. In particular, \(\limsup_{t\downarrow0}\varphi(t)/\psi(t)<+\infty\) yields this implication after reducing \(\delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bound using one growth scale implies a bound using any asymptotically dominating scale.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The corresponding \(\psi\)-error bound holds with modulus \(\kappa C\).

notation.meaning: Local domination of \(\varphi\) by a constant multiple of \(\psi\)

knowledge_statements.title: Error-Bound Transfer under Growth-Scale Domination

children.title: Hölder-to-Lipschitz Transition
children.top_down_role: The boundary between power-scale error bounds and linear error bounds.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At \(q=1\) the Hölder estimate is Lipschitz; for \(q<1\), it generally does not imply a Lipschitz error bound.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The transition occurs exactly at exponent one under the usual power convention.

source_refs.locator: 4.1 Neighborhood Criteria and Exact Bounds p. 378
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
When \(q=1\), the estimate becomes
\[
d(x,S)\leq\kappa r(x),
\]
which is a Lipschitz error bound. For \(0<q<1\), the factor \(r(x)^{q-1}\) diverges as \(r(x)\downarrow0\), so no finite Lipschitz modulus follows in general. Indeed, with \(X=\mathbb R\), \(S=\{0\}\), and \(r(x)=|x|^{1/q}\), one has \(d(x,S)=r(x)^q\), whereas \(d(x,S)/r(x)=|x|^{1-1/q}\to+\infty\) as \(x\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exponent one is precisely the Lipschitz case; smaller Hölder exponents can hold even when every local Lipschitz modulus is infinite.
knowledge_statements.title: Hölder-to-Lipschitz Transition

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1 Neighborhood Criteria and Exact Bounds p. 378
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lipschitz Bounds Imply Lower Hölder Orders Locally
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forward implication across the sharp exponent-one transition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(d(x,S)\leq\kappa r(x)\) and \(0\leq r(x)\leq\delta\), then for every \(q\in(0,1)\), \[d(x,S)\leq\kappa\delta^{1-q}r(x)^q.\] Thus every local Lipschitz error bound yields every lower Hölder order after residual localization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Lipschitz error bound implies every lower Hölder order locally, with an explicit modulus.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An order-\(q\) Hölder error bound holds with modulus \(\kappa\delta^{1-q}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Lipschitz Bounds Imply Lower Hölder Orders Locally

children.title: Nonlinear Scale Degeneracy
children.top_down_role: Growth-scale behavior that prevents meaningful or uniform error-bound control.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The nonlinear bound is exact, but its scale degenerates relative to the linear residual scale at zero.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure arises when the growth function is not bounded above by a linear scale near zero.

source_refs.locator: 4.1 Neighborhood Criteria and Exact Bounds p. 378
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(x\in\mathbb R\),
\[
d(x,S)=|x|=\varphi(r(x)),
\]
so the nonlinear error bound holds globally with equality. However,
\[
\frac{\varphi(t)}{t}=\frac{1}{\sqrt t}\longrightarrow+\infty\qquad\text{as }t\downarrow0.
\]
Consequently, no \(c<\infty\) and no neighborhood of zero satisfy \(\varphi(t)\leq ct\); equivalently, no local Lipschitz error bound \(|x|\leq\kappa x^2\) can hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact square-root error bound may coexist with complete failure of linear residual control near the solution.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonlinear Scale Degeneracy

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1 Neighborhood Criteria and Exact Bounds p. 378
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

children.top_down_role: Canonical residual constructions used to measure feasibility, stationarity, or variational-system violation.

children.title: Constraint-Violation Residuals
children.top_down_role: Residual families for equality, inequality, conic, and set-valued constraints.

assumptions_latex: \(X,Y,Z\) are normed spaces, \(C\subset X\), \(K\subset Z\), and \(Q\subset Y\) are closed, and \(m\in\mathbb N\).
\(h:X\to Y\), \(u:X\to\mathbb R^m\), and \(g:X\to Z\), while \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) has nonempty compact values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The combined residual vanishes exactly at points satisfying every included membership, equality, componentwise inequality, conic, and set-valued intersection constraint.

notation.meaning: Positive part applied componentwise to a vector in Euclidean space

knowledge_statements.scope_note: One scalar residual combines membership, equality, componentwise inequality, conic, and set-valued intersection violations under assumptions ensuring an exact zero set.

source_refs.locator: 4.3 Sensitivity Analysis for Constraint Systems p. 406
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the constraints \(x\in C\), \(h(x)=0\), \(u_i(x)\leq0\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), \(g(x)\in K\), and \(F(x)\cap Q\neq\varnothing\), define
\[
r(x):=\max\bigl\{d(x,C),\|h(x)\|,\|[u(x)]_+\|,d(g(x),K),d(F(x),Q)\bigr\}.
\]
Then \(r(x)\geq0\), and
\[
r(x)=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
x\in C,\ h(x)=0,\ u_i(x)\leq0\ \text{for all }i,\ g(x)\in K,\ F(x)\cap Q\neq\varnothing.
\]
Any constraint not present in the system contributes no term to the maximum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distances, equality norms, and positive parts combine into a scalar residual that is zero exactly at feasible points. Compactness of the set-valued image and closedness of its target make zero set-to-set distance equivalent to intersection.
knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-Violation Residuals

source_witnesses.locator: 4.3 Sensitivity Analysis for Constraint Systems p. 406
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-valued component violations may be aggregated by any finite-dimensional norm without changing feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(v_i:X\to[0,+\infty)\), \(i=1,\ldots,p\), be finitely many exact component violations, and define
\[r_{\max}(x)=\max_i v_i(x),\qquad r_1(x)=\sum_{i=1}^p v_i(x).\]
Then
\[r_{\max}(x)\le r_1(x)\le p\,r_{\max}(x),\qquad r_{\max}(x)=0\iff r_1(x)=0\iff v_i(x)=0\ \forall i.\]
Every norm of the finite vector \((v_1(x),\ldots,v_p(x))\) has the same zero set and is comparable with these aggregates by positive constants.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximum, sum, and every finite-dimensional norm aggregate finite-valued exact component violations into quantitatively equivalent feasibility residuals.
assumptions_latex: \(v_1,ldots,v_p:X\to[0,+\infty)\) are finite-valued nonnegative exact component violations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[r_{\max}\le r_1\le p r_{\max},\qquad Z(r_{\max})=Z(r_1)=\bigcap_{i=1}^p Z(v_i).\]
knowledge_statements.title: Finite Aggregation of Constraint Violations

children.title: Projection-Natural Residual Representation Pair
children.top_down_role: Residual maps induced by projection and fixed-point reformulations.

children.title: Projection Residuals
children.top_down_role: Residual maps built directly from projection onto a feasible or constraint set.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a Hilbert space, \(C\subset H\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, and \(F:C\to H\).
\(\lambda>0\), and \(P_C\) denotes the metric projection onto \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Zeros of the projection residual are exactly solutions of \(0\in F(x)+N_C(x)\).

notation.meaning: Convex normal cone to the constraint set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space projection representation of a constrained variational inequality.

source_refs.locator: 2.1.4 Fixed-point theorems p. 141
source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the projection residual by
\[
R_\lambda(x):=x-P_C(x-\lambda F(x)),\qquad x\in C.
\]
The projection characterization of the convex normal cone gives
\[
R_\lambda(x)=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
x=P_C(x-\lambda F(x))
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
0\in F(x)+N_C(x).
\]
Thus \(\|R_\lambda(x)\|\) is a nonnegative scalar violation measure for the associated variational inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subtracting the projected forward step from the current point yields a residual whose zeros solve the constrained variational inequality.
knowledge_statements.title: Projection Residuals

source_witnesses.locator: 2.1.4 Fixed-point theorems p. 141
source_witnesses.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. I

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lipschitz Stability of the Projection Residual
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuity bound for the vector projection residual under a Lipschitz field.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(F\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz on \(C\), then the projection residual \(R_\lambda(x)=x-P_C(x-\lambda F(x))\) is globally Lipschitz on \(C\), with \[\|R_\lambda(x)-R_\lambda(y)\|\leq(2+\lambda L)\|x-y\|\qquad(x,y\in C).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Lipschitz VI field induces a globally Lipschitz projection-residual vector.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty closed convex subset of a Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Lip}(R_\lambda)\leq2+\lambda L\).
knowledge_statements.title: Lipschitz Stability of the Projection Residual

children.title: Natural Residuals
children.top_down_role: Residual maps associated with natural fixed-point reformulations of structured systems.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a Hilbert space, \(C\subset H\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, and \(F:C\to H\).
\(\lambda>0\), and \(P_C\) is the metric projection onto \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The natural residual is nonnegative and vanishes exactly at solutions of the variational inequality.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar norm of the projection displacement for a variational inequality.

source_refs.locator: 5.10 Residues and Error Bounds p. 475
source_refs.source_title: The Linear Complementarity Problem

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\in C\), define
\[
r_{\mathrm{nat},\lambda}(x):=\|x-P_C(x-\lambda F(x))\|.
\]
Then \(r_{\mathrm{nat},\lambda}(x)\geq0\), and
\[
r_{\mathrm{nat},\lambda}(x)=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
x=P_C(x-\lambda F(x))
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
0\in F(x)+N_C(x).
\]
For \(\lambda=1\), this is the standard unit-step natural residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The natural residual is the norm of the displacement between a point and its projected forward step.
knowledge_statements.title: Natural Residuals

source_witnesses.locator: 5.10 Residues and Error Bounds p. 475
source_witnesses.source_title: The Linear Complementarity Problem

children.title: Fixed-Point Residual Forms
children.top_down_role: Residual representations measuring deviation from a fixed-point condition.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a normed space, \(D\subset X\) is nonempty, and \(T:D\to D\) is a self-map.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The vector residual \(x-T(x)\), its norm, and the fixed-point equation have the same zero set in \(D\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic fixed-point form underlying projection and natural residuals.

source_refs.locator: 1.1.3 Fixed-point theorems and contraction p. 16
source_refs.source_title: Modern Nonconvex Nondifferentiable Optimization

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[
\operatorname{Fix}T:=\{x\in D:T(x)=x\},\qquad R_T(x):=x-T(x),\qquad r_T(x):=\|R_T(x)\|.
\]
Then, for every \(x\in D\),
\[
x\in\operatorname{Fix}T
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
x=T(x)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
R_T(x)=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
r_T(x)=0.
\]
If \(D=C\), where \(C\) is a nonempty closed convex subset of a Hilbert space, and \(T(x)=P_C(x-\lambda F(x))\) for \(\lambda>0\), these forms are respectively the projection residual vector and the natural residual scalar.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed-point problem is equivalently represented by the displacement from a self-map or by the norm of that displacement; both vanish exactly on the fixed-point set.
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Point Residual Forms

children.title: Projection–Natural Residual Equivalence
children.top_down_role: Conditions under which projection-based and natural residuals yield comparable solution measures.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary for step-uniform comparison of projection residuals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty closed convex subset of a Hilbert space and \(R_t(x)=x-P_C(x-tF(x))\). Then \(R_0\equiv0\). For \(C=H\) and a nonzero constant field \(F\), \(\|R_t(x)\|=t\|R_1(x)\|\); hence no positive comparison constants uniform in \(t\) exist over step families approaching \(0\) or \(+\infty\). The standard fixed-step comparison factors are uniform whenever \(0<\underline t\le t\le\overline t<+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero step destroys zero-set exactness, and unrestricted positive steps admit no universal uniform comparison with the unit-step residual.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset H\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_0\equiv0\); compact positive step intervals support uniform comparison, whereas steps tending to zero or infinity do not admit universal uniform constants.

notation.meaning: positive lower and finite upper step bounds

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate and Unbounded Step Families

assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty closed convex subset of a Hilbert space \(H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_t(x)=0\iff R_1(x)=0\), and the two residual norms are globally equivalent for fixed \(t>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space projection residuals for a closed convex feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(x\in C\), define \(R_t(x)=x-P_C(x-tF(x))\) and call \(R_1\) the natural residual. Firm nonexpansiveness of the metric projection yields
\[
\min\{1,t\}\,\|R_1(x)\|\leq \|R_t(x)\|\leq \max\{1,t\}\,\|R_1(x)\|.
\]
Consequently, \(R_t(x)=0\) if and only if \(R_1(x)=0\), equivalently \(0\in F(x)+N_C(x)\). Thus any local error bound stated using one residual transfers to the other after rescaling its constant by a factor depending only on \(t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every positive-step projection residual has the same zeros as the natural residual, and their norms differ by at most explicit step-dependent factors.
knowledge_statements.title: Projection–Natural Residual Equivalence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The equivalence and step-dependent norm bounds are mathematically plausible and fit the property container, but the nontrivial global comparison and error-bound transfer have no cited source.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Projection Nonattainment for a Closed Nonconvex Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of existence of nearest points for a closed nonconvex subset of an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In \(H=\ell^2\), let \(e_n\) be the standard basis and \[C:=\{(1+1/n)e_n:n\in\mathbb N\}.\] The set \(C\) is nonempty and closed, but \(\operatorname{dist}(0,C)=1\) is not attained. Hence \(P_C(0)=\varnothing\), so a projection residual may be undefined even when the constraint set is closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed nonconvex set in an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space can have no nearest point, so its projection residual need not be defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is closed and nonempty, while \(P_C(0)=\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: the nth standard basis vector of \(\ell^2\)
nearest-point projection set at the origin

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonunique Convex Projection Outside Hilbert Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of single-valued metric projection for a closed convex set in a non-strictly-convex normed space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=(\mathbb R^2,\|\cdot\|_\infty)\), \(C=\mathbb R\times\{0\}\), and \(u=(0,1)\). Then \[\operatorname{dist}(u,C)=1,\qquad P_C(u)=\{(t,0):|t|\leq1\}.\] Thus a nonempty closed convex set need not have a single-valued metric projection in a general normed space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even for a closed convex set, projection can be multivalued outside Hilbert or suitably convex Banach geometry.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonunique Convex Projection Outside Hilbert Geometry

assumptions_latex: \(H=\mathbb R\), \(C=\{-1,1\}\), and \(P_C\) denotes the nearest-point projection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_C(x-tF(x))=P_C(0)=\{-1,1\}\), so the projection residual is set-valued.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of convexity can destroy single-valued projection residuals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the closed nonconvex set \(C=\{-1,1\}\), the projection at the origin satisfies \(P_C(0)=\{-1,1\}\). With \(x=1\), \(t=1\), and \(F(1)=1\), one has \(x-tF(x)=0\), hence
\[
R_t(1)=1-P_C(0)=\{0,2\}.
\]
Thus closedness alone does not make the projection residual a single-valued map. Global norm comparisons, Lipschitz estimates, and fixed-point formulations relying on firm nonexpansiveness require convexity, or a local regime in which a chosen projection is single-valued and regular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a closed nonconvex two-point set, projection is multivalued, so the associated projection residual is not a single-valued regular map.
knowledge_statements.title: Projection Regularity Boundaries

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-scale family of normal-map reformulations for convex-set variational inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(z\in H\), set \(x=P_Cz\) and \[M_\lambda(z):=F(x)+\lambda^{-1}(z-x),\qquad r_{N,\lambda}(z):=\|M_\lambda(z)\|.\] Then \[M_\lambda(z)=0\Longleftrightarrow0\in F(x)+N_C(x),\qquad x=P_Cz.\] Conversely, every solution \(x\) corresponds to the zero \(z=x-\lambda F(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every positive scaling gives a normal-map equation whose zeros correspond exactly to VI solutions through projection.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty closed convex subset of a Hilbert space \(H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M_\lambda(z)=0\iff0\in F(P_Cz)+N_C(P_Cz)\), and a solution \(x\) corresponds to \(z=x-\lambda F(x)\).

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset H\) is nonempty, closed, and convex in a Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M(z)=0\iff 0\in F(P_Cz)+N_C(P_Cz)\).

source_refs.locator: 4.1.2 Neighborhood Characterizations of Metric Regularity and Lipschitzian Behavior p. 382
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(z\in H\), set \(x=P_C(z)\) and define the normal map and its scalar residual by
\[
M(z)=F(x)+z-x,\qquad r_N(z)=\|M(z)\|.
\]
The projection characterization \(z-x\in N_C(x)\) implies
\[
M(z)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 0\in F(x)+N_C(x),\qquad x=P_C(z).
\]
Conversely, if \(x\) solves the inclusion, then \(z=x-F(x)\) satisfies \(P_C(z)=x\) and \(M(z)=0\). Hence zeros of the normal-map residual represent precisely the variational-inequality solutions through projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The norm of the normal map is a residual whose zeros project exactly onto solutions of the variational inequality.
knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Map Residuals

children.title: Gap-Function Residuals
children.top_down_role: Scalar residuals derived from gap constructions for equilibrium-type systems.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, compact, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g(x)\geq0\) and \(g(x)=0\iff 0\in F(x)+N_C(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical primal gap on a compact convex feasible set.

source_refs.locator: 10.2.2 The linearized gap function p. 921
source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(x\in C\), the primal gap-function residual is
\[
g(x)=\max_{y\in C}\langle F(x),x-y\rangle.
\]
Compactness makes the maximum finite and attained. Choosing \(y=x\) gives \(g(x)\geq0\). Moreover,
\[
g(x)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \langle F(x),y-x\rangle\geq0\ \text{for every }y\in C
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 0\in F(x)+N_C(x).
\]
Thus \(g\) is an exact scalar residual for the variational inequality on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The primal gap maximizes violation of the variational inequality; it is nonnegative and vanishes exactly at solutions.
knowledge_statements.title: Gap-Function Residuals

source_witnesses.locator: 10.2.2 The linearized gap function p. 921
source_witnesses.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of finite-valued primal gaps on unbounded feasible sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C=\mathbb R\) and \(F(x)=1\). Then for every \(x\in C\),
\[
g(x)=\sup_{y\in\mathbb R}(x-y)=+\infty.
\]
Thus the unregularized primal gap need not be a finite merit function on an unbounded feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On an unbounded set, the classical primal gap may be infinite everywhere.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g(x)=+\infty\) for every \(x\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded-Domain Gap Failure

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Support-Function Representation of the Primal Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural formula and finiteness boundary for the classical primal VI gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a nonempty closed convex set \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) and \(x\in C\), the extended-valued primal gap
\[
g(x)=\sup_{y\in C}\langle F(x),x-y\rangle
\]
satisfies
\[
g(x)=\langle F(x),x\rangle+\sigma_C(-F(x)).
\]
Consequently, \(g(x)<+\infty\) exactly when \(-F(x)\in\operatorname{dom}\sigma_C\). Attainment is equivalent to attainment of the support supremum in direction \(-F(x)\). Compactness of \(C\) is sufficient for finiteness and attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The primal gap is a support-function evaluation, exposing its exact finiteness and attainment conditions.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g(x)=\langle F(x),x\rangle+\sigma_C(-F(x))\), with finiteness equivalent to \(-F(x)\in\operatorname{dom}\sigma_C\).
knowledge_statements.title: Support-Function Representation of the Primal Gap

children.title: Merit-Function Residuals
children.top_down_role: Scalar residuals designed to measure solution quality through merit functions.

assumptions_latex: \(S\) is the solution set of a problem on a domain \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r_m(x)=0\iff x\in S\) precisely when \(m\) is exact.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact nonnegative merit functions viewed as scalar residuals.

source_refs.locator: 10.4 Merit Function Based Algorithms p. 947
source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A merit function \(m:D\to[0,+\infty]\) is exact for the solution set \(S\subset D\) when
\[
m(x)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x\in S.
\]
Its associated scalar residual may be taken as \(r_m(x)=\sqrt{m(x)}\), with the convention \(\sqrt{+\infty}=+\infty\). Then \(r_m\geq0\), \(r_m^{-1}(0)=S\), and minimizing \(m\) is equivalent to minimizing \(r_m\). Exactness identifies solutions but, without an additional growth condition, does not itself imply an error bound relating \(r_m(x)\) to \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative merit function yields an exact residual when its zero set is exactly the solution set; exactness alone gives no error bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Merit-Function Residuals

source_witnesses.locator: 10.4 Merit Function Based Algorithms p. 947
source_witnesses.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Quadratic Merit Growth and Residual Error Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence between quadratic growth of a merit value and a linear error bound for its square-root residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(m:D\to[0,+\infty]\) be exact for a nonempty set \(S\), and set \(r_m=\sqrt m\). On any region \(U\subset D\),
\[
\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le\kappa r_m(x)\quad(x\in U)
\]
is equivalent to
\[
m(x)\ge\kappa^{-2}\operatorname{dist}^2(x,S)\quad(x\in U).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A square-root merit residual controls distance linearly exactly when the merit value grows quadratically away from its zero set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le\kappa r_m(x)\iff m(x)\ge\kappa^{-2}\operatorname{dist}^2(x,S)\) on the same region.
knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Merit Growth and Residual Error Bounds

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Zero-set and minimizer invariance under increasing changes of merit scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(m:D\to[0,+\infty]\) be exact for \(S\), and let \(\theta:[0,+\infty]\to[0,+\infty]\) be strictly increasing with \(\theta(0)=0\). Then \(\widetilde m=\theta\circ m\) is exact for the same set and
\[
\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in D}\widetilde m(x)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in D}m(x)=S.
\]
The associated quantitative residual scale need not be preserved unless \(\theta\) is locally comparable to the identity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strictly increasing reparameterizations preserve exact zeros and minimizers but may change the quantitative residual scale.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\theta\circ m)^{-1}(0)=S\) and \(\arg\min(\theta\circ m)=S\).
knowledge_statements.title: Monotone Reparameterization of Merit Functions

children.title: Variational-Inequality Gap Families
children.top_down_role: Gap residual constructions specialized to variational inequalities.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g_a(x)\geq g_b(x)\geq0\) and \(g_a(x)-g_b(x)=0\iff 0\in F(x)+N_C(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regularized-gap and D-gap family for finite-dimensional variational inequalities.

source_refs.locator: 10.2.1 The regularized gap function p. 913
source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

source_refs.locator: 10.3 The D-Gap Merit Function p. 930
source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(c>0\), define
\[
g_c(x)=\max_{y\in C}\left\{\langle F(x),x-y\rangle-\frac c2\|x-y\|^2\right\}.
\]
The maximizer is \(P_C(x-c^{-1}F(x))\), so \(g_c(x)\) is finite and nonnegative. For \(0<a<b\), the D-gap member
\[
d_{a,b}(x)=g_a(x)-g_b(x)
\]
is nonnegative and satisfies \(d_{a,b}(x)=0\) if and only if \(x=P_C(x-c^{-1}F(x))\), equivalently \(0\in F(x)+N_C(x)\). Hence both regularized-gap and D-gap constructions supply exact scalar residual families.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Regularized gaps are finite projection-based merit functions, while the difference of two parameterized gaps is a nonnegative exact D-gap residual.
knowledge_statements.title: Variational-Inequality Gap Families

source_witnesses.locator: 10.2.1 The regularized gap function p. 913
source_witnesses.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

source_witnesses.locator: 10.3 The D-Gap Merit Function p. 930
source_witnesses.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual-gap member of the finite-dimensional variational-inequality gap family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a nonempty convex set \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\), define
\[
g_D(x)=\sup_{y\in C}\langle F(y),x-y\rangle,
\qquad x\in C.
\]
Then \(g_D(x)\ge0\), and \(g_D(x)=0\) exactly when \(x\) solves the Minty variational inequality. If \(F\) is continuous and monotone on \(C\), the Minty and Stampacchia solution sets coincide. The gap is finite, for example, when \(C\) is compact and \(F\) is continuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual gap certifies Minty solutions; under continuity and monotonicity these are exactly the ordinary VI solutions.
assumptions_latex: For equivalence with the Stampacchia VI, \(F\) is continuous and monotone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g_D(x)=0\iff x\) solves the Minty VI; under continuity and monotonicity this is equivalent to the Stampacchia VI.
knowledge_statements.title: Minty Dual Gap

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative comparison of the D-gap with its two projected displacements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(c>0\), let
\[
y_c(x)=P_C(x-c^{-1}F(x)),\qquad R_c(x)=x-y_c(x),
\]
and define \(g_c\) and \(d_{a,b}=g_a-g_b\) with \(0<a<b\). Then
\[
\frac{b-a}{2}\|R_b(x)\|^2\le d_{a,b}(x)\le\frac{b-a}{2}\|R_a(x)\|^2.
\]
Thus \(\sqrt{d_{a,b}}\) is bounded between explicit multiples of the two projection displacements and has their common VI zero set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The D-gap lies between explicit multiples of the squared projection residuals at its two regularization parameters.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.

notation.meaning: projection displacement associated with parameter c

knowledge_statements.title: D-Gap Residual Sandwich

children.title: Complementarity Merit Families
children.top_down_role: Merit residual constructions specialized to complementarity systems.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Differentiability obtained by squaring the Fischer–Burmeister complementarity equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\phi(a,b)=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}-a-b\) and \(\psi(a,b)=\tfrac12\phi(a,b)^2\). Then \(\psi\in C^1(\mathbb R^2)\), \(\nabla\psi(0,0)=0\), and for \((a,b)\ne(0,0)\),
\[
\nabla\psi(a,b)=\phi(a,b)\left(\frac{a}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}-1,\frac{b}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}-1\right).
\]
Moreover, \(\psi(a,b)=0\) exactly when \(a\ge0\), \(b\ge0\), and \(ab=0\). If \(A,B\) are continuously differentiable vector mappings, the sum of their componentwise \(\psi\)-terms is a continuously differentiable exact complementarity merit function.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Squaring the Fischer–Burmeister equation gives a continuously differentiable merit function with exactly the complementarity zero set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\psi=\frac12\phi^2\in C^1(\mathbb R^2)\) and \(\psi^{-1}(0)=\{(a,b):a\ge0,\ b\ge0,\ ab=0\}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Fischer–Burmeister Merit

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical componentwise minimum representation of orthant complementarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(a,b\in\mathbb R\),
\[
\min\{a,b\}=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad a\ge0,\ b\ge0,\ ab=0.
\]
For arbitrary mappings \(A,B:D\to\mathbb R^m\), define the minimum componentwise and set
\[
r_{\min}(x)=\|\min\{A(x),B(x)\}\|.
\]
Then \(r_{\min}(x)=0\) exactly when every pair \((A_i(x),B_i(x))\) is complementary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The componentwise minimum is an exact residual for nonnegative-orthant complementarity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r_{\min}(x)=0\iff A(x)\ge0,\ B(x)\ge0,\ A_i(x)B_i(x)=0\) for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Function Complementarity Residual
Complementarity Merit Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fischer–Burmeister residuals for componentwise complementarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(a,b\in\mathbb R\), define
\[
\phi(a,b)=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}-a-b.
\]
Then
\[
\phi(a,b)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad a\geq0,\quad b\geq0,\quad ab=0.
\]
Let \(D\) be a nonempty set, let \(m\in\mathbb N\), and let \(A,B:D\to\mathbb R^m\). Define \(\Phi:D\to\mathbb R^m\) componentwise by \(\Phi_i(x)=\phi(A_i(x),B_i(x))\). The residual and merit function
\[
r_{\mathrm{FB}}(x)=\|\Phi(x)\|,
\qquad
m_{\mathrm{FB}}(x)=\frac12\|\Phi(x)\|^2
\]
vanish exactly when \(A_i(x)\geq0\), \(B_i(x)\geq0\), and \(A_i(x)B_i(x)=0\) for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Fischer–Burmeister function represents scalar complementarity as one equation. Applied componentwise, its vector norm and squared norm vanish exactly at componentwise complementary pairs.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is a nonempty set, \(m\in\mathbb N\), and \(A,B:D\to\mathbb R^m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\phi(a,b)=0\iff a\geq0,\ b\geq0,\ ab=0\), and \(r_{\mathrm{FB}}(x)=0\) exactly when all component pairs are complementary.

children.title: Exactness Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Settings where vanishing or small scalar residuals fail to characterize solution proximity sharply.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Small Merit Values Need Not Imply Proximity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global failure of proximity certification by an exact merit function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
On \(D=\mathbb R\), let \(S=\{0\}\) and \(m(x)=x^2e^{-x^2}\). Then \(m\ge0\) and \(m^{-1}(0)=S\). Nevertheless,
\[
m(k)\to0\quad\text{and}\quad\operatorname{dist}(k,S)=k\to+\infty
\]
as \(k\to+\infty\). Thus exactness alone does not make small merit values a global proximity certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact merit function can approach zero along points escaping arbitrarily far from its solution set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m^{-1}(0)=\{0\}\), but \(m(k)\to0\) while \(\operatorname{dist}(k,\{0\})\to+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.title: Small Merit Values Need Not Imply Proximity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effect of scalar residual transformations on exactness and linear error bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(r:D\to[0,+\infty]\) have zero set \(S\), and let \(\psi:[0,+\infty]\to[0,+\infty]\) satisfy \(\psi(0)=0\) and \(\psi(t)>0\) for every \(t>0\). Then \(m=\psi\circ r\) is exact for \(S\). If
\[
\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le\kappa r(x)
\]
locally and \(\psi(t)\ge ct\) for all sufficiently small \(t\), then
\[
\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le(\kappa/c)m(x)
\]
locally. Exactness imposes no such lower linear growth; in particular, \(\psi(t)=t^p\) with \(p>1\) preserves zeros but is not bounded below by a positive multiple of \(t\) near zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive scalar transform preserves residual zeros, but linear error-bound transfer requires at least linear growth of the transform near zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\psi\circ r)^{-1}(0)=S\), while linear error-bound transfer requires an additional local lower linear bound on \(\psi\).
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Transform versus Error-Bound Scale

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m^{-1}(0)=S\), but no \(\kappa,\varepsilon>0\) satisfy \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\leq\kappa m(x)\) for all \(|x|<\varepsilon\).
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact zero sets do not guarantee linear residual error bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S=\{0\}\), \(r(x)=|x|\), and \(m(x)=r(x)^2=x^2\). Then \(m(x)\geq0\) and \(m(x)=0\) exactly when \(x\in S\), so \(m\) is an exact merit function. Nevertheless, a linear error bound using \(m\) would require
\[
|x|=\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\leq\kappa x^2
\]
near \(0\). For every fixed \(\kappa>0\), this inequality fails whenever \(0<|x|<1/\kappa\). Thus exactness is invariant under squaring a residual, whereas a linear error-bound modulus is not.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Squaring an exact residual preserves its zeros but can destroy every local linear error bound based on the resulting merit value.
knowledge_statements.title: Exactness Boundaries

children.title: Subdifferential Stationarity Residuals
children.top_down_role: Residual measures based on distance to a subdifferential stationarity set.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r_{\partial f}(x)=0\iff 0\in\partial f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limiting-subdifferential stationarity in finite dimensions.

source_refs.locator: 2.5.2 Specific Normal and Subdifferential Structures p. 235

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), define
\[
r_{\partial f}(x)=\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x))
=\inf\{\|v\|:v\in\partial f(x)\},
\]
with \(r_{\partial f}(x)=+\infty\) when \(\partial f(x)=\varnothing\). Because the limiting subdifferential value is closed in finite dimensions,
\[
r_{\partial f}(x)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 0\in\partial f(x).
\]
Thus the residual measures first-order generalized stationarity; without convexity, its vanishing need not certify local or global minimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distance from zero to the limiting subdifferential is a stationarity residual, but zero residual need not imply minimality in nonconvex problems.
knowledge_statements.title: Subdifferential Stationarity Residuals
