knowledge_statements.statement_title: Necessity of Subgradient Separation for a Convex Error Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local converse complementing the accepted sufficient convex subdifferential criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, let \(S=\{f\le0\}\ne\varnothing\), and let \(\bar x\in S\). If
\[
\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le\kappa[f(x)]_+
\]
holds near \(\bar x\), then, after shrinking the neighborhood, every nearby \(x\) with \(f(x)>0\) satisfies
\[
\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x))\ge\kappa^{-1}.
\]
Together with the accepted sufficient criterion, local convex error bounds are therefore equivalent, up to arbitrarily small changes of constants and neighborhoods, to uniform separation of zero from nearby infeasible subdifferentials.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex inequality, a local error bound also forces nearby infeasible subgradients to stay uniformly away from zero.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex on \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x))\ge\kappa^{-1}\quad\text{for nearby }x\text{ with }f(x)>0.
knowledge_statements.title: Necessity of Subgradient Separation for a Convex Error Bound

children.title: Primal–Dual Route Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Regimes linking slope criteria with subdifferential criteria.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|\nabla f|(x)=\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x))\), so the primal and dual uniform lower-bound criteria coincide.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact primal–dual identification in the proper lower-semicontinuous convex setting.

source_refs.locator: 4.2.2 Pointbased Characterizations of Covering and Metric Regularity p. 394
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\) with \(f(x)>\inf f\), convexity gives the exact identity
\[
 |\nabla f|(x)=\inf\{\|v\|:v\in\partial f(x)\}
 =\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x)).
\]
Consequently, on any prescribed band of nearby infeasible points, the condition \(|\nabla f|(x)\ge\tau\) is equivalent to \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x))\ge\tau\). The slope and subdifferential routes therefore deliver the same error-bound modulus in this setting.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions, strong slope equals distance to the convex subdifferential, making the primal and dual certificates identical.
knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Route Correspondence

source_witnesses.locator: 4.2.2 Pointbased Characterizations of Covering and Metric Regularity p. 394

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth extension of slope–subdifferential correspondence beyond convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(f:\mathbb R^n	o\mathbb R\) is continuously differentiable, then for every \(x\), \[|
abla f|(x)=\|
abla f(x)\|=\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x)),\] where the limiting and Clarke subdifferentials both equal \(\{
abla f(x)\}\). Thus the slope and subdifferential-separation criteria coincide without convexity in the smooth regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For continuously differentiable functions, strong slope, gradient norm, and distance to the limiting or Clarke subdifferential coincide.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|\nabla f|(x)=\|\nabla f(x)\|=\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x))\).

notation.meaning: limiting or Clarke subdifferential, both singleton in the smooth case

children.title: Route Failure Boundaries

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Clarke Separation Can Fail While the Slope Certificate Is Exact
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonsmooth nonconvex boundary separating the strong-slope route from a Clarke-subdifferential route.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x):=1-|x|\) and \(S:=\{x:f(x)\le0\}=(-\infty,-1]\cup[1,+\infty)\). For \(|x|<1\), \[\operatorname{dist}(x,S)=1-|x|=[f(x)]_+,\qquad |\nabla f|(x)=1.\] At \(x=0\), however, \[\partial_Cf(0)=[-1,1],\qquad\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial_Cf(0))=0.\] Thus the exact slope certificate holds while uniform Clarke-subdifferential separation fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the inverted absolute-value function, strong slope certifies the exact error bound, while the Clarke subdifferential contains zero at an infeasible cusp.
assumptions_latex: \(f(x)=1-|x|\), and the dual route uses the Clarke subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The slope criterion succeeds with constant \(1\), whereas uniform Clarke-subdifferential separation fails.
knowledge_statements.title: Clarke Separation Can Fail While the Slope Certificate Is Exact

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No finite \(\kappa\) gives \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le\kappa[f(x)]_+\) near \(0\).

notation.meaning: strong slope, equal here to the derivative magnitude

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vanishing first-order certificates expose the boundary of linear error bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(x\neq0\),
\[
 \frac{\operatorname{dist}(x,S)}{[f(x)]_+}
 =\frac{|x|}{x^2}=\frac1{|x|}\longrightarrow+\infty
 \quad\text{as }x\to0.
\]
Hence no local linear error bound exists at \(0\). Simultaneously,
\[
 |\nabla f|(x)=2|x|\to0,
 \qquad
 \operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x))=2|x|\to0,
\]
so neither route admits a positive uniform certificate constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The function squared distance to zero has quadratic, not linear, growth; both slope and subdifferential certificate constants vanish near its solution.
knowledge_statements.title: Route Failure Boundaries

children.title: Luo–Tseng Error-Bound Family
children.top_down_role: Proximal and projected residual bounds used in structured optimization.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-point representation underlying proximal and projected Luo–Tseng residuals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be continuously differentiable, let \(g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, closed, and convex, and let \(\gamma>0\). For \[R_\gamma(x):=x-\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma g}(x-\gamma\nabla h(x)),\] one has \[R_\gamma(x)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad0\in\nabla h(x)+\partial g(x).\] If \(h\) is convex, these zeros are exactly the minimizers of \(h+g\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The proximal-gradient residual vanishes exactly at composite stationary points and, when the smooth term is convex, exactly at minimizers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_\gamma(x)=0\iff0\in\nabla h(x)+\partial g(x)\), with equivalence to minimization when \(h\) is convex.

notation.meaning: proximal mapping of the scaled convex function

knowledge_statements.title: Proximal-Gradient Residual Zeros

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specialization of the proximal-gradient residual to a closed convex constraint set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex and set \(g=\delta_C\). Then
\[
\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma g}=P_C,
\qquad R_\gamma(x)=x-P_C(x-\gamma\nabla h(x)).
\]
Thus a Luo–Tseng bound for \(h+\delta_C\) is a projected-gradient residual bound for the constrained stationary set, or for the minimizer set when the problem is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choosing a convex indicator as the nonsmooth term turns the proximal-gradient residual into the projected-gradient residual.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: R_\gamma(x)=x-P_C(x-\gamma\nabla h(x)).
knowledge_statements.title: Projected-Gradient Specialization

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Linear Proximal-Gradient Convergence Under a Luo–Tseng Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical qualitative rate consequence in the convex fixed-stepsize regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F=h+g\) be proper, closed, and convex, where \(h\) is differentiable with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient and \(g\) is proper, closed, and convex. Fix \(0<\gamma<1/L\) and set
\[
x_{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma g}(x_k-\gamma\nabla h(x_k)).
\]
Assume \(X^*=\operatorname*{argmin}F\ne\varnothing\) and that a Luo–Tseng error bound for \(R_\gamma\) holds on the initial sublevel set whenever the residual is sufficiently small. Then the objective gaps converge eventually Q-linearly and the distances \(\operatorname{dist}(x_k,X^*)\) converge R-linearly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For convex fixed-step proximal gradient, a local Luo–Tseng residual bound together with standard descent assumptions yields eventual linear objective and solution-distance convergence.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) is convex, differentiable, and has \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient.
\(0<\gamma<1/L\), \(X^*\ne\varnothing\), and the iterates remain in the initial sublevel set.
A Luo–Tseng error bound for the unscaled residual holds on that sublevel whenever the residual is sufficiently small.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F(x_k)-\min F\text{ converges eventually Q-linearly and }\operatorname{dist}(x_k,X^*)\text{ converges R-linearly}.
knowledge_statements.title: Local Linear Proximal-Gradient Convergence Under a Luo–Tseng Bound

assumptions_latex: \(F=h+g\) on \(\mathbb R^n\), where \(h\) is continuously differentiable and \(g\) is proper, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\le\kappa\|R_\gamma(x)\|\) on a prescribed local level-residual region.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard local level-set form of the Luo–Tseng proximal-residual bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A Luo–Tseng error bound holds on the level \(\zeta>\inf F\) if there exist \(\kappa>0\) and \(\varepsilon>0\) such that
\[
 F(x)\le\zeta,
 \qquad
 \|R_\gamma(x)\|\le\varepsilon
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\le\kappa\|R_\gamma(x)\|.
\]
The family includes projected-gradient bounds by taking \(g\) to be the indicator of a nonempty closed convex feasible set, in which case the proximal mapping is the metric projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Luo–Tseng bound controls distance to the solution set by a small proximal-gradient residual on a fixed objective level set.
knowledge_statements.title: Luo–Tseng Error-Bound Family

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(h(x)=x^2/(1+x^2)\) and \(g\equiv0\), the gradient residual tends to zero as \(|x|\to\infty\) while distance to the unique minimizer diverges. However, \(h\) is nonconvex, so this example does not validate the necessity of level localization under the still-unverified classical Luo–Tseng assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The proposed remote-branch example is mathematically sound but lies outside the likely classical convex composite regime.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The example is deferred as evidence for the classical Luo–Tseng boundary.

assumptions_latex: \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\) are closed subsets of a normed space and \(C:=\bigcap_{i=1}^m C_i\neq\varnothing\).
\(U\) is a specified neighborhood or region.

source_refs.locator: 5.4.1 Linear Subextremality of Set Systems p. 110
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The finite system \(\{C_i\}_{i=1}^m\) is linearly regular on \(U\) if there exists \(\kappa>0\) such that
\[
 \operatorname{dist}\!\left(x,\bigcap_{i=1}^m C_i\right)
 \le \kappa\max_{1\le i\le m}\operatorname{dist}(x,C_i)
 \quad\text{for every }x\in U.
\]
It is locally linearly regular at \(\bar x\in C\) when this inequality holds on some neighborhood of \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linear regularity bounds distance to a finite intersection by the largest distance to an individual set.
knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Regular Set Systems

source_witnesses.locator: 5.4.1 Linear Subextremality of Set Systems p. 110
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tangential Convex Intersection Can Fail Linear Regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonempty intersection and convexity alone do not ensure local linear regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C_1:=\{(u,v)\in\mathbb R^2:v\ge u^2\}\), \(C_2:=\{(u,v)\in\mathbb R^2:v\le0\}\), and \(x_t:=(t,0)\). Then \(C_1\cap C_2=\{(0,0)\}\), \(\operatorname{dist}(x_t,C_2)=0\), \(\operatorname{dist}(x_t,C_1)=O(t^2)\), and \(\operatorname{dist}(x_t,C_1\cap C_2)=|t|\). Hence no finite local linear-regularity modulus exists at the origin.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two closed convex sets meeting tangentially can have quadratic individual violation but linear distance to their intersection, so local linear regularity fails.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The family \(\{C_1,C_2\}\) is not locally linearly regular at \((0,0)\).

notation.meaning: test points approaching the tangential intersection

knowledge_statements.title: Tangential Convex Intersection Can Fail Linear Regularity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex sufficient condition for bounded linear regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\subset\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty closed convex sets with \(\bigcap_i\operatorname{ri}C_i\neq\varnothing\). For every bounded set \(B\subset\mathbb R^n\), there is \(\kappa_B<+\infty\) such that \[\operatorname{dist}\!\left(x,\bigcap_iC_i\right)\le\kappa_B\max_i\operatorname{dist}(x,C_i)\qquad(x\in B).\] Consequently the family is locally linearly regular at every point of its intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite closed convex family having a common relative-interior point is linearly regular on every bounded region.
assumptions_latex: \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\) are nonempty closed convex subsets of \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every bounded \(B\), the linear-regularity inequality holds on \(B\) with some modulus \(\kappa_B\).

notation.meaning: relative interior of a convex set

knowledge_statements.title: Piecewise-Structured Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local metric-subregularity error bound for finite piecewise-polyhedral multifunctions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
There exist a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and a constant \(\kappa>0\) such that
\[
\operatorname{dist}\bigl(x,F^{-1}(\bar y)\bigr)
\le \kappa\operatorname{dist}\bigl(\bar y,F(x)\bigr)
\quad\text{for every }x\in U.
\]
Thus a multifunction whose graph is locally a finite union of closed convex polyhedra is metrically subregular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multifunction with a locally finite piecewise-polyhedral graph admits a local residual error bound at each graph point for the fixed reference value.
assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^m\) has a graph that is locally a finite union of closed convex polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(x,F^{-1}(\bar y))\le\kappa\operatorname{dist}(\bar y,F(x))\) locally at \(\bar x\).

 \operatorname{dist}(x,S)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-equivalence transfer across finite structural representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If
\[
 \operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le\kappa_r r(x)
 \quad\text{for all }x\in U,
\]
then \(r(x)\le a^{-1}q(x)\) implies
\[
 \operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le\frac{\kappa_r}{a}q(x).
\]
Conversely, an estimate \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le\kappa_q q(x)\), together with \(q(x)\le b r(x)\), yields \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le b\kappa_q r(x)\). Thus locally equivalent residuals preserve the existence of an error bound while rescaling its modulus.

children.title: Weak Sharp Minima
children.top_down_role: Linear-growth regimes and their residual interpretations.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Quadratic Growth Is Not Weak Sharpness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar boundary between quadratic and linear objective growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=x^2\) on \(\mathbb R\), \(S=\{0\}\) and \(f(x)-f^*=x^2\). For every \(\alpha>0\) and every neighborhood of \(0\), some \(x\ne0\) in that neighborhood satisfies \(x^2<\alpha|x|\). Hence the minimum is not locally weak sharp despite quadratic growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The squared function has quadratic growth but no positive linear-growth modulus near its minimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No \(\alpha>0\) gives \(x^2\ge\alpha\operatorname{dist}(x,\{0\})\) throughout a neighborhood of \(0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Growth Is Not Weak Sharpness

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global weak sharpness from a uniform slope gap on a complete metric space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,d)\) be complete and let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, bounded below, and attain its infimum on \(S\). If \(|\nabla f|(x)\ge\alpha>0\) for every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\setminus S\), then, for every \(0<\beta<\alpha\), \[f(x)-f^*\ge\beta\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\qquad(x\in X).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A uniform positive strong-slope gap away from the minimizer set certifies global weak sharpness with every smaller modulus.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, bounded below, and attains its infimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(0<\beta<\alpha\), \(f(x)-f^*\ge\beta\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\) for all \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.title: Strong-Slope Certificate for Weak Sharpness

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global weak sharpness for proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions on a Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex on a Hilbert space, with nonempty minimizer set \(S\). For \(\alpha>0\), \[f(x)-f^*\ge\alpha\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\quad(x\in X)\] holds if and only if \[\alpha\mathbb B\cap N_S(s)\subseteq\partial f(s)\quad\text{for every }s\in S.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex objective, weak sharpness is equivalent to every normal direction of size at most the sharpness modulus being a subgradient at each minimizer.
assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Global weak sharpness with modulus \(\alpha\) is equivalent to \(\alpha\mathbb B\cap N_S(s)\subseteq\partial f(s)\) for every \(s\in S\).

notation.meaning: convex normal cone to the minimizer set

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Subgradient Characterization

assumptions_latex: \(f:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is defined on a metric space subset \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)-f^*\ge\alpha\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\) on the specified region.

The minimum of \(f\) is weak sharp with modulus \(\alpha>0\) on a region \(U\subset C\) if

children.title: Quadratic Growth
children.top_down_role: Second-order growth regimes linked to stability and subdifferential regularity.

children.title: Convex Quadratic Growth
children.top_down_role: Quadratic growth for convex functions and monotone subdifferentials.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Flat Convex Minimum without Quadratic Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar failure when a convex objective is flatter than quadratic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f(x)=x^4\) on \(\mathbb R\), the unique minimizer is \(0\), but no \(c,\varepsilon>0\) satisfy
\[
x^4\ge cx^2\qquad( |x|<\varepsilon).
\]
Also \(\partial f(x)=\{4x^3\}\), and no \(\kappa,\varepsilon>0\) satisfy
\[
|x|\le4\kappa|x|^3\qquad(|x|<\varepsilon).
\]
Thus uniqueness and strict convexity do not imply quadratic growth or strong subdifferential subregularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The strictly convex function x to the fourth has a unique minimizer but is too flat for quadratic growth or strong subregularity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\) is the unique minimizer, but quadratic growth and strong metric subregularity of \(\partial f\) both fail at \((0,0)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Flat Convex Minimum without Quadratic Growth

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separation of set-relative quadratic growth from strong convexity and isolated growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f(u,v)=\tfrac12u^2\) on \(\mathbb R^2\),
\[
S=\operatorname*{argmin}f=\{0\}\times\mathbb R,
\qquad
f(u,v)=\tfrac12\operatorname{dist}^2((u,v),S).
\]
Thus convex quadratic growth relative to the full minimizer set holds exactly, although the minimizers are nonisolated and \(f\) is not strongly convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Set-relative convex quadratic growth permits a continuum of minimizers and is strictly weaker than strong convexity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f=\tfrac12\operatorname{dist}^2(\cdot,S)\) with nonisolated \(S\), while \(f\) is not strongly convex.
knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Growth with Nonisolated Minimizers

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local equivalence between growth relative to the minimizer set and subregularity of the convex subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, closed, and convex, let \(S=\operatorname*{argmin}f\ne\varnothing\), and let \(\bar x\in S\). The following local properties at \(\bar x\) are equivalent:
\[
f(x)\ge f^*+c\operatorname{dist}^2(x,S)\quad\text{for some }c>0,
\]
and
\[
\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le\kappa\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x))
\quad\text{for some }\kappa>0.
\]
Equivalently, convex quadratic growth holds exactly when \(\partial f\) is metrically subregular at \((\bar x,0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a closed convex function, local quadratic growth relative to all minimizers is equivalent to metric subregularity of its subdifferential at zero.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, closed, and convex on \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Local quadratic growth at \(\bar x\) is equivalent to metric subregularity of \(\partial f\) at \((\bar x,0)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Convex Quadratic Growth–Subregularity Equivalence

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Isolated-minimizer specialization of convex quadratic growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\) be proper, closed, and convex with \(0\in\partial f(\bar x)\). The local estimate
\[
f(x)\ge f(\bar x)+c\|x-\bar x\|^2
\]
for some \(c>0\) is equivalent to strong metric subregularity of \(\partial f\) at \((\bar x,0)\), namely
\[
\|x-\bar x\|\le\kappa\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x))
\]
locally. Either property makes \(\bar x\) an isolated minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quadratic growth about one isolated convex minimizer is equivalent to strong metric subregularity of the convex subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Isolated quadratic growth at \(\bar x\) is equivalent to strong metric subregularity of \(\partial f\) at \((\bar x,0)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Isolated Convex Growth–Strong Subregularity Equivalence

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)\ge f^*+\frac\alpha2\operatorname{dist}^2(x,S)\) locally around \(\bar x\).
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic growth measured relative to the full convex minimizer set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(f\) has convex quadratic growth at \(\bar x\) with modulus \(\alpha>0\) if there exists a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) such that
\[
 f(x)-f^*\ge\frac{\alpha}{2}\operatorname{dist}^2(x,S)
 \quad\text{for every }x\in U.
\]
The distance is taken to the complete minimizer set, so the condition permits nonisolated minimizers while imposing second-order growth in directions transverse to \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex quadratic growth bounds objective excess below by a positive multiple of squared distance to the entire minimizer set.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex Quadratic Growth

children.title: Prox-Regular Quadratic Growth
children.top_down_role: Quadratic growth in locally nonconvex variationally regular settings.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
\(0\in\partial f(\bar x)\), and \(f\) is prox-regular and subdifferentially continuous at \((\bar x,0)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)\ge f(\bar x)+\frac\alpha2\|x-\bar x\|^2\) locally.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Isolated local quadratic growth in a prox-regular nonconvex setting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Prox-regular quadratic growth at the stationary point \(\bar x\) holds with modulus \(\alpha>0\) if there exists \(\delta>0\) such that
\[
 f(x)
 \ge f(\bar x)+\frac{\alpha}{2}\|x-\bar x\|^2
 \quad\text{whenever }\|x-\bar x\|<\delta.
\]
Together with prox-regularity and subdifferential continuity at \((\bar x,0)\), this is the locally nonconvex quadratic-growth regime associated with an isolated strong local minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the prox-regular setting, quadratic growth requires objective values to rise quadratically away from a stationary local minimizer.
knowledge_statements.title: Prox-Regular Quadratic Growth

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed isolated quadratic-growth condition is coherent, but the exact role of prox-regularity, subdifferential continuity, stationarity, and the asserted association with isolated strong local minimality requires an authoritative source.

children.title: Perturbation-Stable Quadratic Growth Family
children.top_down_role: Growth regimes stable under localized linear perturbations.

children.title: Uniform Quadratic Growth
children.top_down_role: Quadratic growth controlled uniformly over a localized family.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional smooth sufficient condition for uniform quadratic growth under nearby linear tilts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\in C^2\) near \(\bar x\in\mathbb R^n\), with \(\nabla f(\bar x)=0\) and \(\nabla^2f(\bar x)\succeq mI\) for some \(m>0\). For every \(\mu\in(0,m)\), there exist neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(V\) of \(0\) such that, for each \(v\in V\), \(\nabla f(x)=v\) has a unique solution \(x(v)\in U\), and
\[
f(x)-\langle v,x\rangle\ge f(x(v))-\langle v,x(v)\rangle+\frac{\mu}{2}\|x-x(v)\|^2
\quad(x\in U).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-definite Hessian at a stationary point yields a common local quadratic-growth modulus for every sufficiently small linear tilt.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is twice continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\in\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every \(\mu<m\) is locally admissible as a common growth modulus for all sufficiently small tilts.
knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Positive-Definite Hessian Criterion

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Hilbert space and \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
For every \(v\) near \(0\), the localized tilt problem has a selected minimizer \(x(v)\) near \(\bar x=x(0)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_v\) has uniform quadratic growth along \(x(v)\), with constants independent of \(v\).

notation.meaning: selected local minimizer of the tilted objective

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Localized uniform growth for the family of linearly tilted objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Uniform quadratic growth at \((\bar x,0)\) means that there exist neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(V\) of \(0\), and a constant \(\mu>0\), such that for every \(v\in V\), the selected point \(x(v)\in U\) minimizes \(f_v\) locally and
\[
f(x)-\langle v,x\rangle\ge f(x(v))-\langle v,x(v)\rangle+\frac{\mu}{2}\lVert x-x(v)\rVert^2
\]
for every \(x\in U\). The same neighborhoods and modulus \(\mu\) must work for all \(v\in V\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every sufficiently small linear tilt has a nearby selected minimizer, and all tilted objectives grow quadratically away from their minimizers with one common modulus.
knowledge_statements.title: Uniform Quadratic Growth

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the leaf and is internally coherent, but no citation supports the precise uniform localization, selection, and common-modulus formulation. A source is needed to determine whether uniqueness or a more restricted neighborhood around each selected minimizer is required.

children.title: Tilted Quadratic Growth
children.top_down_role: Quadratic growth under localized linear perturbations.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Hilbert space and \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
The localized argmin set below is nonempty for all sufficiently small tilts.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed inequality is the quadratic-growth predicate for the objective tilted by \(v\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic growth expressed relative to the localized minimizer set of each tilt.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and define
\[
M(v):=\mathop{\operatorname{argmin}}_{z\in U}\{f(z)-\langle v,z\rangle\}.
\]
The tilt indexed by \(v\) has quadratic growth on \(U\) with modulus \(\mu_v>0\) if
\[
f(x)-\langle v,x\rangle\ge \inf_{z\in U}\{f(z)-\langle v,z\rangle\}+\frac{\mu_v}{2}\operatorname{dist}(x,M(v))^2
\]
for all \(x\in U\). Uniform tilted quadratic growth additionally requires a positive lower bound for \(\mu_v\) over all sufficiently small \(v\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tilted objective grows at least quadratically with distance from its localized minimizer set; uniformity requires one positive lower modulus for all small tilts.
knowledge_statements.title: Tilted Quadratic Growth

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition is appropriate for the tilted-growth leaf, and the plain and LaTeX statements agree. A source is required for the exact localized-argmin-set formulation and the asserted uniformity criterion.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong Convexity Certificate for All Linear Tilts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mathematically sound but canonically owned by Uniform Quadratic Growth because it supplies one common modulus for every tilt.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and \(\mu\)-strongly convex on a Hilbert space. For any \(v\in X\), if \(x(v)\in\operatorname{argmin}_x\{f(x)-\langle v,x\rangle\}\), then \(x(v)\) is unique and
\[
f(x)-\langle v,x\rangle\ge f(x(v))-\langle v,x(v)\rangle+\frac{\mu}{2}\|x-x(v)\|^2
\quad(x\in X).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong convexity preserves one common quadratic-growth modulus under all attained linear tilts.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and \(\mu\)-strongly convex.
The tilted objective attains its minimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every attained tilt has a unique minimizer and the same growth modulus \(\mu\).
knowledge_statements.title: Strong Convexity Certificate for All Linear Tilts

intermediate_metadata.reason: This leaf owns the quadratic-growth predicate for each localized tilted objective. The proposed all-tilt strong-convexity certificate is deferred as misplaced; common-modulus results belong to Uniform Quadratic Growth, persistence to Perturbation-Stable Growth, and degeneracy to Tilt-Stability Boundaries.

children.title: Perturbation-Stable Growth
children.top_down_role: Persistence of localized growth across nearby tilts.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Hilbert space and \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
A perturbation family \(p\mapsto h_p\) is defined near a reference parameter \(\bar p\), with \(h_{\bar p}=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Quadratic growth persists locally with a parameter-independent positive modulus.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract local persistence predicate; admissible perturbations must be specified in applications.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Quadratic growth of \(f\) at \(\bar x\) is stable for the family \((h_p)\) if there exist neighborhoods \(P\) of \(\bar p\) and \(U\) of \(\bar x\), and \(\mu>0\), such that \(M(p):=\operatorname{argmin}_{z\in U}f_p(z)\) is nonempty for every \(p\in P\) and
\[
f_p(x)\ge \inf_{z\in U}f_p(z)+\frac{\mu}{2}\operatorname{dist}(x,M(p))^2
\]
for every \((p,x)\in P\times U\). Stability includes persistence of localized minimizers and uniformity of \(U\) and \(\mu\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under every admissible nearby perturbation, localized minimizers persist and the perturbed objectives retain quadratic growth with common neighborhoods and modulus.
knowledge_statements.title: Perturbation-Stable Growth

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is a plausible abstract property, but the admissible parameter space, regularity of the perturbations, and meaning of nearby parameters are unspecified. Without a cited definition or fixed perturbation class, the mathematical scope cannot be verified.

children.title: Tilt-Stability Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Regimes where quadratic growth loses uniformity under tilting.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) is given by \(f(x)=x^4\), with reference minimizer \(\bar x=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An isolated minimizer need not be tilt-stable or satisfy quadratic growth.

notation.meaning: minimizer of the linearly tilted quartic

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete boundary showing that strict isolated minimality is weaker than tilt stability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The point \(0\) is the unique global minimizer of \(f(x)=x^4\), but no \(\mu>0\) satisfies \(x^4\ge (\mu/2)x^2\) throughout a neighborhood of \(0\). For the tilted objective \(x\mapsto x^4-vx\), the unique minimizer is
\[
x(v)=\sqrt[3]{v/4}.
\]
Hence \(|x(v)-x(0)|/|v|=4^{-1/3}|v|^{-2/3}\to+\infty\) as \(v\to0\). The localized minimizer mapping is therefore not Lipschitz at \(0\), so \(0\) is not a tilt-stable local minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The quartic has a unique strict minimizer, but lacks quadratic growth; its tilted minimizer varies like the cube root of the tilt and is not Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.title: Tilt-Stability Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The quartic example correctly targets a tilt-stability boundary and the counterexample kind is suitable. Its nontrivial failure claims have no cited source or explicit standard-field rationale, so evidence is still required.

children.title: Tilt Stability
children.top_down_role: Stable locally unique minimizer behavior under linear tilts.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict Minimality Does Not Imply Tilt Stability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar boundary between strict minimality and Lipschitz tilt response.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=x^4\), the origin is a strict global minimizer, while the unique minimizer of \(x^4-vx\) is \(M(v)=\sqrt[3]{v/4}\). Since \(|M(v)-M(0)|/|v|=4^{-1/3}|v|^{-2/3}\to\infty\), \(M\) is not Lipschitz at \(0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The quartic has a strict minimizer, but its minimizer under linear tilts varies only Hölder-continuously, so strict minimality does not imply tilt stability.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M(v)=\sqrt[3]{v/4}\) is not Lipschitz at \(0\), so \(0\) is not tilt-stable.
knowledge_statements.title: Strict Minimality Does Not Imply Tilt Stability

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional twice continuously differentiable objectives at a stationary point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^n	o\mathbb R\) be \(C^2\) near \( ar x\), with \(
abla f( ar x)=0\). Then \( ar x\) is a tilt-stable local minimizer if and only if \(
abla^2f( ar x)\succ0\). In that case the localized minimizer map \(M\) is \(C^1\) near \(0\), and \(DM(0)=
abla^2f( ar x)^{-1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a smooth finite-dimensional objective, tilt stability is equivalent to positive definiteness of the Hessian, and the tilted minimizer varies smoothly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar x\) is tilt-stable if and only if \(\nabla^2f(\bar x)\succ0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Tilt-Stability Criterion

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Hilbert space, \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous, and \(\bar x\) is a local minimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar x\) is tilt-stable exactly when the localized tilt-argmin mapping is single-valued and Lipschitz near \(0\).

notation.meaning: localized minimizer mapping under linear tilts

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard Hilbert-space definition using localized minimizers under linear tilts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The point \(\bar x\) is a tilt-stable local minimizer of \(f\) if there exists \(\varepsilon>0\) such that the mapping
\[
M(v):=\mathop{\operatorname{argmin}}_{\lVert x-\bar x\rVert\le\varepsilon}\{f(x)-\langle v,x\rangle\}
\]
is single-valued and Lipschitz on a neighborhood of \(0\), and \(M(0)=\bar x\). Thus there are \(L>0\) and a neighborhood \(V\) of \(0\) satisfying \(\lVert M(v_1)-M(v_2)\rVert\le L\lVert v_1-v_2\rVert\) for all \(v_1,v_2\in V\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local minimizer is tilt-stable when every small linear tilt has a unique nearby minimizer depending Lipschitz continuously on the tilt.
knowledge_statements.title: Tilt Stability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind and localized tilt-argmin definition fit the topic. A source is needed to verify the Hilbert-space scope and the use of minimization over the closed ball rather than the standard neighborhood-localized formulation.

children.title: Subregularity-Growth Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Implication and equivalence families connecting growth with subgradient-mapping regularity.

children.title: Subdifferential Subregularity
children.top_down_role: Localized subregularity of the subgradient mapping.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a metric space, \(Y\) is a normed space, and \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed local error bound defines metric subregularity of \(F\) at \((\bar x,\bar y)\).

notation.meaning: inverse image of the reference value

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applied to \(F=\partial f\) and usually \(\bar y=0\).

source_refs.locator: 4.1.2 Neighborhood Characterizations of Metric Regularity and Lipschitzian Behavior p. 382
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The mapping \(F\) is metrically subregular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) if there exist \(\kappa\ge0\) and a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) such that
\[
\operatorname{dist}\bigl(x,F^{-1}(\bar y)\bigr)\le\kappa\operatorname{dist}\bigl(\bar y,F(x)\bigr)
\]
for every \(x\in U\), with \(\operatorname{dist}(\bar y,\varnothing)=+\infty\). Subdifferential subregularity of \(f\) at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar v\in\partial f(\bar x)\) means metric subregularity of \(F=\partial f\) at \((\bar x,\bar v)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subdifferential subregularity bounds distance to the critical set by a constant times the residual distance from the reference subgradient to the current subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.title: Subdifferential Subregularity

children.title: Growth Consequences
children.top_down_role: Objective-growth regimes supported by subdifferential subregularity.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Ordinary Subregularity Gives Setwise, Not Pointwise, Isolation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Example distinguishing growth relative to a critical set from isolated quadratic growth at one reference point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R\) be \(f(x,y)=x^2\). Its critical set is \(S=\{0\}\times\mathbb R\), and
\[
\operatorname{dist}((x,y),S)=|x|=\frac12\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x,y)).
\]
Hence \(\partial f\) is metrically subregular at every \(((0,\bar y),0)\), and
\[
f(x,y)=\operatorname{dist}((x,y),S)^2.
\]
Nevertheless, no \(\mu>0\) gives \(f(x,y)\ge f(0,0)+(\mu/2)\|(x,y)\|^2\) near \((0,0)\), because \(f(0,y)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Metric subregularity can yield quadratic growth relative to a nonisolated critical set without isolated quadratic growth at the reference point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Ordinary subregularity does not imply isolated pointwise quadratic growth when the critical set is nonisolated.

notation.meaning: subdifferential, equal here to the gradient

knowledge_statements.title: Ordinary Subregularity Gives Setwise, Not Pointwise, Isolation

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Hilbert space and \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
\(0\in\partial f(\bar x)\), and \(f\) is prox-regular and subdifferentially continuous at \(\bar x\) for \(0\).
\(\partial f\) is strongly metrically subregular at \((\bar x,0)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) has local quadratic growth at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Prox-regular local implication from strong subregularity to quadratic growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Assume additionally that \(\bar x\) is a local minimizer. Then there exist \(\mu>0\) and \(\varepsilon>0\) such that
\[
f(x)\ge f(\bar x)+\frac{\mu}{2}\lVert x-\bar x\rVert^2
\]
whenever \(\lVert x-\bar x\rVert<\varepsilon\). Here strong metric subregularity means that some \(\kappa,\delta>0\) satisfy \(\lVert x-\bar x\rVert\le\kappa\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x))\) for every \(x\) with \(\lVert x-\bar x\rVert<\delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a prox-regular, subdifferentially continuous function, strong subregularity of the subdifferential at a local minimizer yields local quadratic growth.
knowledge_statements.title: Growth Consequences

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem role fits Growth Consequences, but the exact implication from strong metric subregularity to quadratic growth, including its infinite-dimensional Hilbert-space scope and prox-regularity hypotheses, requires an authoritative source.

children.title: Converse Growth Routes
children.top_down_role: Growth conditions supporting subdifferential subregularity.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex Quadratic Growth Implies Subdifferential Subregularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct convex route from setwise quadratic growth to a subgradient residual error bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex on a Hilbert space, let \(S=\operatorname{argmin}f\ne\varnothing\), and suppose that on a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\in S\),
\[
f(x)\ge \min f+\frac{\alpha}{2}\operatorname{dist}(x,S)^2
\quad(\alpha>0).
\]
Then, after possibly shrinking \(U\),
\[
\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le \frac{2}{\alpha}\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x))
\quad(x\in U).
\]
Thus \(\partial f\) is metrically subregular at \((\bar x,0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex function, local quadratic growth relative to its minimizer set implies metric subregularity of the convex subdifferential.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
Local setwise quadratic growth holds with modulus \(\alpha>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial f\) is metrically subregular at \((\bar x,0)\), with admissible modulus \(2/\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.title: Convex Quadratic Growth Implies Subdifferential Subregularity

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Hilbert space and \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
\(f\) is prox-regular and subdifferentially continuous at \(\bar x\) for \(0\in\partial f(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A uniform positive-definiteness condition on the graphical derivative yields strong subregularity and quadratic growth.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-order route supporting a converse from growth-type curvature to subregularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A standard converse route is the uniform positive-definiteness predicate: there exists \(c>0\) such that
\[
\langle z,w\rangle\ge c\lVert w\rVert^2
\]
for every \(w\in X\) and every \(z\in D(\partial f)(\bar x\mid0)(w)\). Under an applicable graphical-derivative criterion for the chosen space and subdifferential, this condition implies local single-valued stability of the inverse subdifferential, hence strong metric subregularity at \((\bar x,0)\), and it supplies a local quadratic-growth conclusion at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A uniformly positive graphical derivative of the subdifferential is a second-order route from curvature information to strong subregularity and quadratic growth.
knowledge_statements.title: Converse Growth Routes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record invokes an unspecified 'applicable graphical-derivative criterion' and then asserts inverse single-valued stability, strong subregularity, and quadratic growth. The necessary finite- or infinite-dimensional assumptions and precise derivative theorem must be sourced before this condition can be accepted.

children.title: Subregularity–Growth Equivalence Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural settings where the two viewpoints coincide.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Qualitative local equivalence using distance to the minimizer set; equality of exact moduli is not asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex on a Hilbert space, let \(S=\operatorname{argmin}f\ne\varnothing\), and fix \(\bar x\in S\). Then the following properties are locally equivalent at \(\bar x\):
\[
\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le \kappa\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x))
\]
for some \(\kappa>0\), and
\[
f(x)\ge \min f+\frac{\alpha}{2}\operatorname{dist}(x,S)^2
\]
for some \(\alpha>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function, subdifferential metric subregularity is locally equivalent to quadratic growth relative to the minimizer set.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial f\) is metrically subregular at \((\bar x,0)\) if and only if \(f\) has local quadratic growth relative to \(S\).
knowledge_statements.title: Convex Subregularity–Quadratic-Growth Equivalence

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Hilbert space and \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
\(f\) is prox-regular and subdifferentially continuous at \(\bar x\) for \(0\in\partial f(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Tilt stability, strong metric regularity of \(\partial f\), and uniform quadratic growth under small tilts are equivalent locally.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Prox-regular equivalence regime for tilt stability and subdifferential regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The following local properties are equivalent: \(\bar x\) is a tilt-stable local minimizer of \(f\); the inverse \((\partial f)^{-1}\) admits a single-valued Lipschitz localization around \((0,\bar x)\); and there exist neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\), \(V\) of \(0\), and \(\mu>0\) such that each small tilt has a unique localized minimizer \(x(v)\in U\) satisfying
\[
f(x)-\langle v,x\rangle\ge f(x(v))-\langle v,x(v)\rangle+\frac{\mu}{2}\lVert x-x(v)\rVert^2
\]
for all \((v,x)\in V\times U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the prox-regular regime, tilt stability, strong metric regularity of the subdifferential, and uniform quadratic growth of tilted objectives are equivalent.
knowledge_statements.title: Subregularity–Growth Equivalence Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem is relevant to an equivalence-regime leaf, but it uses strong metric regularity rather than subregularity and states a Hilbert-space equivalence whose localization and hypotheses require verification. A precise theorem citation is necessary.

children.title: Lipschitz Additive Perturbations
children.top_down_role: Persistence of metric regularity under small Lipschitz additions.

assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are Banach spaces and \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) is metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) with modulus \(\kappa\).
\(g:X\to Y\) is Lipschitz near \(\bar x\) with constant \(\lambda\), and \(\kappa\lambda<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F+g\) is metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y+g(\bar x))\) with modulus at most \(\kappa/(1-\kappa\lambda)\).

notation.meaning: regularity modulus of the original mapping
local Lipschitz constant of the perturbation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard small-Lipschitz perturbation theorem with an explicit modulus bound.

source_refs.locator: 4.2.3 Metric Regularity under Perturbations p. 399
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H(x):=F(x)+g(x)\). Then there are neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(W\) of \(\bar y+g(\bar x)\) such that
\[
\operatorname{dist}(x,H^{-1}(y))\le\frac{\kappa}{1-\kappa\lambda}\operatorname{dist}(y,H(x))
\]
for all \((x,y)\in U\times W\). More generally, if \(\kappa\) and \(\lambda\) are strict upper estimates of the exact regularity and Lipschitz moduli, the displayed quotient is a valid local regularity estimate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Metric regularity survives an additive Lipschitz perturbation when the product of the regularity and Lipschitz moduli is below one, with an explicit degraded modulus.
knowledge_statements.title: Lipschitz Additive Perturbations

source_witnesses.locator: 4.2.3 Metric Regularity under Perturbations p. 399
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sharpness of the Additive Small-Gain Condition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar cancellation at the boundary of the metric-regularity perturbation theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\kappa>0\), \(F(x)=\{x/\kappa\}\), and \(g(x)=-x/\kappa\). Then \(\operatorname{reg}F(0\mid0)=\kappa\), \(\operatorname{lip}(g;0)=1/\kappa\), and \((F+g)(x)=\{0\}\), which is not metrically regular at \((0,0)\). Thus \(\kappa\lambda<1\) cannot generally be weakened to \(\kappa\lambda\le1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At equality in the additive small-gain condition, cancellation can destroy metric regularity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{reg}F(0\mid0)\operatorname{lip}(g;0)=1\), while \(F+g\) is not metrically regular at \((0,0)\).

notation.meaning: exact regularity modulus of the base mapping

knowledge_statements.title: Sharpness of the Additive Small-Gain Condition

children.title: Set-Valued Perturbations
children.top_down_role: Perturbations changing the values of a set-valued mapping.

assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are Banach spaces, \(F,G:X\rightrightarrows Y\), and \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}(F+G)\).
Choose \(\bar z\in G(\bar x)\) with \(\bar y-\bar z\in F(\bar x)\); assume local sum-stability at this decomposition.
\(F\) is metrically regular with modulus \(\kappa\), while \(G\) has the Aubin property with modulus \(\lambda<1/\kappa\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Under the stated decomposition control, the set-valued sum \(F+G\) remains metrically regular locally.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-valued extension requiring control of nearby sum decompositions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Local sum-stability means that every \(y\in(F+G)(x)\) sufficiently near \(\bar y\), with \(x\) near \(\bar x\), admits \(y=u+z\) where \(u\in F(x)\) is near \(\bar y-\bar z\) and \(z\in G(x)\) is near \(\bar z\). Together with the smallness condition \(\kappa\lambda<1\), this decomposition control yields neighborhoods on which \(H=F+G\) is metrically regular. A regularity modulus can be chosen arbitrarily above
\[
\frac{\kappa}{1-\kappa\lambda},
\]
subject to the precise localized moduli used in the hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A small Aubin set-valued perturbation preserves metric regularity when nearby sums admit controlled decompositions and the product of moduli is below one.
knowledge_statements.title: Set-Valued Perturbations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem role is suitable, but the exact sum-stability, Aubin-property, completeness, localization, and modulus hypotheses for a set-valued perturbation theorem are source-sensitive. No citation is supplied.

children.title: Graph Perturbations
children.top_down_role: Perturbations expressed through changes to the mapping graph.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Qualitative convergence of multifunction graphs in metrizable product spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F_n,F:X\rightrightarrows Y\), where \(X\times Y\) is metrizable. Then \(\operatorname{gph}F_n\xrightarrow{PK}\operatorname{gph}F\) exactly when: (i) every convergent sequence \((x_k,y_k)\in\operatorname{gph}F_{n_k}\), with \(n_k\uparrow\infty\), has its limit in \(\operatorname{gph}F\); and (ii) every \((x,y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\) is the limit of a sequence \((x_n,y_n)\in\operatorname{gph}F_n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Graphical convergence requires both exclusion of extraneous graph limits and approximation of every point of the limiting graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{gph}F_n\xrightarrow{PK}\operatorname{gph}F\) if and only if the sequential outer and inner graph conditions both hold.
knowledge_statements.title: Painlevé–Kuratowski Graphical Convergence

assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are metric spaces and \(F,\widetilde F:X\rightrightarrows Y\).
Neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(V\) of \(\bar y\) are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed localized excesses quantify directional graph perturbation; their maximum is the symmetric local graph discrepancy.

notation.meaning: excess of one set over another

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Localized product-space measure of graph displacement, preceding stability estimates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For sets \(A,B\subset X\times Y\), define \(e(A,B):=\sup_{a\in A}\operatorname{dist}(a,B)\), with \(e(\varnothing,B)=0\). Let
\[
A:=\operatorname{gph}F\cap(U\times V),\qquad B:=\operatorname{gph}\widetilde F\cap(U\times V).
\]
The directed local graph perturbation from \(F\) to \(\widetilde F\) is \(e(B,A)\). Its symmetric size is
\[
d_{H,U,V}(F,\widetilde F):=\max\{e(A,B),e(B,A)\},
\]
the Hausdorff discrepancy of the localized graphs in the chosen product metric. Quantitative preservation of metric regularity requires additional slope or Lipschitz control, not merely small graph discrepancy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Graph perturbations are measured by localized excess or Hausdorff distance between graphs; small distance alone does not guarantee preservation of metric regularity.
knowledge_statements.title: Graph Perturbations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits Graph Perturbations and the statement correctly distinguishes graph discrepancy from regularity preservation. A source and a fixed product metric are needed for the quantitative definition and any downstream bounds.

children.title: Coupled Value–Graph Changes
children.top_down_role: Regimes where value variation and graph variation occur together.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph transformation whose output displacement depends on both coordinates of the original graph point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) and \(q:X\times Y\to Y\), define \[\widetilde F(x):=\{y+q(x,y):y\in F(x)\}.\] Equivalently, \(\operatorname{gph}\widetilde F\) is the image of \(\operatorname{gph}F\) under \(T(x,y)=(x,y+q(x,y))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coupled value–graph change maps each graph point to a new output whose displacement depends on both its argument and value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{gph}\widetilde F=T(\operatorname{gph}F)\) for \(T(x,y)=(x,y+q(x,y))\).
knowledge_statements.title: Coupled Value–Graph Transformation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar boundary example for a coupled value-dependent graph transformation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(x)=\{x/\kappa\}\), where \(\kappa>0\), and let \(q(x,y)=-ax-by\), where \(a,b\ge0\), \(b<1\), and \(b+\kappa a=1\). Then \(q\) has coordinatewise Lipschitz constants \(a,b\), while \[\widetilde F(x)=\{(1-b)x/\kappa-ax\}=\{0\}.\] Thus \(\widetilde F\) is not metrically regular at \((0,0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At equality in the proposed coupled small-gain margin, state and value effects can cancel all regularity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widetilde F(x)=\{0\}\), so \(\widetilde F\) is not metrically regular at \((0,0)\).

notation.meaning: Lipschitz constant in the argument coordinate
Lipschitz constant in the value coordinate

knowledge_statements.title: Sharp Coupled-Margin Cancellation

assumptions_latex: \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) is metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) with modulus at most \(\kappa\).
Locally, \(q:X\times Y\to Y\) satisfies \(\|q(x,y)-q(x',y')\|\le a\|x-x'\|+b\|y-y'\|\), where \(b+\kappa a<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widetilde F\) is metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y+q(\bar x,\bar y))\), with modulus at most \(\kappa/(1-b-\kappa a)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lipschitz perturbations acting simultaneously on the graph point and its value.

source_refs.locator: 4.2.3 Metric Regularity under Perturbations p. 399
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the coupled perturbation by \[\widetilde F(x):=\{y+q(x,y):y\in F(x)\}.\] If \(F\) is metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) with modulus at most \(\kappa\), and the local Lipschitz constants \(a\) and \(b\) of \(q\) in its first and second variables satisfy \(b+\kappa a<1\), then \(\widetilde F\) is metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y+q(\bar x,\bar y))\). A valid regularity modulus is \[\operatorname{reg}\widetilde F\bigl(\bar x\mid \bar y+q(\bar x,\bar y)\bigr)\le \frac{\kappa}{1-b-\kappa a}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coupled Lipschitz change of graph points and values preserves metric regularity when its two Lipschitz effects are jointly smaller than the regularity margin.
knowledge_statements.title: Coupled Value–Graph Changes

source_witnesses.locator: 4.2.3 Metric Regularity under Perturbations p. 399

children.title: Graphical Stability Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Graph changes that prevent persistence of metric regularity.

assumptions_latex: For \(t\ge 0\), let \(F_t:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be given by \(F_t(x)=tx\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Although \(\operatorname{gph}F_t\to\operatorname{gph}F_0\) locally as \(t\downarrow0\), the regularity moduli diverge and \(F_0\) is not metrically regular.

notation.meaning: Scalar linear mapping with slope t

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph convergence alone does not provide a uniform metric-regularity margin.

source_refs.locator: 3.2.4 Graphical Regularity of Lipschitzian Mappings p. 327
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(t\ge0\), define \(F_t(x):=tx\) on \(\mathbb R\). For every \(t>0\), the mapping \(F_t\) is metrically regular everywhere and \[\operatorname{reg}F_t(x\mid tx)=\frac1t.\] As \(t\downarrow0\), the graphs \(\operatorname{gph}F_t\) converge locally to \(\operatorname{gph}F_0=\mathbb R\times\{0\}\), but the moduli tend to infinity. The limit mapping \(F_0\) is not metrically regular at any \((x,0)\), since nearby nonzero values have empty inverse images. Thus graphical convergence without a positive uniform regularity margin need not preserve metric regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The graphs of the maps x↦tx converge to the zero-map graph, while their regularity moduli diverge and regularity fails at the limit.
knowledge_statements.title: Graphical Stability Boundaries

children.title: Parameter-Uniform Perturbations
children.top_down_role: Regularity maintained uniformly over parameter neighborhoods.

knowledge_statements.title: Parameter-Uniform Perturbations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform additive perturbation theorem over a fixed parameter neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be Banach spaces, let \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\), let \(p\) range over a neighborhood of \(\bar p\), and set \(F_p(x):=F(x)+q_p(x)\). Suppose fixed neighborhoods witness metric regularity of \(F\) at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) with modulus at most \(\kappa\), and every \(q_p:X\to Y\) satisfies on a common neighborhood \[\|q_p(x)-q_p(x')\|\le\mu\|x-x'\|,\qquad \kappa\mu<1.\] Then every \(F_p\) is metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y+q_p(\bar x))\), with neighborhoods of common radii and the uniform modulus bound \[\operatorname{reg}F_p\bigl(\bar x\mid\bar y+q_p(\bar x)\bigr)\le\frac{\kappa}{1-\kappa\mu}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For mappings between Banach spaces, a parameter family of uniformly small Lipschitz additive perturbations preserves metric regularity with neighborhood radii and a modulus uniform over nearby parameters.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are Banach spaces and \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) is metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) with modulus at most \(\kappa\).
For every nearby parameter \(p\), the mapping \(q_p:X\to Y\) is Lipschitz on one common neighborhood with a common constant \(\mu\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every \(F+q_p\) is metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y+q_p(\bar x))\), with common neighborhood radii and modulus at most \(\kappa/(1-\kappa\mu)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pointwise Smallness Does Not Give Uniform Regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar family demonstrating the need for a common perturbation margin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{0\}\cup\{1/n:n\in\mathbb N\}\), \(F(x)=\{x\}\), \(q_0(x)=0\), and \(q_{1/n}(x)=-(1-1/n)x\). Then \(F_0(x)=x\) and \(F_{1/n}(x)=x/n\), so every \(F_p=F+q_p\) is metrically regular at \((0,0)\), but \(\operatorname{reg}F_{1/n}(0\mid0)=n\). No modulus is uniform on a parameter neighborhood of \(0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pointwise strict perturbation margins do not imply a uniform metric-regularity modulus.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each \(F_p\) is metrically regular at \((0,0)\), but \(\sup_{p\to0}\operatorname{reg}F_p(0\mid0)=+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.title: Pointwise Smallness Does Not Give Uniform Regularity

children.title: Radius of Metric Regularity
children.top_down_role: Distance to perturbations that destroy metric regularity.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Perturbation radius and distance-to-irregularity framework

assumptions_latex: \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) is metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\).
Perturbations are single-valued local Lipschitz maps \(h:X\to Y\) satisfying \(h(\bar x)=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The radius is the infimum of local Lipschitz seminorms of perturbations for which \(F+h\) is not metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\).

notation.meaning: Local Lipschitz seminorm at the reference point

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Radius relative to additive single-valued Lipschitz perturbations fixing the reference value.

source_refs.locator: 4.2.3 Metric Regularity under Perturbations p. 399
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For additive local Lipschitz perturbations fixing the reference value, define \[\operatorname{rad}_{\mathrm{MR}}F(\bar x\mid\bar y):=\inf\left\{\operatorname{lip}(h;\bar x):h(\bar x)=0,\ F+h\ \text{is not metrically regular at }(\bar x,\bar y)\right\}.\] Here \(\operatorname{lip}(h;\bar x)\) is the infimum of local Lipschitz constants of \(h\) near \(\bar x\). The infimum of the empty set is \(+\infty\). The perturbation class is part of the definition; changing it can change the radius.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The radius is the smallest local Lipschitz size of an allowed additive perturbation that destroys metric regularity at the reference point.
knowledge_statements.title: Radius of Metric Regularity

source_witnesses.locator: 4.2.3 Metric Regularity under Perturbations p. 399
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reciprocal-Modulus Lower Bound for the Regularity Radius
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower bound for additive local-Lipschitz perturbations fixing the reference value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X,Y\) be Banach spaces and let \(r:=\operatorname{reg}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)<+\infty\). Every local Lipschitz \(h:X\to Y\) with \(h(\bar x)=0\) and \(\operatorname{lip}(h;\bar x)<1/r\) preserves metric regularity. Consequently \[\operatorname{rad}_{\mathrm{MR}}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)\ge\frac{1}{\operatorname{reg}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)},\] with \(1/0:=+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The additive Lipschitz radius is at least the reciprocal exact regularity modulus.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) with finite exact modulus.
Perturbations are local Lipschitz maps \(h\) satisfying \(h(\bar x)=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rad}_{\mathrm{MR}}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)\ge1/\operatorname{reg}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)\).

notation.meaning: radius for the specified perturbation class

knowledge_statements.title: Reciprocal-Modulus Lower Bound for the Regularity Radius

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Scalar Sharpness of the Additive Lipschitz Radius
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact calibration for the identity mapping under additive local-Lipschitz perturbations fixing the reference value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\), \(F(x)=x\), at \((0,0)\), \[\operatorname{reg}F(0\mid0)=1,\qquad \operatorname{rad}_{\mathrm{MR}}F(0\mid0)=1.\] Every admissible perturbation with \(\operatorname{lip}(h;0)<1\) preserves metric regularity, while the threshold perturbation \(h(x)=-x\) gives \(F+h\equiv0\), which is not metrically regular at \((0,0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the scalar identity, the additive Lipschitz radius is one, and exact cancellation destroys regularity at that threshold.
assumptions_latex: The perturbation class consists of local Lipschitz maps \(h:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) satisfying \(h(0)=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rad}_{\mathrm{MR}}F(0\mid0)=1=1/\operatorname{reg}F(0\mid0)\).

notation.meaning: threshold perturbation cancelling the identity mapping

knowledge_statements.title: Scalar Sharpness of the Additive Lipschitz Radius

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Radius for a Surjective Linear Operator
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Hilbert-space formula for bounded linear additive perturbations, a subclass of the declared local-Lipschitz perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A:X\to Y\) be a surjective linear operator between finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces, with admissible perturbations \(H:X\to Y\) linear. Then
\[\inf\{\|H\|:A+H\text{ is not surjective}\}=\min_{\|y\|=1}\|A^*y\|=\frac{1}{\operatorname{reg}A}.\]
A rank-one perturbation attains this infimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a surjective finite-dimensional linear operator, the exact linear-perturbation radius is its adjoint minimum gain and the reciprocal regularity modulus.
assumptions_latex: Admissible perturbations are bounded linear maps \(H:X\to Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rad}_{\mathrm{MR}}^{\mathrm{lin}}A=\min_{\|y\|=1}\|A^*y\|=1/\operatorname{reg}A\).

notation.meaning: radius restricted to linear additive perturbations

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Radius for a Surjective Linear Operator

children.title: Implicit Mappings under Metric Regularity
children.top_down_role: Set-valued implicit solution behavior without local uniqueness.

knowledge_statements.title: Implicit Mappings under Metric Regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-valued inverse behavior; no local uniqueness is assumed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be normed spaces, let \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\), and define \(S:Y\rightrightarrows X\) by \(S(y):=F^{-1}(y)\). If \(F\) is metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) with modulus at most \(\kappa\), then there are neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(V\) of \(\bar y\) such that \[S(y)\cap U\subset S(y')+\kappa\|y-y'\|\mathbb B_X\qquad\text{for all }y,y'\in V.\] Thus \(S\) has the Aubin property at \((\bar y,\bar x)\). Its localized values may contain multiple points, so metric regularity alone does not provide a unique implicit branch.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For mappings between normed spaces, metric regularity makes the set-valued implicit solution map Lipschitz-like, but it does not make nearby solutions unique.
assumptions_latex: \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) is metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) with modulus at most \(\kappa\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The solution mapping \(S\) has the Aubin property at \((\bar y,\bar x)\) with Lipschitz bound at most \(\kappa\), without an assertion of local uniqueness.

notation.meaning: Closed unit ball of the normed space X

children.title: Implicit Mappings under Strong Metric Regularity
children.top_down_role: Stable locally unique implicit solution branches.

knowledge_statements.title: Implicit Mappings under Strong Metric Regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Locally unique Lipschitz implicit branch obtained from strong metric regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be normed spaces and let \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) be strongly metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\). Then there are neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(V\) of \(\bar y\) and a Lipschitz mapping \(s:V\to U\) such that \[F^{-1}(y)\cap U=\{s(y)\}\qquad\text{for every }y\in V,\] with \(s(\bar y)=\bar x\). Consequently, the inclusion \(y\in F(x)\) has exactly one solution in \(U\) for every \(y\in V\), and that solution varies Lipschitz continuously with \(y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a mapping between normed spaces, strong metric regularity yields a unique nearby implicit solution for every nearby right-hand side, varying Lipschitz continuously with the data.

children.title: Inverse-Branch Stability
children.top_down_role: Persistence and sensitivity of localized inverse branches.

knowledge_statements.title: Inverse-Branch Stability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stability of a unique inverse branch under a small additive Lipschitz perturbation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be Banach spaces, and suppose a localization of \(F^{-1}\) at \((\bar y,\bar x)\) is single-valued and Lipschitz with constant \(\kappa\). Let \(h:X\to Y\) satisfy \(h(\bar x)=0\) and be Lipschitz on a neighborhood of \(\bar x\) with constant \(\mu\), where \(\kappa\mu<1\). Then a localization of \((F+h)^{-1}\) at \((\bar y,\bar x)\) is single-valued. Its branch \(s_h\) satisfies locally \[\|s_h(y)-s_h(y')\|\le\frac{\kappa}{1-\kappa\mu}\|y-y'\|.\] Thus local uniqueness and Lipschitz dependence persist under perturbations below the inverse-branch margin.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For mappings between Banach spaces, a unique Lipschitz inverse branch survives an additive perturbation having an actual local Lipschitz constant smaller than the reciprocal branch constant.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are Banach spaces and \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\).
A localization of \(F^{-1}\) at \((\bar y,\bar x)\) is single-valued and Lipschitz with constant \(\kappa\).
\(h:X\to Y\) satisfies \(h(\bar x)=0\) and is locally Lipschitz with a constant \(\mu\) satisfying \(\kappa\mu<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((F+h)^{-1}\) has a single-valued local branch at \((\bar y,\bar x)\) with Lipschitz constant at most \(\kappa/(1-\kappa\mu)\).

notation.meaning: Lipschitz constant of the original inverse branch

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Robinson strong regularity defined through the partially linearized generalized equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the generalized equation \[0\in f(x)+Q(x),\] define its partial linearization at \(\bar x\) by \[L_{\bar x}(x):=f(\bar x)+Df(\bar x)(x-\bar x)+Q(x).\] The generalized equation is strongly regular at \(\bar x\) if there exist neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(V\) of \(0\) such that, for every \(y\in V\), the inclusion \(y\in L_{\bar x}(x)\) has exactly one solution \(x=s(y)\in U\), and the mapping \(s:V\to U\) is Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A generalized equation is strongly regular when its partial linearization has a locally unique solution that depends Lipschitz continuously on the forcing term.

knowledge_statements.title: Mapping-Theoretic Strong Metric Regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mapping-level definition through a single-valued Lipschitz inverse localization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be normed spaces and let \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) satisfy \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\). The mapping \(F\) is strongly metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) if there are neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(V\) of \(\bar y\) and a Lipschitz mapping \(s:V\to U\) such that \[F^{-1}(y)\cap U=\{s(y)\}\qquad\text{for every }y\in V.\] The strong metric-regularity modulus is the infimum of the local Lipschitz constants over all such inverse localizations. This property combines metric regularity with local uniqueness of the inverse.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a mapping between normed spaces, strong metric regularity means that its inverse admits a locally single-valued Lipschitz branch through the reference graph point; its modulus is the infimum of the branch constants.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is strongly metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) exactly when \(F^{-1}\) has a single-valued Lipschitz localization at \((\bar y,\bar x)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Mapping-Theoretic Formulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mapping-theoretic definition through a localized inverse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The mapping \(F\) is strongly metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) if there exist neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(V\) of \(\bar y\), a mapping \(s:V\to U\), and \(\kappa\geq 0\) such that \[F^{-1}(y)\cap U=\{s(y)\}\quad\text{for every }y\in V,\] and \[\|s(y_1)-s(y_2)\|\leq\kappa\|y_1-y_2\|\quad\text{for all }y_1,y_2\in V.\] The strong metric regularity modulus is the infimum of such local Lipschitz constants over all admissible localizations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong metric regularity means that the inverse mapping admits a locally unique Lipschitz selection near the reference output; its modulus is the infimum of the admissible local Lipschitz constants.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The following local formulations are equivalent, after possibly shrinking \(U\) and \(V\). First, there is \(\kappa\geq0\) such that \[\operatorname{dist}(x,F^{-1}(y))\leq\kappa\operatorname{dist}(y,F(x))\] for \(x\in U\) and \(y\in V\), and every set \(F^{-1}(y)\cap U\) is a singleton. knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local metric error bound combined with inverse uniqueness is equivalent, after localization, to a single-valued Lipschitz inverse branch.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x,y\in\mathbb R\), \[F^{-1}(y)=\{y,-y\}\quad\text{and}\quad \operatorname{dist}(x,F^{-1}(y))=\operatorname{dist}(y,F(x)).\] Hence \(F\) is globally metrically regular with modulus \(1\). Nevertheless, for every pair of neighborhoods \(U\) and \(V\) of zero, sufficiently small nonzero \(y\in V\) satisfies \[F^{-1}(y)\cap U=\{y,-y\},\] which is not a singleton. Thus \(F^{-1}\) has no single-valued localization at \((0,0)\), so \(F\) is not strongly metrically regular there.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The mapping taking x to {x,-x} is metrically regular with modulus one, but its two inverse branches prevent strong metric regularity at zero.

abla h_j( ar x):1\leq j\leq q\}\) are linearly independent and there exists \(d\in\mathbb R^n\) such that \[

\[\sum_{i\in I(\bar x)}\lambda_i\nabla g_i(\bar x)+\sum_{j=1}^q\mu_j\nabla h_j(\bar x)=0,\quad \lambda_i\ge0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad(\lambda,\mu)=(0,0).\]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Smooth Degeneracy Can Destroy the Feasibility Error Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar smooth inequality showing that smoothness alone does not imply a linear residual bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the constraint \(g(x)=x^2\le0\) at \(\bar x=0\), the feasible set is \(S=\{0\}\), while
\[\operatorname{dist}(x,S)=|x|,\qquad (g(x))_+=x^2.\]
Consequently, no finite \(\kappa\) satisfies \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le\kappa(g(x))_+\) locally, and MFCQ fails because \(\nabla g(0)=0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S(b,d)=\{x:Ax\le b,\ Cx=d\}\), and let \(H=H(A,C)\) be a Hoffman constant. If \(S(b,d)\) and \(S(b',d')\) are nonempty, then every \(x\in S(b,d)\) satisfies
\[\operatorname{dist}(x,S(b',d'))\le H\left\|\big((b-b')_+,d-d'\big)\right\|.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hoffman’s bound makes the polyhedral feasible-set mapping globally Lipschitz-like with respect to feasible right-hand-side perturbations for fixed matrices.
assumptions_latex: \(H(A,C)\) is a Hoffman constant for the selected norms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S(b,d)\subset S(b',d')+H\|((b-b')_+,d-d')\|\mathbb B.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Right-Hand-Side Lipschitz Stability of Polyhedral Feasible Sets

children.title: Conic Constraint Systems
