knowledge_statements.title: Conic Constraint Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Robinson qualification for a smooth cone constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Robinson's constraint qualification for \(g(x)\in K\) at \(\bar x\) is \[0\in\operatorname{int}\big(g(\bar x)+Dg(\bar x)\mathbb R^n-K\big).\] If this condition holds, then the set-valued residual mapping \[\Phi(x):=g(x)-K\] is metrically regular at \((\bar x,0)\). In particular, there exist a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and a constant \(\kappa\geq0\) such that \[\operatorname{dist}(x,\Phi^{-1}(0))\leq\kappa\operatorname{dist}(0,\Phi(x))\quad\text{for every }x\in U.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Robinson's interior condition for a smooth cone constraint yields metric regularity of the conic residual mapping and, consequently, a local feasibility error bound.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subset\mathbb R^m\) is a closed convex cone, and \(g:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Robinson's constraint qualification implies metric regularity of \(\Phi(x)=g(x)-K\) at \((\bar x,0)\), which implies a local error bound.

notation.meaning: Derivative range at the reference point

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent Primal and Dual Forms of Robinson CQ
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth finite-dimensional constraint into a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\subset\mathbb R^m\) be a closed convex cone, let \(g\) be differentiable at a feasible point \(\bar x\), and put \(z=g(\bar x)\). Robinson's constraint qualification is equivalent to
\[Dg(\bar x)\mathbb R^n+T_K(z)=\mathbb R^m,\]
and also to
\[\lambda\in N_K(z),\quad Dg(\bar x)^T\lambda=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\lambda=0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Robinson CQ is equivalent to linearized tangent surjectivity and to the absence of a nonzero cone-normal multiplier annihilated by the constraint Jacobian.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subset\mathbb R^m\) is a closed convex cone.
\(g\) is differentiable at \(\bar x\) and \(g(\bar x)\in K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\in\operatorname{int}(z+Dg(\bar x)\mathbb R^n-K)\iff Dg(\bar x)\mathbb R^n+T_K(z)=\mathbb R^m\iff\ker Dg(\bar x)^T\cap N_K(z)=\{0\}.\)

notation.meaning: tangent cone to K at z
convex normal cone to K at z

children.title: Generalized-Equation Solution Maps
children.top_down_role: Solution mappings generated by parameterized generalized equations.

assumptions_latex: \(P,X,Y\) are finite-dimensional spaces, \(f:P\times X\to Y\), and \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\).
The generalized equation is parameterized by \(p\in P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The parameterized generalized equation defines the solution multifunction \(S:P\rightrightarrows X\).

source_refs.locator: 4.4 Sensitivity Analysis for Variational Systems p. 421

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The solution map associated with the parameterized generalized equation \[0\in f(p,x)+F(x)\] is the multifunction \[S(p):=\{x\in X:0\in f(p,x)+F(x)\}.\] Its graph is therefore \[\operatorname{gph}S=\{(p,x)\in P\times X:-f(p,x)\in F(x)\}.\] Local existence, uniqueness, calmness, the Aubin property, and strong regularity are properties of this multifunction at a chosen reference pair \((\bar p,\bar x)\in\operatorname{gph}S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A generalized-equation solution map assigns each parameter all states satisfying the corresponding set-valued inclusion.
knowledge_statements.title: Generalized-Equation Solution Maps

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closedness of the Generalized-Equation Solution Graph
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic graph property inherited from a continuous single-valued term and a closed-graph set-valued term.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose \(f:P\times X\to Y\) is continuous and \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) has closed graph. For
\[
S(p)=\{x:0\in f(p,x)+F(x)\},
\]
\(\operatorname{gph}S\) is closed. Equivalently, if \(p_k\to p\), \(x_k\to x\), and \(x_k\in S(p_k)\), then \(x\in S(p)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Continuity of the single-valued term and closedness of the set-valued term make the generalized-equation solution graph closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{gph}S\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.title: Closedness of the Generalized-Equation Solution Graph

children.title: Variational-Inequality Solution Maps
children.top_down_role: Stability regimes for parameterized variational inequalities.

knowledge_statements.title: Variational-Inequality Solution Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex-set variational inequality in generalized-equation form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(p\in P\), define \[S_{\mathrm{VI}}(p):=\{x\in C:\langle G(p,x),z-x\rangle\geq0\ \text{for every }z\in C\}.\] With the convex normal cone convention \[N_C(x):=\{v\in\mathbb R^n:\langle v,z-x\rangle\leq0\ \text{for every }z\in C\}\quad\text{for }x\in C,\] the solution map has the equivalent generalized-equation representation \[S_{\mathrm{VI}}(p)=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:0\in G(p,x)+N_C(x)\}.\] Thus stability of the variational inequality is stability of this parameterized generalized-equation solution map.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The solution map of a convex variational inequality is exactly the solution map of a generalized equation formed with the convex normal cone.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(G:P\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\) is a parameterized field.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(p\in P\), the variational inequality over \(C\) is equivalent to \(0\in G(p,x)+N_C(x)\).

notation.meaning: Convex normal cone to C at x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of local uniqueness under ordinary monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=[0,1]\subset\mathbb R\) and \(G(p,x)\equiv0\). The field is continuous and monotone, but \[S_{\mathrm{VI}}(p)=C\] for every \(p\). Thus monotonicity alone does not imply a single-valued, isolated, or locally unique VI solution map.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The zero field on a nontrivial convex set is monotone, yet every feasible point solves the VI.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S_{\mathrm{VI}}(p)=[0,1]\text{ despite monotonicity of }G(p,\cdot).
knowledge_statements.title: Monotonicity Does Not Imply Uniqueness

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed feasible set in finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(G\) is continuous on \(P\times C\), then \(\operatorname{gph}S_{\mathrm{VI}}\) is closed. In particular, if \(p_k\to p\), \(x_k\to x\), and \(x_k\in S_{\mathrm{VI}}(p_k)\), then \(x\in S_{\mathrm{VI}}(p)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Joint continuity of the field and closedness of the fixed feasible set make the VI solution map closed-graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{gph}S_{\mathrm{VI}}\text{ is closed}.
knowledge_statements.title: Closed Graph under Joint Continuity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed closed convex feasible set with uniformly strongly monotone parameterized fields.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose each \(G(p,\cdot)\) is \(\alpha\)-strongly monotone on \(C\), with a common \(\alpha>0\). If \(x_p\in S_{\mathrm{VI}}(p)\) and \(x_q\in S_{\mathrm{VI}}(q)\), then \[\alpha\|x_p-x_q\|\leq\|G(p,x_q)-G(q,x_q)\|.\] Consequently, each solution set contains at most one point. If additionally \(\|G(p,x)-G(q,x)\|\leq Ld(p,q)\) on the relevant solution neighborhood, then \[\|x_p-x_q\|\leq(L/\alpha)d(p,q).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform strong monotonicity gives uniqueness and converts Lipschitz parameter dependence of the field into Lipschitz dependence of existing VI solutions.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
Each \(G(p,\cdot)\) is strongly monotone on \(C\) with common modulus \(\alpha>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S_{\mathrm{VI}}(p)\text{ is at most singleton and }\|x_p-x_q\|\leq\alpha^{-1}\|G(p,x_q)-G(q,x_q)\|.
knowledge_statements.title: Strong-Monotonicity Stability Bound

children.title: KKT Solution Maps
children.top_down_role: Localized primal-dual mappings for KKT systems.

knowledge_statements.title: KKT Solution Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal-dual map for smooth parameterized nonlinear programs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the program with objective \(\varphi(p,x)\), inequalities \(g(p,x)\leq0\), and equalities \(h(p,x)=0\), define \[L(p,x,\lambda,\mu):=\varphi(p,x)+\lambda^\top g(p,x)+\mu^\top h(p,x).\] Its KKT solution map is \[S_{\mathrm{KKT}}(p):=\{(x,\lambda,\mu)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R_+^m\times\mathbb R^q:\nabla_xL(p,x,\lambda,\mu)=0,\ g(p,x)\leq0,\ h(p,x)=0,\ \lambda_i g_i(p,x)=0\ \text{for every }i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\}.\] This map retains both primal and multiplier sensitivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The KKT solution map assigns each parameter every primal point and multiplier pair satisfying stationarity, primal feasibility, dual feasibility, and complementarity.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a finite-dimensional parameter space, and \(n,m,q\) are nonnegative integers.
\(\varphi:P\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\), \(g:P\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\), and \(h:P\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^q\) are continuously differentiable with respect to \(x\).
The inequalities use \(g(p,x)\leq0\), with multipliers \(\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^m\), and equality multipliers satisfy \(\mu\in\mathbb R^q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_{\mathrm{KKT}}:P\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R_+^m\times\mathbb R^q\) collects all primal-dual triples satisfying the KKT system.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: KKT System as a Generalized Equation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact primal-dual generalized-equation representation retaining equality and inequality multipliers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(z=(x,\lambda,\mu)\). The seed's KKT conditions are equivalent to
\[
0\in
\begin{pmatrix}
\nabla_xL(p,x,\lambda,\mu)\\
-g(p,x)\\
h(p,x)
\end{pmatrix}
+
\begin{pmatrix}
0\\N_{\mathbb R_+^m}(\lambda)\\0
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Thus \(S_{\mathrm{KKT}}(p)\) is the solution map of this generalized equation in the joint variable \(z\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The full KKT map is a generalized-equation solution map whose normal-cone block encodes dual feasibility and complementarity.
assumptions_latex: The smooth nonlinear program and sign conventions are those of the seed definition.
\(N_{\mathbb R_+^m}\) is the convex-analysis normal cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed generalized equation has solution map exactly \(S_{\mathrm{KKT}}\).
knowledge_statements.title: KKT System as a Generalized Equation

children.title: Multiplier Solution Maps
children.top_down_role: Parameter-dependent mappings of admissible multipliers.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiplier Solution Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplier fiber associated with a fixed feasible primal point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each feasible pair \((p,x)\in P\times\mathbb R^n\), define the multiplier solution map by \[\Lambda(p,x):=\{(\lambda,\mu)\in\mathbb R_+^m\times\mathbb R^q:\nabla_xL(p,x,\lambda,\mu)=0,\ \lambda_i g_i(p,x)=0\ \text{for every }i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\}.\] It is exactly the multiplier fiber of the KKT solution map over \(x\): \[\Lambda(p,x)=\{(\lambda,\mu)\in\mathbb R_+^m\times\mathbb R^q:(x,\lambda,\mu)\in S_{\mathrm{KKT}}(p)\}.\] Consequently, local uniqueness of a primal solution does not by itself imply that \(\Lambda(p,x)\) is a singleton.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The multiplier map consists of the dual variables completing a fixed feasible primal point to a KKT triple; primal uniqueness need not imply multiplier uniqueness.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a finite-dimensional parameter space, and \(n,m,q\) are nonnegative integers.
\(\varphi:P\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\), \(g:P\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\), and \(h:P\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^q\) are continuously differentiable with respect to \(x\).
\(L\) and \(S_{\mathrm{KKT}}\) use the conventions of the prerequisite KKT-map record.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Lambda(p,x)\) is the multiplier fiber of \(S_{\mathrm{KKT}}(p)\) over \(x\) and may be set-valued even when the primal solution is unique.

notation.meaning: Multiplier solution map at a parameter-primal pair
Lagrangian of the parameterized nonlinear program

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniqueness of an existing multiplier at a fixed feasible point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\{\nabla_xg_i(p,x):i\in I(p,x)\}\cup\{\nabla_xh_j(p,x):1\le j\le q\}\) is linearly independent, then \(\Lambda(p,x)\) contains at most one element. Hence, if a KKT multiplier exists, LICQ makes the multiplier fiber a singleton.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linear independence of the active inequality and equality gradients makes any existing KKT multiplier unique.
assumptions_latex: The active inequality gradients together with all equality gradients are linearly independent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |\Lambda(p,x)|\leq 1.
knowledge_statements.title: LICQ Implies Multiplier Uniqueness

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed feasible point of a smooth finite-dimensional nonlinear program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(I(p,x):=\{i:g_i(p,x)=0\}\). Then \[\Lambda(p,x)=\left\{(\lambda,\mu):\lambda_{I(p,x)}\geq0,\ \lambda_i=0\ (i
otin I(p,x)),\ 
abla_x\varphi(p,x)+\sum_{i\in I(p,x)}\lambda_i
abla_xg_i(p,x)+\sum_{j=1}^q\mu_j
abla_xh_j(p,x)=0ight\}.\] Thus \(\Lambda(p,x)\) is a possibly empty or unbounded closed convex polyhedron.

children.title: Primal–Dual Localization
children.top_down_role: Joint localization of primal solutions and associated multipliers.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^q\to\mathbb{R}\) and \(g:\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^q\to\mathbb{R}^m\) are continuously differentiable near \((\bar x,\bar p)\).
\((\bar x,\bar\lambda)\) satisfies the KKT system at \(\bar p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_{U,V}\) is the primal-dual localization of the KKT solution map at \((\bar p,\bar x,\bar\lambda)\).

notation.meaning: Neighborhoods of the reference primal and dual solutions

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional inequality-constrained KKT systems localized jointly in primal and multiplier variables.

source_refs.locator: 3.3.3 Local uniqueness in terms of KKT triples p. 279
source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(V\) of \(\bar\lambda\), define
\[
S_{U,V}(p):=\left\{(x,\lambda)\in U\times V:\nabla_xL(x,\lambda,p)=0,\ g(x,p)\leq0,\ \lambda\geq0,\ \langle\lambda,g(x,p)\rangle=0\right\}.
\]
This localization retains precisely the KKT pairs near \((\bar x,\bar\lambda)\). It is single-valued around \(\bar p\) when there are neighborhoods \(P,U,V\) such that \(S_{U,V}(p)\) contains exactly one pair for every \(p\in P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The localized map collects KKT primal-multiplier pairs near a reference pair and is locally single-valued when each nearby parameter has exactly one such pair.
knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Localization

children.title: Multiplier Nonuniqueness Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Regimes where multiplier multiplicity obstructs stable single-valued localization.

assumptions_latex: The optimization problem has two identical active inequality constraints \(g_1(x)=x\leq0\) and \(g_2(x)=x\leq0\).
The objective is \(f(x)=-x\), and the reference solution is \(\bar x=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The primal solution is locally unique, but its multiplier set is the nontrivial segment \(\{\lambda\geq0:\lambda_1+\lambda_2=1\}\); hence no primal-dual localization is single-valued.

notation.meaning: Multiplier vector for the duplicated constraints

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Redundant active constraints exhibit the boundary between primal uniqueness and primal-dual uniqueness.

source_refs.locator: 3.3.4 Local uniqueness theory in NLP p. 283
source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider
\[
\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}}-x\quad\text{subject to}\quad g_1(x)=x\leq0,\qquad g_2(x)=x\leq0.
\]
The unique feasible minimizer is \(\bar x=0\). The KKT stationarity and complementarity conditions at \(\bar x\) reduce to
\[
-1+\lambda_1+\lambda_2=0,\qquad \lambda_1,\lambda_2\geq0.
\]
Thus every \(\lambda\) in the segment \(\{\lambda\in\mathbb{R}_+^2:\lambda_1+\lambda_2=1\}\) is a multiplier. Redundancy destroys multiplier uniqueness despite primal uniqueness, so the primal-dual KKT map cannot possess a single-valued localization at any selected multiplier.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Duplicating an active constraint preserves the unique primal solution but creates a segment of multipliers, preventing locally unique primal-dual KKT pairs.
knowledge_statements.title: Multiplier Nonuniqueness Boundaries

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3.4 Local uniqueness theory in NLP p. 283
source_witnesses.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. I

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear independence is the standard sufficient boundary excluding multiplier multiplicity at a fixed KKT point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At a feasible point \(\bar x\), let \(I(\bar x)=\{i:g_i(\bar x)=0\}\). If
\[
\{\nabla g_i(\bar x):i\in I(\bar x)\}\cup\{\nabla h_j(\bar x):1\le j\le q\}
\]
is linearly independent, then at most one pair \((\lambda,\mu)\) can satisfy KKT stationarity and complementarity at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: LICQ makes the KKT multiplier associated with a fixed primal point unique.
assumptions_latex: The objective and constraints are differentiable at \(\bar x\).
The active inequality and equality gradients satisfy LICQ.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |\Lambda(\bar x)|\leq1.

notation.meaning: KKT multiplier set at the fixed primal point

knowledge_statements.title: LICQ Guarantees Multiplier Uniqueness

knowledge_statements.statement_title: LICQ Failure Need Not Produce Multiple Multipliers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the standard sufficient condition is not equivalent to multiplier nonuniqueness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider
\[
\min_{x\in\mathbb R}x^2\quad\text{subject to}\quad x\le0,\quad 2x\le0.
\]
The unique minimizer is \(\bar x=0\). The active gradients \(1\) and \(2\) are dependent, so LICQ fails. KKT stationarity is
\[
\lambda_1+2\lambda_2=0,\qquad \lambda_1,\lambda_2\ge0,
\]
which forces \(\lambda_1=\lambda_2=0\). Thus the multiplier remains unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dependent active constraints can still have a unique multiplier; LICQ failure permits but does not force multiplier multiplicity.
assumptions_latex: The stated one-dimensional nonlinear program is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{LICQ}\text{ fails at }0\text{ while }\Lambda(0)=\{(0,0)\}.
knowledge_statements.title: LICQ Failure Need Not Produce Multiple Multipliers

children.title: Complementarity Solution Maps
children.top_down_role: Local uniqueness, nondegeneracy, and stability of complementarity systems.

assumptions_latex: Parameters and solutions are restricted to neighborhoods of \((\bar p,\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S(p)=\{x:0\leq x\perp F(x,p)\geq0\}\) is the complementarity solution map, equivalently the zero-set map of \(\Phi\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional nonlinear complementarity problems represented by a componentwise residual equation.

source_refs.locator: 3.3 Local Uniqueness of Solutions p. 266
source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each parameter \(p\in\mathbb{R}^q\), define
\[
S(p):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:x\geq0,\ F(x,p)\geq0,\ \langle x,F(x,p)\rangle=0\}.
\]
Because both vectors are componentwise nonnegative, the inner-product condition is equivalent to \(x_iF_i(x,p)=0\) for every \(i\). Consequently,
\[
x\in S(p)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \Phi(x,p)=0,
\qquad \Phi_i(x,p):=\min\{x_i,F_i(x,p)\}.
\]
Local uniqueness, isolation, and stability of complementarity solutions can therefore be formulated as corresponding local properties of this parameterized zero-set map.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A complementarity solution map is the parameterized zero set of the componentwise minimum residual, enabling local uniqueness and stability analysis.
knowledge_statements.title: Complementarity Solution Maps

source_witnesses.locator: 3.6 Nondegenerate Matrices and Local Uniqueness p. 162

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact generalized-equation representation of the nonlinear complementarity solution map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
With the convex-analysis normal cone \(N_{\mathbb R_+^n}\),
\[
0\le x\perp F(x,p)\ge0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
0\in F(x,p)+N_{\mathbb R_+^n}(x).
\]
Consequently,
\[
S(p)=\{x:0\in F(x,p)+N_{\mathbb R_+^n}(x)\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonlinear complementarity problem is exactly a generalized equation with the normal cone to the nonnegative orthant.
assumptions_latex: \(N_{\mathbb R_+^n}\) uses the convex-analysis outward-normal convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The complementarity and normal-cone generalized-equation solution maps coincide.

notation.meaning: Normal-cone mapping to the nonnegative orthant

knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Cone Representation of Complementarity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical global uniqueness characterization for linear-complementarity solution maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(M\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), define
\[
S_M(q):=\{x\ge0:Mx+q\ge0,\ x^\top(Mx+q)=0\}.
\]
Then \(M\) is a \(P\)-matrix if and only if \(S_M(q)\) is a singleton for every \(q\in\mathbb R^n\). Under these equivalent conditions, the resulting solution function is continuous, piecewise affine, and globally Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An LCP has exactly one solution for every right-hand side precisely when its matrix is a P-matrix; its solution map is then piecewise affine and globally Lipschitz.
assumptions_latex: A \(P\)-matrix has every principal minor positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M\text{ is a }P\text{-matrix}\iff |S_M(q)|=1\ \forall q\in\mathbb R^n.

notation.meaning: Matrix with all principal minors positive

knowledge_statements.title: P-Matrix Global Uniqueness Theorem

children.title: Hadamard Well-Posedness
children.top_down_role: Classical existence, uniqueness, and continuous-dependence organization.

assumptions_latex: \(G:P\rightrightarrows X\) is the solution map of the parameterized problem, and \(\bar x\in G(\bar p)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The problem is locally Hadamard well-posed at \((\bar p,\bar x)\) precisely when nearby solutions exist uniquely and depend continuously on the parameter.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local metric-space version of Hadamard's existence, uniqueness, and continuous-dependence requirements.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Characterizations of Well-Posedness and Sensitivity Analysis p. 377
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The parameterized problem is locally Hadamard well-posed at \((\bar p,\bar x)\) if there are neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar p\) and \(V\) of \(\bar x\) and a function \(s:U\to V\) such that
\[
G(p)\cap V=\{s(p)\}\quad\text{for every }p\in U,
\qquad s(\bar p)=\bar x,
\]
and \(s\) is continuous at \(\bar p\). Thus the localized problem has a solution, that solution is unique, and whenever \(p_k\to\bar p\), the corresponding localized solutions satisfy \(s(p_k)\to\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local Hadamard well-posedness means that every nearby parameter has exactly one nearby solution and that solution converges to the reference solution with the parameter.
knowledge_statements.title: Hadamard Well-Posedness

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 4. Characterizations of Well-Posedness and Sensitivity Analysis p. 377
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary showing that Hadamard continuous dependence need not be Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=X=\mathbb R\) and \(G(p)=\{\sqrt[3]{p}\}\). The unique solution selection \(s(p)=\sqrt[3]{p}\) is continuous at \(0\), so the problem is locally Hadamard well-posed at \((0,0)\). It is not locally Lipschitz there, since \[\frac{|s(p)-s(0)|}{|p|}=|p|^{-2/3}\to\infty\quad\text{as }p\to0,\ p\ne0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The unique cube-root solution depends continuously on the parameter and is Hadamard well-posed, but its dependence is not locally Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\) is locally Hadamard well-posed at \((0,0)\) but its solution selection is not locally Lipschitz there.
knowledge_statements.title: Qualitative Versus Lipschitz Dependence

children.top_down_role: Local uniqueness and isolated-solution regimes.

children.title: Local Solution Uniqueness
children.top_down_role: Uniqueness of a solution within a localized neighborhood.

assumptions_latex: \(S:P\rightrightarrows X\) is a solution map between metric spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar x\) is locally unique at \(\bar p\) exactly when it is the sole member of \(S(\bar p)\) in some neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniqueness at the reference parameter, restricted to a neighborhood of the reference solution.

source_refs.locator: 3.3 Local Uniqueness of Solutions p. 266
source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A solution \(\bar x\in S(\bar p)\) is locally unique for the reference problem if there exists a neighborhood \(V\) of \(\bar x\) such that
\[
S(\bar p)\cap V=\{\bar x\}.
\]
This condition concerns only the fiber at \(\bar p\): it neither requires solutions to exist for parameters near \(\bar p\) nor controls their displacement. If one neighborhood \(V\) satisfies the equality, every sufficiently small neighborhood of \(\bar x\) contained in \(V\) also satisfies it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reference solution is locally unique when no other solution of the same unperturbed problem lies sufficiently near it.
knowledge_statements.title: Local Solution Uniqueness

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3 Local Uniqueness of Solutions p. 266

children.title: Stable Solution Isolation
children.top_down_role: Persistence of isolated solution behavior under perturbation.

assumptions_latex: \(S:P\rightrightarrows X\) is a solution map between metric spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed estimate defines stable isolation, equivalently isolated calmness of \(S\) at \((\bar p,\bar x)\).

notation.meaning: Metric balls in the parameter and solution spaces
Distance metrics on the parameter and solution spaces

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stable isolation is formulated as isolated calmness of a set-valued solution map.

source_refs.locator: 4.1.2 Neighborhood Characterizations of Metric Regularity and Lipschitzian Behavior p. 382
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The solution \(\bar x\in S(\bar p)\) is stably isolated if there exist radii \(r_P,r_X>0\) and a constant \(\kappa\geq0\) such that
\[
x\in S(p)\cap B_X(\bar x,r_X),\quad p\in B_P(\bar p,r_P)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
d_X(x,\bar x)\leq\kappa d_P(p,\bar p).
\]
At \(p=\bar p\), the estimate forces \(S(\bar p)\cap B_X(\bar x,r_X)=\{\bar x\}\). The definition permits an empty localized fiber for some nearby parameters; existence is an additional requirement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A solution is stably isolated when every nearby solution moves from it at most linearly with the parameter perturbation; nearby solution existence is separate.
knowledge_statements.title: Stable Solution Isolation

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1.2 Neighborhood Characterizations of Metric Regularity and Lipschitzian Behavior p. 382
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local displacement-ratio representation of the least stable-isolation constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \((\bar p,\bar x)\in\operatorname{gph}S\), set
\[
\operatorname{isol}S(\bar p\mid\bar x):=\limsup_{\substack{p\to\bar p,\ p\ne\bar p\\x\to\bar x,\ x\in S(p)}}\frac{d_X(x,\bar x)}{d_P(p,\bar p)},
\]
using value \(0\) when no such nearby graph points exist. Then \(\bar x\) is stably isolated exactly when it is locally unique in \(S(\bar p)\) and this modulus is finite. When finite, it equals the infimum of the admissible constants in the stable-isolation estimate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stable isolation is reference-fiber isolation plus a finite local displacement ratio; the ratio limsup is its exact modulus.
assumptions_latex: \(S:P\rightrightarrows X\) is a multifunction between metric spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar x\text{ is stably isolated}\iff S(\bar p)\text{ is locally singleton at }\bar x\text{ and }\operatorname{isol}S(\bar p\mid\bar x)<\infty.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Stable-Isolation Modulus

children.title: Uniqueness–Isolation Relations
children.top_down_role: Regimes connecting local uniqueness with stable isolation.

knowledge_statements.title: Uniqueness–Isolation Relations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical comparison of fiberwise local uniqueness and perturbation-uniform stable isolation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Stable isolation of \(\bar x\) for \(S\) at \(\bar p\) implies local uniqueness of \(\bar x\) in \(S(\bar p)\). The converse is false. For \(P=X=\mathbb{R}\), the map \(T(p)=\{\sqrt{|p|}\}\) has the locally unique reference solution \(0\in T(0)\), but \(0\) is not stably isolated because no finite \(\kappa\) satisfies \(\sqrt{|p|}\leq \kappa|p|\) for all sufficiently small nonzero \(p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stable isolation implies local uniqueness, but local uniqueness does not imply stable isolation; the square-root solution branch is a counterexample.
assumptions_latex: \(S:P\rightrightarrows X\) is a solution map between metric spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Stable isolation implies local uniqueness, whereas local uniqueness alone does not imply stable isolation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Stable Isolation Does Not Imply Nearby Single-Valuedness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stable isolation bounds every localized branch but does not restrict the number of branches away from the reference parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(S:\mathbb R\rightrightarrows\mathbb R\) by \(S(p)=\{-|p|,|p|\}\). Then \(S(0)=\{0\}\), and every \(x\in S(p)\) satisfies \(|x|=|p|\). Thus \(0\) is stably isolated at \(p=0\) with modulus \(1\), although \(S(p)\) has two distinct values for every \(p\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stable isolation can coexist with two nearby branches because it bounds displacement without requiring a unique perturbed solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\) is stably isolated at \((0,0)\) but has no single-valued localization on any parameter neighborhood of \(0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Stable Isolation Does Not Imply Nearby Single-Valuedness

children.title: Isolation Loss Regimes
children.top_down_role: Branching or accumulation phenomena that destroy stable isolation.

assumptions_latex: The scalar parameter and solution spaces are \(P=X=\mathbb{R}\).
The solution map is generated by the equation \(x^2=p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The isolated reference solution at \(p=0\) loses local single-valuedness under arbitrarily small positive perturbations and is not stably isolated.

notation.meaning: Solution map of the scalar equation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A scalar fold illustrates loss of branch uniqueness and linear isolation at a singular reference point.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Characterizations of Well-Posedness and Sensitivity Analysis p. 377
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[
S(p):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}:x^2=p\}.
\]
At \(p=0\), the solution \(\bar x=0\) is globally unique and hence isolated. For every \(p>0\), however,
\[
S(p)=\{-\sqrt p,\sqrt p\},
\]
so arbitrarily small positive perturbations split the reference branch into two nearby solutions. Moreover, stable isolation would require \(\sqrt p\leq\kappa p\) for all sufficiently small \(p>0\), which is impossible. The vanishing derivative of \(x\mapsto x^2\) at \(0\) marks the loss regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At the fold equation x-squared equals p, the unique isolated zero splits into two solutions and violates every linear displacement bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Isolation Loss Regimes

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 4. Characterizations of Well-Posedness and Sensitivity Analysis p. 377
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Static accumulation is an isolation-loss mechanism distinct from perturbation-induced branch splitting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S:\mathbb R\rightrightarrows\mathbb R\) be constant with \(S(p)=\{0\}\cup\{1/n:n\in\mathbb N\}\). Every neighborhood of \(0\) contains a distinct point \(1/n\in S(0)\). Hence \(0\) is not locally isolated and cannot be stably isolated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distinct reference solutions accumulating at the selected solution destroy isolation without any parameter perturbation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\) is neither locally unique in \(S(0)\) nor stably isolated.
knowledge_statements.title: Accumulation Destroys Reference Isolation

children.top_down_role: Stable solution-set behavior used in variational-inequality error-bound theory.

children.title: Semistability
children.top_down_role: Localized semistable behavior relevant to variational systems.

assumptions_latex: \(S:P\rightrightarrows X\) has nonempty values near \(\bar p\) in metric spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar x\) is semistable when \(\operatorname{dist}(\bar x,S(p))\to0\) as \(p\to\bar p\).

notation.meaning: Distance from a point to a set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semistability is taken here as persistence of one reference solution under parameter perturbations.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Characterizations of Well-Posedness and Sensitivity Analysis p. 377
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A reference solution \(\bar x\in S(\bar p)\) is semistable with respect to parameter perturbations if
\[
\lim_{p\to\bar p}\operatorname{dist}(\bar x,S(p))=0.
\]
Equivalently, for every sequence \(p_k\to\bar p\), there exist choices \(x_k\in S(p_k)\) such that \(x_k\to\bar x\). This is inner semicontinuity of \(S\) at the graph point \((\bar p,\bar x)\). It asserts persistence of the selected solution but neither uniqueness of nearby solutions nor exclusion of additional branches far from \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reference solution is semistable when every small parameter perturbation admits some solution converging to that selected solution.
knowledge_statements.title: Semistability

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 4. Characterizations of Well-Posedness and Sensitivity Analysis p. 377
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The distance condition precisely describes inner semicontinuity at a graph point, but “semistability” is terminology-sensitive and overloaded. The broad chapter locator does not establish that this source uses the term in exactly this sense.

children.title: Solution-Set Stability
children.top_down_role: Persistence of nearby solution sets under perturbation.

assumptions_latex: \(S:P\rightrightarrows X\) has nonempty compact values near \(\bar p\).
\(X\) is a metric space and \(d_H\) denotes Hausdorff distance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The solution set is stable at \(\bar p\) when \(d_H(S(p),S(\bar p))\to0\) as \(p\to\bar p\).

notation.meaning: Excess of one set over another

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hausdorff stability of nonempty compact solution sets in a metric solution space.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Characterizations of Well-Posedness and Sensitivity Analysis p. 377
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For nonempty compact sets \(A,B\subset X\), define
\[
e(A,B):=\sup_{a\in A}\operatorname{dist}(a,B),
\qquad d_H(A,B):=\max\{e(A,B),e(B,A)\}.
\]
The solution-set map \(S\) is Hausdorff stable at \(\bar p\) if
\[
\lim_{p\to\bar p}d_H\bigl(S(p),S(\bar p)\bigr)=0.
\]
The two excess terms encode distinct requirements: every perturbed solution must approach the reference solution set, and every reference solution must be approximated by perturbed solutions. Thus set stability permits multiple solutions while controlling the entire compact solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solution-set stability means the whole compact solution set converges in Hausdorff distance, controlling both disappearing reference solutions and emerging perturbed branches.
knowledge_statements.title: Solution-Set Stability

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 4. Characterizations of Well-Posedness and Sensitivity Analysis p. 377

children.title: Semistability-to-Set Transfer
children.top_down_role: Regimes transferring semistable behavior to solution-set control.

knowledge_statements.title: Semistability-to-Set Transfer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compact-valued transfer from pointwise persistence plus outer semicontinuity to Hausdorff set stability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a metric space, let \(K\) be a compact metric space, and let \(S:P\rightrightarrows K\) have nonempty closed values in a neighborhood of \(\bar p\in P\). Suppose that, for every \(x\in S(\bar p)\), \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S(p))\to0\) as \(p\to\bar p\). Suppose also that \(S\) is outer semicontinuous at \(\bar p\): whenever \(p_k\to\bar p\), \(x_k\in S(p_k)\), and \(x_k\to x\), one has \(x\in S(\bar p)\). Then \(d_H\bigl(S(p),S(\bar p)\bigr)\to0\) as \(p\to\bar p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For solution sets in a common compact metric range, persistence of every reference solution together with outer semicontinuity implies Hausdorff stability of the entire solution set.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a metric parameter space and \(K\) is a compact metric solution space.
\(S:P\rightrightarrows K\) has nonempty closed values near \(\bar p\).
Every \(x\in S(\bar p)\) is semistable, and \(S\) is outer semicontinuous at \(\bar p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_H\bigl(S(p),S(\bar p)\bigr)\to0\) as \(p\to\bar p\).

notation.meaning: Common compact metric range containing all nearby solution sets
Hausdorff distance on nonempty compact subsets of the solution space

children.title: Set-Stability Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Perturbation regimes where solution-set control breaks down.

assumptions_latex: The parameter and solution spaces are \(P=X=\mathbb{R}\).
The solution map is \(S(0)=\{0\}\) and \(S(p)=\{0,1\}\) for \(p\neq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The reference solution \(0\) is semistable, but \(S\) is not outer semicontinuous or Hausdorff stable at \(0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An emerging branch shows why pointwise semistability alone does not ensure solution-set stability.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Characterizations of Well-Posedness and Sensitivity Analysis p. 377
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(S:\mathbb{R}\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}\) by
\[
S(0)=\{0\},
\qquad S(p)=\{0,1\}\quad\text{for }p\neq0.
\]
The reference solution \(0\in S(0)\) is semistable because \(\operatorname{dist}(0,S(p))=0\) for every \(p\). Nevertheless, for every nonzero \(p\),
\[
d_H(S(p),S(0))=1.
\]
Hence the solution sets do not converge to \(S(0)\). The constant perturbed branch \(x=1\) also violates outer semicontinuity at \(0\). Pointwise persistence of a selected reference solution therefore cannot by itself exclude emerging branches or imply set stability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A persistent reference solution does not prevent an extra perturbed branch; semistability can therefore hold while outer and Hausdorff set stability fail.
knowledge_statements.title: Set-Stability Failure Boundaries

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 4. Characterizations of Well-Posedness and Sensitivity Analysis p. 377
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the compact-range hypothesis in the semistability-to-set transfer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(S:\mathbb R\rightrightarrows\mathbb R\) by \[S(0)=\{0\},\qquad S(p)=\{0,|p|^{-1}\}\quad(p\ne0).\] The reference solution persists because \(0\in S(p)\) for every \(p\). Moreover, \(S\) is outer semicontinuous at \(0\): if \(p_k\to0\), \(x_k\in S(p_k)\), and \(x_k\to x\), then the unbounded branch cannot occur infinitely often, so \(x=0\in S(0)\). Nevertheless, \[d_H(S(p),S(0))=|p|^{-1}\to\infty.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A perturbed branch can escape to infinity without violating sequential outer semicontinuity, destroying Hausdorff stability when compact containment is absent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every reference solution persists and \(S\) is outer semicontinuous at \(0\), but \(d_H(S(p),S(0))\not\to0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Escape without Compact Containment

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of Hausdorff stability when only some reference solutions persist.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(S:\mathbb R\rightrightarrows\mathbb R\) by \[S(0)=\{0,1\},\qquad S(p)=\{0\}\quad(p\ne0).\] The selected reference solution \(0\) persists, and \(S\) is outer semicontinuous at \(0\). However, \(1\in S(0)\) is not approximated at nonzero parameters, and \[d_H(S(p),S(0))=1\qquad(p\ne0).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Outer semicontinuity and persistence of one reference solution do not prevent another reference branch from disappearing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\) is outer semicontinuous at \(0\) and \(0\) persists, but \(S\) is not Hausdorff stable at \(0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Disappearing Reference Branch

children.title: Set-Valued Stability without Uniqueness
children.top_down_role: Stable solution sets in the absence of isolated branches.

assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a metric space with metric \(d_P\), and \(X\) is a normed space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exist neighborhoods \(V\) of \(\bar p\) and \(U\) of \(\bar x\), and \(L\geq 0\), such that \(S(p_1)\cap U\subset S(p_2)+L d_P(p_1,p_2)\mathbb B_X\) for all \(p_1,p_2\in V\).

notation.meaning: closed unit ball of the normed space

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Aubin stability of a localized solution set, allowing multiple solutions.

source_refs.locator: 4.1.2 Neighborhood Characterizations of Metric Regularity and Lipschitzian Behavior p. 382
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The solution mapping \(S\) is set-valuedly Lipschitz stable at \((\bar p,\bar x)\) if there exist neighborhoods \(V\) of \(\bar p\) and \(U\) of \(\bar x\), and a constant \(L\geq 0\), such that for all \(p_1,p_2\in V\), \[S(p_1)\cap U\subset S(p_2)+L d_P(p_1,p_2)\mathbb B_X.\] This property neither requires \(S(p)\cap U\) to be a singleton nor selects an isolated solution branch.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nearby parameters produce localized solution sets whose one-sided excess changes at most Lipschitzly, without requiring a unique or isolated solution.
knowledge_statements.title: Set-Valued Stability without Uniqueness

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1.2 Neighborhood Characterizations of Metric Regularity and Lipschitzian Behavior p. 382
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Example showing that set-valued Lipschitz stability does not imply a unique local branch.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=X=\mathbb R\) and define \(S(p)=[-1,1]\) for every \(p\). At \((\bar p,\bar x)=(0,0)\), for every neighborhood \(U\) of \(0\) and all \(p_1,p_2\), \[S(p_1)\cap U\subset S(p_2)=S(p_2)+0\,|p_1-p_2|\mathbb B.\] Hence \(S\) has the Aubin property with modulus \(0\), while every sufficiently small neighborhood of \(0\) contains infinitely many points of \(S(p)\); no unique localized branch is selected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constant interval-valued solution map is Lipschitz stable with modulus zero while retaining infinitely many nearby solutions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\) is set-valuedly Lipschitz stable at \((0,0)\) with modulus \(0\), but its localization is not single-valued.
knowledge_statements.title: Aubin Stability with Persistent Multiplicity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Smooth Manifolds as Partly Smooth Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic subclass common to standard finite-dimensional set conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) agree locally near \(\bar x\) with a \(C^2\) embedded manifold \(M\). Then \(C\) is prox-regular near \(\bar x\), \(N_C(x)=N_M(x)\) varies continuously along \(M\), and \[\operatorname{span}N_C(\bar x)=N_M(\bar x).\] Consequently, \(C\) is partly smooth at \(\bar x\) relative to \(M\) under the standard finite-dimensional set conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth embedded manifold is a partly smooth set relative to itself.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) agrees locally with a \(C^2\) embedded manifold \(M\) near \(\bar x\).
A standard finite-dimensional set partial-smoothness convention is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\text{ is partly smooth at }\bar x\text{ relative to }M.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Manifolds as Partly Smooth Sets

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is locally closed and \(\bar x\in C\).
\(M\subset C\) is a \(C^2\) manifold around \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is partly smooth at \(\bar x\) relative to \(M\).

notation.meaning: limiting normal cone to the set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional local definition relative to a prescribed smooth manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The set \(C\) is partly smooth at \(\bar x\) relative to \(M\) when: \(C\) is prox-regular at \(\bar x\); the mapping \(x\mapsto N_C(x)\) is continuous at \(\bar x\) when \(x\) is restricted to \(M\); and the sharpness identity \[N_M(\bar x)=\operatorname{span}N_C(\bar x)\] holds. Here continuity is set-valued continuity along \(M\), and the equality makes the normal variation of \(C\) exactly transverse to the active manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set is partly smooth when it is prox-regular, has continuously varying normals along a smooth manifold, and its normal span equals the manifold normal space.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical convex finite-dimensional example at a point with fixed support.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=\|x\|_1\) and \(\bar x\in\mathbb R^n\), let \(I=\{i:\bar x_i\ne0\}\) and \[M=\{x:x_{I^c}=0,\ \operatorname{sign}(x_I)=\operatorname{sign}(\bar x_I)\}.\] Locally at \(\bar x\), \(M\) is a smooth manifold, \(f|_M\) is smooth, and \[\operatorname{par}\partial f(\bar x)=\{v:v_I=0\}=N_M(\bar x).\] Thus the \(\ell_1\) norm is partly smooth relative to the fixed-support, fixed-sign manifold under the standard convex convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The ℓ1 norm is partly smooth along the manifold preserving the support and signs of the reference vector.
assumptions_latex: The standard convex partly smooth function convention is used.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f\) is partly smooth at \((\bar x,\bar v)\) relative to \(M\) if \(f|_M\) is \(C^2\) near \(\bar x\), \(f\) is prox-regular and subdifferentially continuous at \((\bar x,\bar v)\), the restriction of \(\partial f\) to \(M\) is continuous there, and \[\operatorname{par}\partial f(\bar x)=N_M(\bar x).\] The last equality is the sharpness condition identifying directions of nonsmooth variation with directions normal to \(M\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Partly smooth structure transfers between object classes through canonical geometric representations. children.title: Active Manifolds

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-localization convention for an active manifold at a stationary point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and lower semicontinuous, let \(0\in\partial f(\bar x)\), and let \(M\) be a \(C^2\) manifold through \(\bar x\). The manifold \(M\) is a stationary active manifold for \(f\) at \(\bar x\) if \(f|_M\) is \(C^2\) near \(\bar x\) and there exist a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(\eta>0\) such that \[x\in U\setminus M\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x))\geq\eta.\] Equivalently, every \(x\in U\) satisfying \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x))<\eta\) lies in \(M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stationary active manifold is a smooth stratum containing every sufficiently nearby point with sufficiently small stationarity residual.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f|_M\) is locally \(C^2\) and nearby points outside \(M\) have stationarity residual bounded below by a positive constant.

notation.meaning: Stationarity residual, with distance to the empty set interpreted as positive infinity.

children.title: Identifiable Manifolds

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential and localized formulations of subdifferential identifiability at a specified graph pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and lower semicontinuous, let \((\bar x,\bar v)\in\operatorname{gph}\partial f\), and let \(M\) be a manifold through \(\bar x\). The manifold \(M\) is identifiable for \(f\) at \((\bar x,\bar v)\) in the function-value-attentive sense if every sequence \((x_k,v_k)\in\operatorname{gph}\partial f\) satisfying \[(x_k,v_k,f(x_k))\to(\bar x,\bar v,f(\bar x))\] has \(x_k\in M\) eventually. Equivalently, there are neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(V\) of \(\bar v\), and \(\varepsilon>0\), such that \[x\in U,\quad v\in V\cap\partial f(x),\quad |f(x)-f(\bar x)|<\varepsilon\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x\in M.\] If \(f\) is subdifferentially continuous at \((\bar x,\bar v)\), the value-convergence clause is automatic, so identifiability is equivalent to local containment of \(\operatorname{gph}\partial f\) in \(M\times\mathbb R^n\) near \((\bar x,\bar v)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An identifiable manifold eventually contains every primal component of a function-value-compatible subgradient sequence approaching the reference pair; under subdifferential continuity this reduces to ordinary local graph containment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (x_k,v_k,f(x_k))\to(\bar x,\bar v,f(\bar x))\Longrightarrow x_k\in M\ \text{eventually},
knowledge_statements.title: Function-Value-Attentive Identifiable Manifold

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The manifold \(M\) is identifiable for \(f\) at \((\bar x,\bar v)\) if, for every sequence \((x_k,v_k)\in\operatorname{gph}\partial f\) satisfying \[(x_k,v_k)\to(\bar x,\bar v)\quad\text{and}\quad f(x_k)	o f(\bar x),\] there exists \(k_0\) such that \(x_k\in M\) for every \(kgeq k_0\).
