children.title: Regularity Condition Measures
children.top_down_role: Exact regularity and openness moduli as local condition measures.

assumptions_latex: \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) maps metric spaces and \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\).
The infimum of an empty set of admissible constants is defined as \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{reg}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)=\inf\!\left\{\kappa>0:\operatorname{dist}(x,F^{-1}(y))\le\kappa\operatorname{dist}(y,F(x))\ \text{locally}\right\},\] and \(\operatorname{sur}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)=1/\operatorname{reg}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)\) under reciprocal extended-real conventions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact local moduli for metric regularity and linear openness.

source_refs.locator: 1.2.3 Metric Regularity and Covering p. 56
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

source_refs.locator: 4.1.2 Neighborhood Characterizations of Metric Regularity and Lipschitzian Behavior p. 382
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The exact regularity modulus is the infimum of all \(\kappa>0\) for which neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(V\) of \(\bar y\) exist such that \[\operatorname{dist}(x,F^{-1}(y))\le
\kappa\operatorname{dist}(y,F(x))
\quad((x,y)\in U\times V).\] The exact linear-openness modulus is the supremal local covering rate and satisfies \[\operatorname{sur}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)=
\frac{1}{\operatorname{reg}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)},\] with \(1/0=+\infty\) and \(1/(+\infty)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exact regularity modulus is the smallest local residual-to-solution constant; its reciprocal is the exact linear-openness modulus.
knowledge_statements.title: Regularity Condition Measures

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2.3 Metric Regularity and Covering p. 56
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1.2 Neighborhood Characterizations of Metric Regularity and Lipschitzian Behavior p. 382
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact quantitative correspondence between metric regularity and Lipschitz-like behavior of the inverse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A multifunction \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) is metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) if and only if \(F^{-1}\) has the Aubin property at \((\bar y,\bar x)\). Their exact moduli coincide:
\[
\operatorname{reg}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)=\operatorname{lip}F^{-1}(\bar y\mid\bar x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exact regularity condition measure equals the exact Lipschitz-like modulus of the inverse solution mapping.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{reg}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)=\operatorname{lip}F^{-1}(\bar y\mid\bar x).

notation.meaning: Exact Aubin modulus of the inverse multifunction

knowledge_statements.title: Inverse Aubin Modulus Identity

children.title: Error-Bound Condition Measures
children.top_down_role: Residual-to-distance moduli as feasibility and stationarity condition measures.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hölder Error-Bound Moduli and Limiting-Ratio Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order-dependent extension and intrinsic ratio representation of the exact local residual-to-distance modulus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(q>0\), define
\[
\operatorname{eb}_q(r;\bar x):=\inf\left\{\kappa>0:\exists U\ni\bar x\ \forall x\in U,\ \operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le\kappa r(x)^q\right\}.
\]
Then
\[
\operatorname{eb}_q(r;\bar x)=\limsup_{\substack{x\to\bar x\\x\notin S}}\frac{\operatorname{dist}(x,S)}{r(x)^q}.
\]
The case \(q=1\) is the linear error-bound modulus. The empty limiting supremum is interpreted as \(0\), and a quotient with \(r(x)=+\infty\) as \(0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exact order-q error-bound measure is the limiting worst-case ratio of distance to the zero set over the qth power of the residual.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{eb}_q(r;\bar x)=\limsup_{x\to\bar x,\ x\notin S}\frac{\operatorname{dist}(x,S)}{r(x)^q}.
knowledge_statements.title: Hölder Error-Bound Moduli and Limiting-Ratio Representation

assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a metric space, \(r:X\to[0,+\infty]\), and \(S:=\{x:r(x)=0\}\) contains \(\bar x\).
The infimum of an empty set of admissible constants is defined as \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{eb}(r;\bar x):=\inf\!\left\{\kappa>0:\exists U\ni\bar x\ \forall x\in U,\ \operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le\kappa r(x)\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact local residual-to-distance modulus for an arbitrary nonnegative residual.

source_refs.locator: 5.4.1 Linear Subextremality of Set Systems p. 110
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The exact local error-bound modulus of \(r\) at \(\bar x\in S\) is \[\operatorname{eb}(r;\bar x):=
\inf\left\{\kappa>0:
\begin{array}{l}
\text{there exists a neighborhood }U\text{ of }\bar x\text{ such that}\\
\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le\kappa r(x)\text{ for every }x\in U
\end{array}
\right\}.\] A finite value quantifies local residual conditioning; smaller values mean that a given residual controls distance to the solution set more sharply.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The error-bound condition measure is the smallest local constant converting a feasibility or stationarity residual into distance to its zero set.
knowledge_statements.title: Error-Bound Condition Measures

source_witnesses.locator: 5.4.1 Linear Subextremality of Set Systems p. 110
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition itself is precise and the content kind fits the container, but the cited section concerns linear subextremality of set systems and does not clearly support the claimed exact modulus for an arbitrary extended-valued residual. A directly supporting error-bound source or confirmed full-text passage is required.

children.title: Distance to Ill-Posedness
children.top_down_role: Perturbation distance to loss of regularity or stable solvability.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal P\) is a normed space of problem data.
\(\mathcal R\subseteq\mathcal P\) is the set of data whose associated solution mapping has the prescribed regularity property.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_{\mathrm{ill}}(p)=\inf_{q\in\Sigma}\|p-q\|_{\mathcal P}\), where \(\Sigma=\mathcal P\setminus\mathcal R\).

notation.meaning: Set of ill-posed or nonregular data.
Distance from the datum to ill-posedness.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract perturbation-space definition; the selected regularity property and data norm are application-dependent.

source_refs.locator: 4.2.3 Metric Regularity under Perturbations p. 399
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let each \(p\in\mathcal P\) determine a solution mapping \(F_p\), and let \(\mathcal R\) consist of the data for which \(F_p\) possesses the designated local regularity or stable-solvability property. The ill-posed set is \(\Sigma:=\mathcal P\setminus\mathcal R\). The distance to ill-posedness of \(p\) is
\[
d_{\mathrm{ill}}(p):=\operatorname{dist}(p,\Sigma)=\inf_{q\in\Sigma}\|p-q\|_{\mathcal P},
\]
with \(d_{\mathrm{ill}}(p):=+\infty\) if \(\Sigma=\varnothing\). A positive value certifies that every perturbation of norm strictly below \(d_{\mathrm{ill}}(p)\) remains in \(\mathcal R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distance to ill-posedness is the smallest data perturbation, in a specified norm, that destroys the chosen regularity or stable-solvability property.
knowledge_statements.title: Distance to Ill-Posedness

source_witnesses.locator: 4.2.3 Metric Regularity under Perturbations p. 399
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Metric Geometry of the Ill-Posedness Distance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General metric properties of distance to the selected ill-posed data set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every nonempty \(\Sigma\subseteq\mathcal P\), the function \(d_{\mathrm{ill}}(p)=\operatorname{dist}(p,\Sigma)\) is \(1\)-Lipschitz. Moreover, \(d_{\mathrm{ill}}(p)=0\) exactly when \(p\in\overline\Sigma\), and \(d_{\mathrm{ill}}(p)>0\) exactly when an open ball centered at \(p\) contains no ill-posed datum. Thus zero distance need not mean that \(p\in\Sigma\) unless the ill-posed set is closed at \(p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distance to ill-posedness is 1-Lipschitz and is positive exactly when the datum has a nonzero robust regularity radius.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal P\) is a normed data space.
\(\varnothing\ne\Sigma\subseteq\mathcal P\) is the selected ill-posed set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |d_{\mathrm{ill}}(p)-d_{\mathrm{ill}}(q)|\le\|p-q\|,\qquad d_{\mathrm{ill}}(p)=0\iff p\in\overline\Sigma.

notation.meaning: Distance from the datum to the ill-posed set

knowledge_statements.title: Metric Geometry of the Ill-Posedness Distance

children.title: Representation-Scaling Conditioning Coupling
children.top_down_role: Dependence of residual and regularity condition measures on model representation and scaling.

children.title: Representation Effects
children.top_down_role: Dependence of regularity measures on equivalent model formulations.

assumptions_latex: \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) is metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\).
\(U\) and \(V\) are locally bi-Lipschitz coordinate changes near \(\bar x\) and \(\bar y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\dfrac{\operatorname{reg}F}{\operatorname{lip}(U^{-1})\operatorname{lip}(V)}\leq\operatorname{reg}G\leq\operatorname{lip}(U)\operatorname{reg}F\operatorname{lip}(V^{-1})\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantifies how bi-Lipschitz changes of variables alter the exact metric-regularity modulus.

source_refs.locator: 4.1.2 Neighborhood Characterizations of Metric Regularity and Lipschitzian Behavior p. 382
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G:=V\circ F\circ U^{-1}\), \(\bar u:=U(\bar x)\), and \(\bar v:=V(\bar y)\). If the displayed local Lipschitz moduli are finite, then \(G\) is metrically regular at \((\bar u,\bar v)\), and its exact modulus satisfies
\[
\frac{\operatorname{reg}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)}{\operatorname{lip}(U^{-1})(\bar u)\operatorname{lip}(V)(\bar y)}
\leq \operatorname{reg}G(\bar u\mid\bar v)
\leq \operatorname{lip}(U)(\bar x)\operatorname{reg}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)\operatorname{lip}(V^{-1})(\bar v).
\]
Thus equivalent representations preserve regularity but can distort its numerical modulus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bi-Lipschitz coordinate changes preserve metric regularity, while their Lipschitz distortion factors bound the change in its numerical modulus.
knowledge_statements.title: Representation Effects

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1.2 Neighborhood Characterizations of Metric Regularity and Lipschitzian Behavior p. 382
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

children.title: Scaling Effects
children.top_down_role: Dependence of residual measures on variable or constraint scaling.

assumptions_latex: \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) is metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{reg}G(a\bar x\mid b\bar y)=\dfrac{a}{b}\operatorname{reg}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)\).

notation.meaning: Mapping obtained by scaling variables and residuals.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact scalar-scaling law for normed domain and range spaces.

source_refs.locator: 1.2.3 Metric Regularity and Covering p. 56
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(G:aX\rightrightarrows bY\) by \(G(u):=bF(u/a)\). Then \(G^{-1}(v)=aF^{-1}(v/b)\), so the exact metric-regularity moduli obey
\[
\operatorname{reg}G(a\bar x\mid b\bar y)=\frac{a}{b}\operatorname{reg}F(\bar x\mid\bar y).
\]
Consequently, scaling the domain by \(a\) enlarges the modulus by \(a\), whereas scaling the range by \(b\) reduces it by \(b\). Metric regularity itself is unchanged because \(a/b\) is finite and positive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scaling domain coordinates by a positive factor and range coordinates by another multiplies the metric-regularity modulus by their ratio.
knowledge_statements.title: Scaling Effects

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2.3 Metric Regularity and Covering p. 56
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual and Variable Scaling Law for Error-Bound Moduli
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact scaling law for residual-to-distance condition measures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S=r^{-1}(0)\), let \(a,c>0\), and define \(\widetilde r(u)=c\,r(u/a)\), whose zero set is \(aS\). Then
\[
\operatorname{eb}(\widetilde r;a\bar x)=\frac{a}{c}\operatorname{eb}(r;\bar x).
\]
More generally, for the order-\(q\) modulus,
\[
\operatorname{eb}_q(\widetilde r;a\bar x)=\frac{a}{c^q}\operatorname{eb}_q(r;\bar x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scaling variables multiplies an error-bound modulus by the variable scale, while scaling the residual divides the order-q modulus by the qth power of the residual scale.
assumptions_latex: \(r:X\to[0,+\infty]\) is a residual on a normed space and \(\bar x\in r^{-1}(0)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{eb}_q(c\,r(\cdot/a);a\bar x)=a c^{-q}\operatorname{eb}_q(r;\bar x).

notation.meaning: Residual after variable and residual scaling

knowledge_statements.title: Residual and Variable Scaling Law for Error-Bound Moduli

children.title: Representation-Invariant Quantities
children.top_down_role: Conditioning information stable across selected reformulations.

assumptions_latex: \(G=V\circ F\circ U^{-1}\) for local bi-Lipschitz homeomorphisms \(U,V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{reg}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)<+\infty\iff\operatorname{reg}G(U\bar x\mid V\bar y)<+\infty\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(G:=V\circ F\circ U^{-1}\), the graph germ transforms as
\[
\operatorname{gph}G=(U\times V)(\operatorname{gph}F)
\]
locally around \((U(\bar x),V(\bar y))\). Hence the membership relation \(\bar y\in F(\bar x)\), local closedness of the graph, and the finiteness of the exact regularity modulus are invariant under the representation change. In particular,
\[
\operatorname{reg}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)<+\infty
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\operatorname{reg}G(U(\bar x)\mid V(\bar y))<+\infty.
\]
The numerical value of the modulus is generally not invariant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bi-Lipschitz representations preserve graph membership, local graph closedness, and whether metric regularity holds, but not generally its numerical modulus.
knowledge_statements.title: Representation-Invariant Quantities

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Invariance of Subregularity and Strong Metric Regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additional qualitative regularity properties preserved by local bi-Lipschitz coordinate changes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=V\circ F\circ U^{-1}\), where \(U\) and \(V\) are local bi-Lipschitz homeomorphisms near \(\bar x\) and \(\bar y\). Metric subregularity of \(F\) at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) is equivalent to metric subregularity of \(G\) at \((U(\bar x),V(\bar y))\). Likewise, strong metric regularity of \(F\) at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) is equivalent to strong metric regularity of \(G\) at the transformed point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local bi-Lipschitz representation changes preserve metric subregularity and strong metric regularity as qualitative properties.
assumptions_latex: \(U\) and \(V\) are local bi-Lipschitz homeomorphisms near the reference points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ has metric subregularity or strong metric regularity}\iff G\text{ has the corresponding property at the transformed point}.

children.title: Scaling-Distortion Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Scaling regimes that distort residual or regularity comparisons.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{\operatorname{reg}G_{a,b}(a\bar x\mid b\bar y):a,b>0\}=(0,+\infty)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(a,b>0\), set \(G_{a,b}(u):=bF(u/a)\). Its exact modulus is
\[
\operatorname{reg}G_{a,b}(a\bar x\mid b\bar y)=\frac{a}{b}\kappa,
\qquad \kappa:=\operatorname{reg}F(\bar x\mid\bar y).
\]
Because \(a/b\) may be any positive number, equivalent scaled representations realize every modulus in \((0,+\infty)\) while retaining metric regularity. Thus an absolute modulus has no representation-independent conditioning meaning unless admissible scalings have uniformly bounded distortion or a normalization is imposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without bounded scaling distortion or normalization, equivalent regular formulations can have arbitrarily small or large numerical regularity moduli.

assumptions_latex: \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) is metrically subregular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) with modulus at most \(\kappa\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S:=F^{-1}(\bar y)\) and define the residual \(r(x):=\operatorname{dist}(\bar y,F(x))\), with distance to the empty set interpreted as \(+\infty\). Metric subregularity at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) gives a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) such that
\[
\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\leq\kappa r(x)\qquad(x\in U).
\]
Therefore, any evaluated point \(x\in U\) with \(r(x)\leq\varepsilon\) carries the verifiable local certificate \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\leq\kappa\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local error bound converts a computable feasibility residual into an upper bound on distance to the feasible set.

knowledge_statements.title: Stationarity-Distance Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies the subregularity error bound to a stationarity mapping without assuming attainment of the set distance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a normed space, let \(M:X\rightrightarrows X^*\), and define the stationary set \(S:=M^{-1}(0)\) and residual \(r_M(x):=\operatorname{dist}(0,M(x))\). If \(M\) is metrically subregular at \((\bar x,0)\) with modulus at most \(\kappa\), then there is a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) such that
\[
\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\leq \kappa r_M(x)\qquad(x\in U).
\]
Consequently, for every \(x\in U\), the inequality \(r_M(x)\leq\varepsilon\) certifies \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\leq\kappa\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subregularity of a stationarity mapping converts its residual into a certified local upper bound on distance to the stationary set.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a normed space and \(M:X\rightrightarrows X^*\).
\(M\) is metrically subregular at \((\bar x,0)\) with modulus at most \(\kappa\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(x,M^{-1}(0))\leq\kappa\operatorname{dist}(0,M(x))\) locally near \(\bar x\).

knowledge_statements.title: Perturbed-Solution Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local a posteriori certificate under strong metric regularity, using the localized graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be normed spaces. Strong metric regularity of \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) provides neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(V\) of \(\bar y\), together with a single-valued Lipschitz localization \(s:V\to U\) satisfying
\[
F^{-1}(y)\cap U=\{s(y)\}\qquad(y\in V).
\]
After shrinking the neighborhoods if necessary, a regularity constant \(\kappa\) gives
\[
\|x-s(y)\|\leq\kappa\operatorname{dist}\bigl(y,F(x)\cap V\bigr)
\qquad(x\in U,\ y\in V),
\]
where distance to the empty set is \(+\infty\). Moreover,
\[
\|s(y)-s(y')\|\leq\kappa\|y-y'\|
\qquad(y,y'\in V).
\]
Thus the localized inclusion residual and the data perturbation provide local solution-displacement certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong metric regularity gives a unique nearby perturbed solution and bounds its sensitivity and approximation error using a consistently localized residual.
assumptions_latex: \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) is strongly metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\).
\(s:V\to U\) is the resulting single-valued localization of \(F^{-1}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|x-s(y)\|\leq\kappa\operatorname{dist}(y,F(x)\cap V)\) for nearby \(x\) and \(y\).

notation.meaning: Unique solution in the domain localization satisfying \(y\in F(s(y))\).

knowledge_statements.title: Exact-Penalty Threshold Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient local exact-penalty cutoff obtained from a residual error bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a normed space, let \(r:X\to[0,+\infty]\), and set \(C:=\{x\in X:r(x)=0\}\). Suppose \(\bar x\in C\), the local error bound
\[
\operatorname{dist}(x,C)\leq\kappa r(x)
\]
holds near \(\bar x\), \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) is locally \(L\)-Lipschitz near \(\bar x\), and \(\bar x\) is a local minimizer of \(f\) over \(C\). Then every \(\rho>L\kappa\) is a sufficient local exact-penalty parameter: \(\bar x\) locally minimizes
\[
x\longmapsto f(x)+\rho r(x).
\]
Thus \(L\kappa\) is a sufficient lower cutoff for selecting the penalty parameter; it is not asserted to be necessary or minimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An error-bound modulus times the objective’s Lipschitz constant is a sufficient lower cutoff: every strictly larger penalty parameter gives local exactness.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a normed space, \(r:X\to[0,+\infty]\), and \(C:=\{x\in X:r(x)=0\}\).
\(\bar x\in C\) and \(\operatorname{dist}(x,C)\leq\kappa r(x)\) locally near \(\bar x\).
\(f:X\to\mathbb R\) is locally \(L\)-Lipschitz near \(\bar x\), and \(\bar x\) locally minimizes \(f\) over \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho>L\kappa\Longrightarrow \bar x\) locally minimizes \(x\mapsto f(x)+\rho r(x)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sharpness Below the Universal Penalty Cutoff
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar example showing that no universally sufficient threshold below \(L\kappa\) follows from the seed assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix \(L>0\) and \(\kappa>0\). On \(X=\mathbb R\), let \(C=\{0\}\), \(r(x)=|x|/\kappa\), and \(f(x)=-L|x|\). Then \(\operatorname{dist}(x,C)=\kappa r(x)\), \(f\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz, and \(0\) minimizes \(f\) over \(C\). For every \(\rho<L\kappa\),
\[
f(x)+\rho r(x)=\left(\frac{\rho}{\kappa}-L\right)|x|,
\]
so \(0\) is not a local minimizer of the penalized objective. Thus the universal sufficient cutoff cannot be lowered below \(L\kappa\) using only the stated Lipschitz and error-bound constants.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scalar example shows that every penalty below the Lipschitz-constant–error-bound product can fail.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\) is not a local minimizer of \(f+\rho r\).

notation.meaning: Universal cutoff furnished by the available Lipschitz and error-bound constants.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
There exist a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and a constant \(C>0\) such that, for every \(x_0\in U\), the Newton iterates
\[
x_{k+1}:=x_k-DF(x_k)^{-1}F(x_k)
\]
are well defined, remain in \(U\), and converge to \(\bar x\). They satisfy
\[
\|x_{k+1}-\bar x\|\leq C\|x_k-\bar x\|^2.
\]
Nonsingularity of \(DF(\bar x)\) supplies local inverse stability, while local Lipschitz continuity of the Jacobian yields the quadratic rate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth equation with a nonsingular, locally Lipschitz Jacobian admits well-defined nearby Newton iterates converging quadratically to the solution.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional equivalence connecting smooth Newton nonsingularity with strong metric regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\) be continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\). Then \(DF(\bar x)\) is nonsingular if and only if \(F^{-1}\) has a single-valued locally Lipschitz localization at \((F(\bar x),\bar x)\); equivalently, \(F\) is strongly metrically regular at \((\bar x,F(\bar x))\).

Then Newton's iteration is well defined from every sufficiently close initial point and satisfies \[\|x_{k+1}-\bar x\|\le C\|x_k-\bar x\|^{1+\alpha}.\] The case \(\alpha=1\) is the quadratic result in the accepted seed.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every sufficiently close \(x_0\) and every choice \(V_k\in\partial F(x_k)\), the iteration
\[
x_{k+1}:=x_k-V_k^{-1}F(x_k)
\]
is well defined and converges to \(\bar x\). Semismoothness and uniform inverse boundedness imply
\[
\|x_{k+1}-\bar x\|=o(\|x_k-\bar x\|),
\]
so convergence is superlinear. If \(F\) is strongly semismooth, meaning its linearization remainder is \(O(\|h\|^2)\), then for some \(C>0\),
\[
\|x_{k+1}-\bar x\|\leq C\|x_k-\bar x\|^2,
\]
and convergence is quadratic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform nonsingularity of generalized Jacobians makes semismooth Newton locally superlinear; a quadratic remainder strengthens the rate to quadratic.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Q-linear counterpart of the accepted vanishing-residual superlinear theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(F\) is strongly metrically subregular at \(\bar x\) for \(0\) with constant \(\kappa\), the iterates remain in its error-bound neighborhood, and eventually \[\operatorname{dist}(0,F(x_{k+1}))\le\varepsilon\|x_{k+1}-x_k\|,\qquad \|x_{k+1}-x_k\|\le M\|x_k-\bar x\|.\] If \(q:=\kappa M\varepsilon<1\), then \[\|x_{k+1}-\bar x\|\le q\|x_k-\bar x\|,\] so the iterates converge Q-linearly to \(\bar x\) with factor at most \(q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed relative Newton residual gives Q-linear convergence when its product with the subregularity and step constants is below one.
assumptions_latex: \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) is strongly metrically subregular at \(\bar x\) for \(0\) with constant \(\kappa\).
The iterates remain in the strong-subregularity neighborhood.
The relative residual and step bounds hold with constants \(\varepsilon\ge0\) and \(M>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|x_{k+1}-\bar x\|\le(\kappa M\varepsilon)\|x_k-\bar x\|\) eventually.
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Accuracy Linear Newton Rate

assumptions_latex: The local error bound \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\leq\kappa r(x)\) holds for some \(\kappa>0\).
The iterates remain in the error-bound neighborhood and satisfy \(r(x_{k+1})\leq a_k\operatorname{dist}(x_k,S)\), where \(a_k\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(x_{k+1},S)\leq\kappa a_k\operatorname{dist}(x_k,S)\) for every sufficiently large \(k\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The local residual error bound and the one-step residual estimate yield \[\operatorname{dist}(x_{k+1},S)\leq\kappa a_k\operatorname{dist}(x_k,S)\] for every sufficiently large \(k\). If \(a_k\leq a\) eventually and \(\kappa a<1\), the solution distances converge Q-linearly. If \(a_k\to0\), their nonzero successive ratios converge to zero, giving Q-superlinear convergence of the distances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local residual error bound transfers one-step residual improvement into linear or superlinear convergence of distance to the solution set.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order-p extension of the accepted residual-transfer principle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=F^{-1}(0)\), and suppose \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le\kappa\operatorname{dist}(0,F(x))\) locally. If, for some \(p>1\) and \(c>0\), the iterates remain local and satisfy \[\operatorname{dist}(0,F(x_{k+1}))\le c\operatorname{dist}(x_k,S)^p,\] then \[\operatorname{dist}(x_{k+1},S)\le\kappa c\operatorname{dist}(x_k,S)^p.\] Thus the solution-set distances have Q-order at least \(p\) whenever they converge to zero and are eventually nonzero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local error bound transfers a residual estimate of order p directly into solution-distance convergence of order p.
assumptions_latex: \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\), \(S=F^{-1}(0)\neq\varnothing\), and the local error bound holds with constant \(\kappa\).
The iterates remain in the error-bound neighborhood.

children.title: Newton-Rate Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Regimes where strong subregularity alone does not secure the expected rate.

assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) is defined by \(F(x)=x^2\), with reference solution \(\bar x=0\).
Newton's method is initialized at \(x_0\neq0\) sufficiently near \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{k+1}=x_k/2\), the convergence is Q-linear with factor \(1/2\), and strong metric subregularity fails at \((0,0)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar loss of superlinear Newton convergence at a multiple root.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the scalar equation \(F(x)=x^2\), Newton's iteration satisfies \[x_{k+1}=\frac{x_k}{2}\] whenever \(x_k\neq0\). Hence it converges to \(0\) Q-linearly with exact factor \(1/2\), rather than Q-superlinearly. At the same reference point, no constants \(\kappa>0\) and \(\delta>0\) satisfy \[|x|\leq\kappa|x|^2\qquad\text{for every }|x|<\delta,\] so strong metric subregularity fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At the multiple root of x squared, Newton's method halves the error and strong metric subregularity fails, providing a boundary for the superlinear-rate mechanism.
knowledge_statements.title: Newton-Rate Failure Boundaries

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong Subregularity Alone Does Not Imply an Iteration Rate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical boundary showing that a residual error bound must be coupled with an iteration-specific improvement estimate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be \(F(x)=x\) and \(\bar x=0\). Then \(F\) is strongly metrically subregular at \((0,0)\) with modulus \(1\). Nevertheless, the convergent sequence \(x_k=1/(k+1)\) satisfies \[\frac{|x_{k+1}|}{|x_k|}=\frac{k+1}{k+2}\longrightarrow1.\] Thus strong subregularity alone implies neither Q-linear convergence with a factor below one nor Q-superlinear convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The identity mapping is strongly subregular, but a sequence can approach its zero sublinearly; regularity alone supplies no algorithmic rate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is strongly subregular, while \(|x_{k+1}|/|x_k|\to1\).

notation.meaning: Sequence lacking a Newton residual-improvement condition.

knowledge_statements.title: Strong Subregularity Alone Does Not Imply an Iteration Rate

children.title: Descent-to-Distance Rate Transfer
children.top_down_role: Conversion of residual or objective progress into solution-distance convergence.

assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) has local minimum value \(f_*\) on a nonempty solution set \(S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(x_k,S)\leq CA^\theta(q^\theta)^k\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conversion of geometric objective descent through a Hölder growth error bound.

source_refs.locator: 5.4 Subextremality and Suboptimality at Linear Rate p. 109
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Whenever \(x_k\) lies in the neighborhood where the growth error bound holds, \[\operatorname{dist}(x_k,S)\leq C(f(x_k)-f_*)^\theta\leq CA^\theta q^{\theta k}.\] Therefore geometric decay of the objective gap transfers to R-linear decay of solution distance with factor \(q^\theta\). More generally, any bound \(f(x_k)-f_*\leq\eta_k\) transfers as \(\operatorname{dist}(x_k,S)\leq C\eta_k^\theta\); thus the exponent \(\theta\) determines the rate conversion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Hölder growth error bound converts objective-gap decay into solution-distance decay, raising the objective rate to the growth exponent.
knowledge_statements.title: Descent-to-Distance Rate Transfer

children.title: Proximal Rate Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Local rate consequences for proximal solver families.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is differentiable with locally Lipschitz gradient, \(g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, and \(S=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:0\in\nabla f(x)+\partial g(x)\}\neq\varnothing\).

For \(\gamma>0\), define \(R_\gamma(x)=\gamma^{-1}(x-\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma g}(x-\gamma\nabla f(x)))\), and suppose \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\leq\kappa\|R_\gamma(x)\|\) locally for some \(\kappa>0\).
The iterates remain local and satisfy \(\|R_\gamma(x_{k+1})\|\leq a\operatorname{dist}(x_k,S)\) for some \(a\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(x_{k+1},S)\leq\kappa a\operatorname{dist}(x_k,S)\) for every sufficiently large \(k\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-valued proximal-gradient residual interface for local distance rates.

source_refs.locator: 2.5.3 The proximal Newton method p. 97
source_refs.source_title: Modern Nonconvex Nondifferentiable Optimization

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the stated local error bound and residual estimate, \[\operatorname{dist}(x_{k+1},S)\leq\kappa a\operatorname{dist}(x_k,S)\] for every sufficiently large \(k\). Thus \(\kappa a<1\) gives local Q-linear convergence of the solution distances. If the constant \(a\) is replaced by factors \(a_k\to0\), the solution distances converge Q-superlinearly along nonzero successive ratios.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local error bound for a single-valued proximal-gradient residual converts next-residual control into linear or superlinear solution-distance convergence.
knowledge_statements.title: Proximal Rate Interfaces

source_witnesses.locator: 2.5.3 The proximal Newton method p. 97

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-point and stationarity interpretations of the residual used by the accepted proximal rate interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(g\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, let \(f\) be differentiable, and let \(\gamma>0\). For
\[
R_\gamma(x):=\gamma^{-1}\bigl(x-\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma g}(x-\gamma\nabla f(x))\bigr),
\]
one has
\[
R_\gamma(x)=0
\iff x=\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma g}(x-\gamma\nabla f(x))
\iff 0\in\nabla f(x)+\partial g(x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zeros of the proximal-gradient residual are exactly fixed points of the forward–backward map and stationary points of the composite objective.
assumptions_latex: \(g\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: R_\gamma^{-1}(0)=\{x:0\in\nabla f(x)+\partial g(x)\}.
knowledge_statements.title: Proximal-Gradient Residual Zero Set

children.title: Splitting Rate Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Local rate consequences for operator-splitting families.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local distance contraction for an averaged fixed-point splitting operator under a residual error bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(T:X\to X\) be \(\alpha\)-averaged on a Hilbert space, where \(0<\alpha<1\), and let \(S=\operatorname{Fix}T\neq\varnothing\). Suppose \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\leq\kappa\|x-Tx\|\) on a neighborhood \(U\) of \(S\). If \(x_{k+1}=Tx_k\) remains in \(U\), then
\[
\operatorname{dist}(x_{k+1},S)^2\leq\left(1-\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha\kappa^2}\right)\operatorname{dist}(x_k,S)^2.
\]
At every nonfixed point in \(U\), the assumptions imply \((1-\alpha)/(\alpha\kappa^2)\leq1\). Hence the distance contracts Q-linearly with factor \(q=\sqrt{1-(1-\alpha)/(\alpha\kappa^2)}<1\); the endpoint \(q=0\) gives one-step arrival in \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Averagedness and a fixed-point residual error bound give an explicit local linear distance rate for splitting iterations.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Hilbert space and \(T:X\to X\) is \(\alpha\)-averaged, with \(0<\alpha<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(x_{k+1},S)\leq q\operatorname{dist}(x_k,S)\), where \(q=\sqrt{1-(1-\alpha)/(\alpha\kappa^2)}<1\), with \(q=0\) interpreted as one-step arrival.
knowledge_statements.title: Averaged-Splitting Linear Rate

assumptions_latex: \(T:X\to X\) is a local fixed-point operator with \(S=\operatorname{Fix}T\) and residual \(R=I-T\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(x_{k+1},S)\leq\kappa a\operatorname{dist}(x_k,S)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-point residual interface shared by local splitting analyses.

source_refs.locator: 7.4.1 Problem Formulation and Splitting p. 400
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any splitting scheme represented locally by \(x_{k+1}=T(x_k)\), the fixed-point residual error bound gives \[\operatorname{dist}(x_{k+1},S)\leq\kappa\|R(x_{k+1})\|\leq\kappa a\operatorname{dist}(x_k,S).\] Thus \(\kappa a<1\) implies local Q-linear convergence of distance to \(S\). The interface is operator-independent: the particular splitting method enters only through its operator \(T\) and the estimate on its next residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Representing a splitting method as a fixed-point iteration lets a residual error bound convert next-residual control into local linear convergence.
knowledge_statements.title: Splitting Rate Interfaces

children.title: Shared Regularity Mechanisms
children.top_down_role: Subregularity, growth, or tame geometry shared across both solver families.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a normed space, \(S\subset X\) is nonempty and closed, and \(r:X\to[0,+\infty]\) vanishes exactly on \(S\) locally.
The local error bound \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\leq\kappa r(x)\) holds for some \(\kappa>0\).
The iterates remain local and satisfy \(r(x_{k+1})\leq\phi_k(\operatorname{dist}(x_k,S))\), where \(\phi_k:[0,+\infty)\to[0,+\infty]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(x_{k+1},S)\leq\kappa\phi_k(\operatorname{dist}(x_k,S))\) for every sufficiently large \(k\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Common error-bound mechanism behind proximal and splitting rate transfers.

source_refs.locator: 4.1.2 Neighborhood Characterizations of Metric Regularity and Lipschitzian Behavior p. 382
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The error bound and the method-specific next-residual estimate give \[\operatorname{dist}(x_{k+1},S)\leq\kappa\phi_k(\operatorname{dist}(x_k,S))\] for every sufficiently large \(k\). A bound \(\phi_k(t)\leq at\) along the iterates with \(\kappa a<1\) gives Q-linear convergence in distance. If \[\frac{\phi_k(\operatorname{dist}(x_k,S))}{\operatorname{dist}(x_k,S)}\longrightarrow0\] along indices with \(\operatorname{dist}(x_k,S)>0\), the distance convergence is Q-superlinear.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Proximal and splitting rate results share a residual error-bound mechanism; linear or superlinear rates follow from the corresponding one-step residual majorant.
knowledge_statements.title: Shared Regularity Mechanisms

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1.2 Neighborhood Characterizations of Metric Regularity and Lipschitzian Behavior p. 382
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hölder-error-bound extension of the accepted shared residual mechanism.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose locally that
\[
\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le\kappa r(x)^\theta,
\qquad \kappa>0,\quad0<\theta\le1,
\]
and that local iterates satisfy
\[
r(x_{k+1})\le a\operatorname{dist}(x_k,S)^p
\]
for some \(a>0\) and \(p>0\). Then
\[
\operatorname{dist}(x_{k+1},S)\le\kappa a^\theta\operatorname{dist}(x_k,S)^{p\theta}.
\]
Consequently, \(p\theta=1\) with \(\kappa a^\theta<1\) gives Q-linear distance convergence, while \(p\theta>1\) gives Q-order at least \(p\theta\) along nonzero errors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Hölder residual error bound multiplies the one-step residual order by its Hölder exponent when transferring progress to solution distance.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is closed and the iterates remain where the Hölder error bound holds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{dist}(x_{k+1},S)\le\kappa a^\theta\operatorname{dist}(x_k,S)^{p\theta}.

notation.meaning: Hölder exponent of the residual error bound.
Order of the one-step residual majorant.

knowledge_statements.title: Hölder Residual Rate Transfer

children.title: Rate-Transfer Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Settings where regularity information does not transfer to local solver rates.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of linear rate transfer when an exact residual error bound holds but the iteration lacks uniform relative progress.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S=\{0\}\), \(r(x)=|x|\), and
\[
x_{k+1}=x_k-x_k^3,\qquad 0<|x_0|<1.
\]
The exact error bound \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)=r(x)\) holds globally. The iterates converge to zero, but
\[
\frac{\operatorname{dist}(x_{k+1},S)}{\operatorname{dist}(x_k,S)}=1-x_k^2\longrightarrow1.
\]
Thus an error bound alone does not imply Q-linear convergence; a contractive one-step residual or distance estimate is also required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even an exact residual error bound does not imply a linear rate when the iteration makes asymptotically vanishing relative progress.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{dist}(x,S)=r(x),\qquad |x_{k+1}|/|x_k|\to1.

notation.meaning: Residual satisfying the exact distance error bound.

knowledge_statements.title: Regularity Without One-Step Progress

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Flat Natural Residual and Sublinear Fixed-Point Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A natural fixed-point residual that loses a local linear error bound and whose associated iteration is not Q-linear.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(T:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be \(T(x)=x-x^5\), let \(S=\operatorname{Fix}T=\{0\}\) locally, and define the natural displacement residual \(r(x)=|x-T(x)|=|x|^5\). For \(0<|x_0|<1\), the iteration \(x_{k+1}=T(x_k)\) converges to zero, but
\[
\frac{\operatorname{dist}(x_{k+1},S)}{\operatorname{dist}(x_k,S)}=1-|x_k|^4\longrightarrow1.
\]
Moreover,
\[
\frac{r(x)}{\operatorname{dist}(x,S)}=|x|^4\longrightarrow0,
\]
so no local linear residual error bound \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le\kappa r(x)\) holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A flat natural fixed-point residual can be arbitrarily small relative to solution distance while its iteration converges to the fixed point slower than Q-linearly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_k\to0,\qquad \frac{|x_{k+1}|}{|x_k|}\to1,\qquad \frac{r(x)}{\operatorname{dist}(x,S)}\to0\ \text{as }x\to0.
knowledge_statements.title: Flat Natural Residual and Sublinear Fixed-Point Convergence

assumptions_latex: \(T:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) is defined by \(T(x)=x-x^3\), with fixed-point set locally equal to \(S=\{0\}\).
The iteration starts with \(0<|x_0|<1\) and uses \(x_{k+1}=T(x_k)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_k\to0\) but \(|x_{k+1}|/|x_k|\to1\), and no local bound \(|x|\leq\kappa|x-T(x)|\) holds.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of linear transfer when the fixed-point residual lacks an error bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Here \(x-T(x)=x^3\). A local residual error bound would require \(|x|\leq\kappa|x|^3\) for all sufficiently small \(x\), which is impossible. For \(0<|x_k|<1\), \(|x_{k+1}|=|x_k|(1-x_k^2)<|x_k|\), so the iterates converge to \(0\). Nevertheless, \[\frac{|x_{k+1}|}{|x_k|}=1-x_k^2\longrightarrow1,\] excluding Q-linear convergence with any factor strictly below \(1\). Thus residual decay alone does not furnish a linear distance rate when the regularity error bound fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The iteration x minus x cubed converges to zero, but its residual is too flat to control distance, so convergence is not Q-linear.
knowledge_statements.title: Rate-Transfer Failure Boundaries

children.title: Post-Identification Local Rates
children.top_down_role: Rate transitions after stable active-structure identification.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Neutral restricted derivative showing that finite identification alone does not imply fast convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M=\mathbb R\), \(T_M(x)=x-x^3\), and \(0<|x_0|<1\). The manifold is identified from the outset and \(DT_M(0)=1\). The iteration converges to \(0\), but
\[
\frac{|x_{k+1}|}{|x_k|}=1-x_k^2\longrightarrow1,
\]
so it is not Q-linearly convergent with any factor below one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Immediate manifold identification does not imply a linear rate when the restricted derivative is neutral.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: DT_M(0)=1,\qquad x_k\to0,\qquad |x_{k+1}|/|x_k|\to1.
knowledge_statements.title: Identification Without a Linear Rate

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Restricted-Map Rate Theorem After Finite Identification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local fixed-point rates determined by the derivative and remainder of an iteration restricted to an identified manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M\) be a finite-dimensional \(C^1\) manifold, let \(\bar x\in M\), and suppose that for some \(K\), \(x_k\in M\) and \(x_{k+1}=T_M(x_k)\) for all \(k\ge K\), where \(T_M:M\to M\), \(T_M(\bar x)=\bar x\), and \(x_k\to\bar x\). If \(T_M\) is differentiable at \(\bar x\), then in local coordinates
\[
e_{k+1}=Ae_k+o(\|e_k\|),\qquad A=DT_M(\bar x).
\]
If \(\|A\|<1\), the iterates are eventually Q-linearly convergent. If \(\rho(A)<1\), they are R-linearly convergent in any fixed norm. If \(A=0\), convergence is Q-superlinear; if additionally \(\|T_M(x)-\bar x\|\le C\|x-\bar x\|^p\) locally for some \(p>1\), the Q-order is at least \(p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After finite manifold identification, the derivative of the restricted iteration determines linear or superlinear local rates, while a higher-order zero-linear-part remainder gives the corresponding Q-order.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) is a finite-dimensional \(C^1\) manifold and the iterates identify it after a finite index.
The post-identification iteration is represented by a self-map \(T_M:M\to M\) differentiable at the fixed point \(\bar x\).
The order-\(p\) conclusion assumes a zero linear part through the stated higher-order bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \|A\|<1\Rightarrow Q\text{-linear};\quad \rho(A)<1\Rightarrow R\text{-linear};\quad A=0\Rightarrow Q\text{-superlinear}.

notation.meaning: Iteration map restricted to the identified manifold.
Derivative of the restricted map at the limit.
Spectral radius of the restricted derivative.

knowledge_statements.title: Restricted-Map Rate Theorem After Finite Identification

assumptions_latex: \(T\) identifies a \(C^1\) manifold \(M\) after a finite index \(K\): \(x_k\in M\) and \(x_{k+1}=T(x_k)\) for \(k\geq K\).
\(T(\bar x)=\bar x\), \(x_k\to\bar x\), and the restriction \(T|_M\) is differentiable at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(\|D(T|_M)(\bar x)\|<1\), convergence is locally Q-linear; if \(D(T|_M)(\bar x)=0\), it is Q-superlinear.

notation.meaning: derivative of the restricted iteration map

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rate transition for a differentiable iteration restricted to an identified manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A=D(T|_M)(\bar x)\). Differentiability on the identified manifold gives \[x_{k+1}-\bar x=A(x_k-\bar x)+o(\|x_k-\bar x\|)\qquad(k\geq K).\] If \(\|A\|=q<1\), then for every \(\widehat q\in(q,1)\), all sufficiently large iterates satisfy \(\|x_{k+1}-\bar x\|\leq\widehat q\|x_k-ar x\|\), hence convergence is Q-linear. If \(A=0\), then \(\|x_{k+1}-\bar x\|/\|x_k-ar x\|\to0\), hence convergence is Q-superlinear. If additionally the remainder is \(O(\|x-ar x\|^p)\) for \(p>1\), the local order is at least \(p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After finite manifold identification, the derivative of the restricted iteration controls the local rate: contractive derivatives give linear rates and a zero derivative gives superlinear convergence.
knowledge_statements.title: Post-Identification Local Rates

The derivative \(Df(\bar x):\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is not surjective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is not metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\).

notation.meaning: Jacobian derivative at the reference point

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional smooth failure of metric regularity through nonsurjective linearization.

source_refs.locator: 4.2.2 Pointbased Characterizations of Covering and Metric Regularity p. 394

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a continuously differentiable single-valued mapping in finite dimensions, metric regularity at \((\bar x,f(\bar x))\) requires surjectivity of \(Df(\bar x)\). Equivalently, it requires \[\ker Df(\bar x)^*=\{0\}.\] Therefore a derivative range defect, \(\operatorname{range}Df(\bar x)\neq\mathbb R^m\), supplies a nonzero vector \(y^*\) satisfying \(Df(\bar x)^*y^*=0\) and prevents metric regularity. The scalar mapping \(f(x)=x^2\) at \(\bar x=0\) is the elementary instance: \(Df(0)=0\), and no uniform local openness estimate is possible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a smooth finite-dimensional mapping, a nonsurjective Jacobian prevents metric regularity; equivalently, the adjoint Jacobian has a nonzero kernel vector.
knowledge_statements.title: Derivative Range Defects

children.title: Coderivative Kernel Obstructions
children.top_down_role: Dual singularity mechanisms preventing metric regularity.

assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^m\) has locally closed graph around \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\).
\(D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)\) denotes the limiting coderivative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Metric regularity holds exactly when \(0\in D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)\) implies \(y^*=0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Mordukhovich coderivative criterion and its obstruction form.

source_refs.locator: 4.2.2 Pointbased Characterizations of Covering and Metric Regularity p. 394
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The coderivative kernel at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) is \[\ker D^*F(\bar x,\bar y):=\{y^*\in\mathbb R^m:0\in D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)\}.\] For a multifunction with locally closed graph in finite-dimensional spaces, metric regularity around \((\bar x,\bar y)\) is equivalent to \[\ker D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)=\{0\}.\] Consequently, any nonzero \(y^*\) with \(0\in D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)\) is a dual certificate obstructing metric regularity. For a smooth single-valued mapping, this reduces to the adjoint-Jacobian kernel condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Metric regularity holds exactly when the limiting coderivative has no nonzero dual vector mapped to a set containing zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Coderivative Kernel Obstructions

children.title: Loss of Transversality
children.top_down_role: Tangential intersection geometry incompatible with stable feasibility.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No constants \(\kappa,\varepsilon>0\) satisfy \(d(z,A\cap B)\leq\kappa r(z)\) whenever \(\|z\|<\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: Distance from a point to a set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete tangential-intersection obstruction to a local linear feasibility error bound.

source_refs.locator: 1.2.3 Metric Regularity and Covering p. 56

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At \(\bar z=(0,0)\), the sets have the common tangent line \(\mathbb R\times\{0\}\) and opposing nonzero normals. For \(z_t=(t,0)\), one has \(d(z_t,A\cap B)=|t|\), while \(d(z_t,B)=0\) and \(d(z_t,A)=O(t^2)\) as \(t\to0\). Consequently, \(d(z_t,A\cap B)/r(z_t)\to+\infty\), so tangential contact destroys every local linear residual bound at \(\bar z\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A parabola tangent to a line has quadratic feasibility residual but linear distance to their intersection, so no local linear error bound exists.
knowledge_statements.title: Loss of Transversality

children.title: Stable-Branch Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Obstructions to stable local branches even when weaker regularity survives.

children.title: Branching Inverse Maps
children.top_down_role: Multiple nearby inverse branches preventing strong metric regularity.

knowledge_statements.title: Branching Inverse Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar model of inverse branching at a fold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(y>0\), \(F^{-1}(y)=\{-\sqrt{y},\sqrt{y}\}\). Both inverse branches approach \(0\) as \(y\downarrow0\), so no neighborhoods of \(0\) can make the localized inverse single-valued. Moreover, either branch has quotient \(|\sqrt{y}-\bar x|/|y-\bar y|=1/\sqrt{y}\), which is unbounded. Thus the single-valued Lipschitz localization required by strong metric regularity fails at the fold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near the fold of the squaring map, two inverse branches approach the reference solution and neither yields a Lipschitz inverse.
assumptions_latex: The reference graph point is \((\bar x,\bar y)=(0,0)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The mapping \(F\) is not strongly metrically regular at \((0,0)\).

children.title: Nonisolated Solution Sets
children.top_down_role: Solution geometry incompatible with strong subregularity or isolated calmness.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonisolated Solution Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Accumulating solutions obstruct strong metric subregularity at the reference solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Strong metric subregularity at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) would provide \(\kappa,\rho>0\) such that \(d(x,\bar x)\leq\kappa d(\bar y,F(x))\) for every \(x\) with \(d(x,\bar x)<\rho\). Taking \(x=x_k\) gives a strictly positive left-hand side and a zero right-hand side because \(\bar y\in F(x_k)\). Hence every sufficiently small neighborhood violates the defining estimate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If distinct solutions accumulate at the reference solution, the residual vanishes there while distance to the reference remains positive, precluding strong subregularity.
assumptions_latex: \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) is a mapping between metric spaces and \(\bar y\in F(\bar x)\).
There exist distinct \(x_k\in F^{-1}(\bar y)\) with \(x_k\to\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The mapping \(F\) is not strongly metrically subregular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\).

children.title: Multiplier Nonuniqueness
children.top_down_role: Dual branching affecting KKT and primal-dual solution-map stability.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiplier Nonuniqueness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Redundant equalities produce an accumulating continuum of KKT multipliers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The KKT conditions are \(x=0\) and \(\lambda_1+2\lambda_2=0\). Therefore every triple \((x,\lambda_1,\lambda_2)=(0,-2t,t)\), with \(t\in\mathbb R\), is a KKT solution. These distinct primal-dual solutions converge to \((0,0,0)\) as \(t\to0\). The reference KKT solution is consequently nonisolated, contradicting the isolation required by strong metric subregularity and the single-valued localization required by strong metric regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Redundant equality constraints create a continuum of nearby multipliers for one primal point, preventing isolated or single-valued primal-dual stability.
assumptions_latex: Consider minimizing the zero objective subject to \(x=0\) and \(2x=0\) in \(\mathbb R\).
Let \((\lambda_1,\lambda_2)\in\mathbb R^2\) denote the equality multipliers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The primal-dual KKT mapping cannot be strongly metrically subregular, and hence cannot be strongly metrically regular, at \((0,0,0)\).

children.title: Noncompact Escape Obstruction Family
children.top_down_role: Noncompact directions that prevent global residual control.

children.title: Escape Directions
children.top_down_role: Directions along which residual control deteriorates away from localized regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Escape Directions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An escaping sequence defeats global residual control despite a unique zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x_k=k\), one has \(d(x_k,S)=k\to+\infty\), whereas \(|F(x_k)|=k/(1+k^2)\to0\). Hence \(d(x_k,S)/|F(x_k)|=1+k^2\to+\infty\). This escaping sequence rules out every uniform global error-bound constant, although the equation has the unique solution \(0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Points can escape to infinity while their residuals approach zero, making any uniform global distance-to-solution estimate impossible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No finite \(\kappa\) satisfies \(d(x,S)\leq\kappa|F(x)|\) for all \(x\in\mathbb R\).

notation.meaning: Zero set of the residual mapping

children.title: Unbounded-Level-Set Obstructions
children.top_down_role: Unbounded level geometry preventing global error-bound control.

knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded-Level-Set Obstructions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual sublevels extending arbitrarily far from the solution set obstruct global error bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If a global error bound held with constant \(\kappa<+\infty\), then every point satisfying \(r(x)\leq\alpha\) would satisfy \(d(x,S)\leq\kappa\alpha\). Thus the entire residual sublevel set \(\{x:r(x)\leq\alpha\}\) would lie in the closed \(\kappa\alpha\)-neighborhood of \(S\). A sequence in that sublevel whose distance from \(S\) diverges contradicts this necessary containment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded residual sublevel cannot contain points arbitrarily far from the solution set if a global linear error bound holds.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is a nonempty closed subset of a metric space \(X\), and \(r:X\to[0,+\infty]\) vanishes on \(S\).
For some \(\alpha<+\infty\), there are \(x_k\) with \(r(x_k)\leq\alpha\) and \(d(x_k,S)\to+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is no finite \(\kappa\) such that \(d(x,S)\leq\kappa r(x)\) for every \(x\in X\).

children.title: Coercivity-Loss Regimes
children.top_down_role: Loss of confinement associated with noncompact solution behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Coercivity-Loss Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of linear growth at infinity destroys a global objective-gap error bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x_k=k\), the objective gaps satisfy \(f(x_k)-f^*=k^2/(1+k^2)<1\), while \(d(x_k,S)=k\to+\infty\). Consequently, \((f(x_k)-f^*)/d(x_k,S)=k/(1+k^2)\to0\). The objective therefore lacks the uniform linear growth, or weak-sharpness modulus, required to control global distance to its minimizer set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded objective gap along points escaping from the minimizer defeats every global linear growth estimate.
assumptions_latex: Its minimum is \(f^*=0\), attained exactly on \(S=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is no \(c>0\) such that \(f(x)-f^*\geq c\,d(x,S)\) for every \(x\in\mathbb R\).

children.title: Global Residual-Control Failure
children.top_down_role: Breakdown of global residual estimates caused by noncompact geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Global Residual-Control Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential characterization of failure of a finite global linear error-bound modulus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite global residual-control modulus exists exactly when \(\sup_{x\notin S}d(x,S)/r(x)<+\infty\), with the convention that a positive numerator divided by zero is \(+\infty\). Accordingly, global residual control fails exactly when this supremum is infinite; equivalently, for every \(k\in\mathbb N\) there is \(x_k\notin S\) satisfying \(d(x_k,S)>k\,r(x_k)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Global residual control fails precisely when distance-to-residual ratios are unbounded, as witnessed by a sequence of increasingly severe violations.
assumptions_latex: \(S\neq\varnothing\) is the zero set of a residual \(r:X\to[0,+\infty]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The global residual estimate \(d(x,S)\leq\kappa r(x)\) fails for every finite \(\kappa\).

children.title: Degenerating Regularity Moduli
children.top_down_role: Loss of uniform conditioning along solution or parameter sequences.

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerating Regularity Moduli
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar family exhibiting pointwise regularity with diverging conditioning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(p>0\), the inverse is \(F_p^{-1}(y)=y/p\), whose exact Lipschitz modulus is \(1/p\). Hence \(F_p\) is strongly metrically regular at \((0,0)\) for each fixed parameter. Along any sequence \(p_k\downarrow0\), however, the moduli \(1/p_k\to+\infty\). Thus pointwise regularity does not supply a uniform neighborhood estimate over the parameter family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linear maps with slopes approaching zero remain individually regular, but their inverse Lipschitz moduli diverge, eliminating uniform conditioning.
assumptions_latex: Each mapping is considered at the graph point \((0,0)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every \(F_p\) is strongly metrically regular at \((0,0)\), but no regularity modulus is uniform as \(p\downarrow0\).

children.title: Representation-Dependent Residual Failure
children.top_down_role: Residual scaling or formulation that obscures true solution distance.

assumptions_latex: Both residuals have exactly the same zero set \(S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The residual \(r\) gives an exact global error bound, whereas \(\widetilde r\) gives no local linear error bound at \(0\).

notation.meaning: Rescaled residual with the same zeros

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonlinear residual rescaling can erase linear distance control without changing solutions.

source_refs.locator: 4.1.2 Neighborhood Characterizations of Metric Regularity and Lipschitzian Behavior p. 382
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The identity \(d(x,S)=r(x)\) gives a global error bound with modulus \(1\). If \(d(x,S)\leq\kappa\widetilde r(x)\) held near \(0\), then every sufficiently small \(x\neq0\) would satisfy \(|x|\leq\kappa x^2\), or \(1\leq\kappa|x|\). This is impossible as \(x\to0\). Thus error-bound validity depends on residual calibration, not merely on its zero set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Squaring an exact distance residual preserves its zeros but destroys every local linear error bound at the solution.
knowledge_statements.title: Representation-Dependent Residual Failure

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1.2 Neighborhood Characterizations of Metric Regularity and Lipschitzian Behavior p. 382
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.scope_note: General same-zero-set rescalings that are sublinear relative to distance near zero destroy local linear error bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\subset X\) be nonempty and closed, let \(r(x)=d(x,S)\), and let \(\phi:[0,+\infty)\to[0,+\infty)\) satisfy \(\phi(0)=0\), \(\phi(t)>0\) for \(t>0\), and \(\phi(t)/t\to0\) as \(t\downarrow0\). Define \(\widetilde r=\phi\circ r\). If points outside \(S\) occur arbitrarily close to \(S\), then \(r\) and \(\widetilde r\) have the same zero set, while no neighborhood of \(S\) admits a finite constant \(\kappa\) with \(d(x,S)\leq\kappa\widetilde r(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any positive rescaling that flattens faster than linearly at zero preserves the solution set of the distance residual but destroys local linear distance control.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is a nonempty closed subset of a metric space \(X\), and \(X\setminus S\) contains points with distance to \(S\) arbitrarily close to zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{x:\widetilde r(x)=0\}=S,\qquad \sup_{0<d(x,S)<\varepsilon}\frac{d(x,S)}{\widetilde r(x)}=+\infty\quad\text{for every }\varepsilon>0.

notation.meaning: Flattened residual with the same zero set

knowledge_statements.title: Superlinear Residual Flattening Boundary

children.title: Infinite-Dimensional Calculus Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Topological and infinite-dimensional obstructions to dual criteria and regularity calculus.

children.title: Unstable Graphical Limits
children.top_down_role: Graph-limit behavior incompatible with stable local regularity analysis.

assumptions_latex: For \(n\in\mathbb N\), let \(F_n:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be \(F_n(x)=x/n\).
Let \(F:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be the graphical limit \(F(x)=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strong metric regularity at \((0,0)\) is not stable under this graphical convergence without uniform modulus control.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graphical convergence alone does not preserve strong metric regularity.

source_refs.locator: 3.2.4 Graphical Regularity of Lipschitzian Mappings p. 327
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The graphs \(\operatorname{gph}F_n=\{(x,x/n):x\in\mathbb R\}\) converge to \(\operatorname{gph}F=\mathbb R\times\{0\}\). Each \(F_n\) is strongly metrically regular at \((0,0)\), with inverse \(F_n^{-1}(y)=ny\). The limit satisfies \(F^{-1}(0)=\mathbb R\), so its inverse admits no single-valued localization at \((0,0)\). The failure accompanies the unbounded inverse moduli \(n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strongly regular linear maps can converge graphically to a constant map whose inverse is nonisolated when their inverse moduli are unbounded.
knowledge_statements.title: Unstable Graphical Limits

children.title: Failure of Sequential Normal Compactness
children.top_down_role: Escaping dual sequences obstructing limiting coderivative calculus.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space and \(C=\{0\}\subset H\).
Let \((e_k)\) be an orthonormal sequence in \(H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The set \(C\) fails sequential normal compactness at \(0\).

source_refs.locator: 1.1.4 Sequential Normal Compactness of Sets p. 27

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(k\), take \(x_k=0\) and \(x_k^*=e_k\in\widehat N_C(0)=H\). Then \(x_k\to0\) and \(x_k^*\rightharpoonup0\), while \(\|x_k^*\|=1\) for all \(k\). Sequential normal compactness would require \(\|x_k^*\|\to0\) whenever normals converge weakly to zero along points converging to the reference point. This normal sequence violates that implication.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At the singleton in an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space, orthonormal normals converge weakly to zero but retain unit norm, violating sequential normal compactness.

children.title: Failure of Calculus Qualifications
children.top_down_role: Loss of exact normal and coderivative transfer rules.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: An infinite-dimensional linear inverse image exhibits strict failure of exact normal transfer when the abnormal-multiplier qualification is absent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=\ell^2\), let \(T:H\to H\) be given by \((Tx)_n=x_n/n\), set \(Y=H\oplus\mathbb R\), and define \(A:H\to Y\) by \(Ax=(Tx,0)\). For \(Q=\{0\}\subset Y\), \(A^{-1}(Q)=\{0\}\), \(N_{A^{-1}(Q)}(0)=H\), and \(A^*N_Q(0)=\operatorname{ran}T\subsetneq H\). Moreover, \((0,1)\in N_Q(0)\cap\ker A^*\) is a nonzero abnormal multiplier.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a compact diagonal embedding into a larger Hilbert space, failure of the abnormal-multiplier qualification makes the formal inverse-image normal formula strictly underestimate the true normal cone.
assumptions_latex: Normal cones are Mordukhovich limiting normal cones.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N_{A^{-1}(Q)}(0)=H\supsetneq A^*N_Q(0)=\operatorname{ran}T,\qquad N_Q(0)\cap\ker A^*\ne\{0\}.

notation.meaning: Compact injective diagonal operator on ell-squared
Linear mapping into the enlarged Hilbert space

knowledge_statements.title: Infinite-Dimensional Inverse-Image Calculus Failure

assumptions_latex: Normal cones are Mordukhovich limiting normal cones in \(\mathbb{R}^2\).
No normal-cone qualification is imposed on the intersection.

notation.meaning: Epigraph and hypograph sets used in the counterexample.
Mordukhovich limiting normal cone to a closed set.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A concrete failure of the exact normal-intersection rule when its qualification is removed.

source_refs.locator: 3.1.1 Calculus of Normal Cones p. 262
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C_1=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2:y\ge x^2\}\) and \(C_2=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2:y\le -x^2\}\). Then \(C_1\cap C_2=\{(0,0)\}\), so \(N_{C_1\cap C_2}(0,0)=\mathbb{R}^2\). Individually, \(N_{C_1}(0,0)=\{(0,-\lambda):\lambda\ge0\}\) and \(N_{C_2}(0,0)=\{(0,\lambda):\lambda\ge0\}\); hence their sum is \(\{0\}\times\mathbb{R}\). The failed qualification is visible from \(N_{C_1}(0,0)\cap[-N_{C_2}(0,0)]\ne\{0\}\). Thus an exact normal-cone intersection formula, and consequently coderivative transfers derived from it, cannot be asserted without an appropriate qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without a normal qualification, the normal cone to an intersection can strictly exceed the sum of the individual normal cones.
knowledge_statements.title: Failure of Calculus Qualifications

children.title: Degenerate or Delayed Identification
children.top_down_role: Failure or instability of finite active-structure discovery.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Degenerate Active Constraint Never Identified by Projected Gradient
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional projected-gradient example with convergence but no finite active-set identification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Minimize \(f(x)=\tfrac12x^2\) over \(C=[0,+\infty)\). The unique solution is \(\bar x=0\), and the constraint is active there with zero multiplier. Projected gradient with \(0<\alpha<1\) and \(x_0>0\) gives \[x_{k+1}=P_C(x_k-\alpha x_k)=(1-\alpha)x_k,\qquad x_k=(1-\alpha)^kx_0>0.\] Thus \(x_k\to0\) geometrically, but no finite iterate belongs to the active structure \(M=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a degenerate active constraint, projected gradient can converge geometrically to the solution while never reaching the active boundary at a finite iteration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_k=(1-\alpha)^kx_0\to0\quad\text{while}\quad x_k\notin\{0\}\ \text{for every finite }k.

notation.meaning: Euclidean projection onto the feasible half-line
active boundary structure at the solution

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Active Constraint Never Identified by Projected Gradient

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite, Delayed, and Failed Structure Identification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algorithm-relative terminology for a prescribed active structure and a specified family of runs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a prescribed active set or manifold containing \(\bar x\), and let \(x_k\to\bar x\). The run identifies \(M\) finitely if its identification time \[\tau_M:=\inf\{K:x_k\in M\text{ for every }k\ge K\}\] is finite. Identification fails when \(\tau_M=+\infty\). For a specified family of problem instances, initializations, or perturbations, identification is delayed when every run under consideration has finite \(\tau_M\) but these times are not uniformly bounded over the family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite identification is eventual permanent membership in a prescribed active structure; failure means no such index exists, while delay means finite but nonuniform discovery times across a specified family.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) is a specified active set or manifold containing \(\bar x\).
Any assertion of delayed identification specifies the family of runs over which identification times are compared.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\tau_M<+\infty\) characterizes finite identification, \(\tau_M=+\infty\) characterizes failure, and unbounded finite \(\tau_M\) characterizes delay over a family.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite, Delayed, and Failed Structure Identification

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Failure of Nondegeneracy Is Not a Converse Identification Test
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical boundary on conclusions drawn from failure of a relative-interior condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: When a finite-identification theorem assumes \(-\nabla g(\bar x)\in\operatorname{ri}\partial h(\bar x)\), failure of this condition removes that theorem's guarantee. It does not by itself imply delayed identification or nonidentification for every algorithm, initialization, or stepsize rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Loss of the usual nondegeneracy condition removes a sufficient finite-identification guarantee but does not universally force identification to fail.
assumptions_latex: A finite-identification theorem uses \(-\nabla g(\bar x)\in\operatorname{ri}\partial h(\bar x)\) as a sufficient hypothesis.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: -\nabla g(\bar x)\notin\operatorname{ri}\partial h(\bar x)\ \text{does not imply universal failure of finite identification}.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[x_k=(1-\alpha)^k x_0>0\quad\text{for every finite }k,\qquad x_k\to0.\]
review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports finite-identification failure under degeneracy.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of finite support identification at a degenerate one-dimensional composite minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(F(x)=\tfrac12(x-1)^2+|x|\), whose unique minimizer is \(\bar x=0\). The nondegeneracy condition is strict complementarity, namely \(-g'(\bar x)\in\operatorname{ri}\partial|\bar x|\); here \(-g'(0)=1\notin(-1,1)\), so it fails. Proximal gradient with step \(\alpha\) gives \(x_{k+1}=S_\alpha((1-\alpha)x_k+\alpha)\). For every \(x_k>0\), this reduces to \(x_{k+1}=(1-\alpha)x_k\). Consequently \(x_k\to0\) but \(x_k\ne0\) for every finite \(k\). Thus the active structure \(\{0\}\) is approached asymptotically but never identified in finite time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a degenerate sparse minimizer, proximal gradient may converge to zero without ever identifying the zero structure in finite time.
knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate or Delayed Identification

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proximal-gradient calculation and finite-identification failure are precise and fit the terminal container, but no inspectable source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Nonunique Active Structures
children.top_down_role: Ambiguous local geometry leading to unstable manifold selection.

assumptions_latex: Active indices of a finite maximum are those attaining its value.

notation.meaning: The maximum function used to exhibit competing active pieces.
Set of indices attaining the maximum at \(z\).

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports active-structure nonuniqueness.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A finite-max model exhibiting incompatible active structures along arbitrarily close approaches.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x,y)=\max\{x,y\}\) and define \(I(x,y)=\{i\in\{1,2\}:f(x,y)=f_i(x,y)\}\), where \(f_1(x,y)=x\) and \(f_2(x,y)=y\). At \(\bar z=(0,0)\), both pieces are active and \(\partial f(\bar z)=\operatorname{conv}\{(1,0),(0,1)\}\). For every \(t>0\), however, \(I(t,0)=\{1\}\) while \(I(0,t)=\{2\}\). Hence arbitrarily near \(\bar z\), distinct approaches select incompatible active pieces. Without an additional uniqueness or nondegeneracy condition, no single locally stable active structure is determined by the limiting point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two sequences approaching the same point can select different active pieces, so the limiting point does not determine a unique stable structure.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonunique Active Structures

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-maximum example correctly exhibits unstable selection of competing active pieces and fits the failure-boundary container, but it has no cited source or locator.

children.title: Non-Tame Descent Pathologies
children.top_down_role: Oscillation, multiple cluster points, or absent rate control outside desingularizable regimes.

assumptions_latex: Let \((a_k)\) be any strictly decreasing positive sequence with \(a_k\to0\).
Only monotonic decrease and boundedness of the iterates are required.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f(z_{k+1})<f(z_k),\qquad \operatorname{cluster}(z_k)=\{(0,1),(0,-1)\},\qquad f(z_k)=a_k^2.\]

notation.meaning: A bounded descent sequence with alternating second coordinate.
Objective recording only the first coordinate.

review_flags: This record isolates insufficiency of descent alone; a sourced algorithm-generated non-tame example remains needed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary example showing that bounded monotone descent alone provides neither iterate convergence nor a universal rate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}\) be \(f(x,y)=x^2\), and let \(z_k=(a_k,(-1)^k)\), where \(a_k\downarrow0\) strictly. Then \((z_k)\) is bounded and \(f(z_{k+1})<f(z_k)\) with \(f(z_k)\to0\), yet its cluster set is exactly \(\{(0,1),(0,-1)\}\), so the iterates do not converge. Moreover, by choosing \((a_k)\) arbitrarily slowly, the objective residual \(f(z_k)=a_k^2\) has no universal decay rate. Therefore bounded monotone descent, without a compatible update condition and desingularizing inequality, does not ensure convergence to one point or quantitative rate control.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bounded monotone descent can oscillate between cluster points and converge arbitrarily slowly when no update geometry or desingularizing inequality controls the path.
knowledge_statements.title: Non-Tame Descent Pathologies

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The arbitrary sequence proves only that monotone objective decrease is insufficient. It is not generated by a descent algorithm, and its objective is the tame semialgebraic function f(x,y)=x^2, so it does not exhibit pathology outside desingularizable regimes as required by the exact terminal container.
